title: ‘I could not save the rest’: Hero nurse remembers Pakistan’s nursery fire
excerpt: Islamabad, Pakistan – Staff nurse Razia Noreen was at a medicine cupboard on the nursery ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Islamabad’s largest public-sector hospital. She was ...
body_text:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Staff nurse Razia Noreen was at a medicine cupboard on the nursery ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Islamabad’s largest public-sector hospital. She was two doors from the babies in her care, preparing the morning’s injections.

As she shut the cupboard door, she saw through the nursery’s glass panel a light too sharp and too red to be anything ordinary. She did not wait to understand what it was.

It was 6:38am on Wednesday, August 26. Elsewhere in the ward, her colleague, Sister Nasreen, was already running out, shouting for help.

At 56 seconds past 6:38am, according to security camera timestamps later logged by a government inquiry committee, Noreen rushed into the nursery.

Eight seconds later, she emerged carrying a baby. She tried to go back in. She could not. By 6:40am, the room was gone, swallowed by smoke so thick that the security cameras could no longer see through it.

Noreen was recalling this eight days later, in a plain office beside the hostel warden’s room at PIMS, dressed in a pale pink shalwar kameez, her dupatta loose over one shoulder.

“There was a proper blast,” she told Al Jazeera. “Everything turned to smoke.”

Fifteen newborns had been in that nursery. Fourteen died. The baby Noreen carried out was the only one who lived.

On Thursday, Noreen was given an award by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif for her courage. But for the nurse, the trauma of that Wednesday morning was still raw.

Barely two hours after meeting the prime minister, she sat down and talked, at length, about what happened inside.

Noreen had been on duty since 8pm the previous night, working a routine dawn medication round with Sister Nasreen, with less than two hours left before the end of her shift.

When she saw the light through the nursery glass, she says she did not stop to work out what it was.

“I just told my sister nurse, save the babies,” she told Al Jazeera. “I went in. I didn’t think about what would happen next.”

Noreen said the fire was coming out of the side of the air-conditioning unit facing her.

“The AC was right in front of me, and the fire was coming out of its side,” she said. “We don’t know what was happening behind it. That’s just what I saw.”

The government’s interim inquiry, submitted on August 28, states that the precise cause of the fire “is not yet conclusively established”, with evidence pointing variously to the air conditioner, an incubator or an electrical short circuit.

Inside the nursery, Noreen reached the nearest baby. There was no time to choose between 15. She carried the infant out and handed her to Dr Abdul Rehman, a doctor who had been inserting a feeding tube in the next room and emerged into the corridor moments after her. Then she turned back.

“I thought I’d get five, six, seven, eight more of them out,” she said. “But the fire was moving faster than I was.”

A second doctor, Dr Rimsha, who had been doing rounds nearby and saw the same light Noreen had, followed her in.

The two of them, and later Sister Nasreen, tried to crawl back through the smoke below the worst of the heat. A sudden loss of power plunged the room into darkness. They could not get through.

Noreen’s phone, left behind on the medication table when she ran in, sat inside the burned ward overnight. Hospital guards found it and returned it to her the next afternoon. Its case is still scorched and cracked.

Noreen, Dr Rimsha and Sister Nasreen instead moved to where a separate rescue team was lowering babies from an adjoining gynaecology ward. They stood there catching newborns and running them to the neonatal intensive care unit until the smoke became too thick to remain.

The government’s inquiry later found that the available evidence “does not support generalised allegations that front-line medical and nursing staff simply abandoned the newborns”.

Ask Noreen what a nurse is to a newborn separated from its mother, and she has one answer: its first mother.

“A mother who gives birth endures a pain no one else can stand in for,” she said. “But once a baby is in our hands, no one else is watching over it the way we are, checking their oxygen, their feeding, whether they’re breathing right, every two hours, whatever else is happening around us. That is why we are their first mother.”

Noreen, 38, has spent 21 years in government nursing, the last 17 of them at PIMS. She trained in Karachi right after school, at the age of 17, before a transfer brought her to PIMS in 2009. She has never married.

“Thank God, I am very happy with the children,” she said, when asked about it directly.

Born in Punjab’s city of Sahiwal, she was one of seven children. Her father, Victor John, was a pastor; he died when she was in the eighth grade. Two of her sisters have died; a third, also a nurse, lives in Lahore.

Her mother, 83, a retired government school teacher who is hard of hearing, lives in Lahore with one of Noreen’s brothers.

Noreen herself has lived in the PIMS staff hostel, across from the ward where she works, for most of the past two decades.

With her own phone trapped inside the burning ward, Noreen could not call her family herself.

Noreen’s niece happened to be staying with her that week. It was the niece the warden found, and who got word to the family in Lahore: Noreen was safe.

On the morning of the fire, Noreen and Sister Nasreen were the only two nurses on duty in a nursery holding 15 babies, backed by two doctors, one of them two rooms away. She says it was not an unusual night.

“Sometimes there are 20 babies, sometimes 25,” she said. “It’s always the two of us.”

Doctors on her ward work 36-hour shifts, she said, arriving at 8am and going off duty at 2pm the following day.

Handover between nursing shifts, checking each baby’s medication, feeding and vital signs, takes roughly 45 minutes given the numbers involved. The cost of drugs can also run to tens of thousands of Pakistani rupees per injection, all provided by PIMS to its patients.

“Sometimes we get a break, sometimes we don’t,” she said. “When the workload is heavy, even the water we carry with us goes back home untouched.”

No fire drill had been run in the nursery before August 26, not even after an earlier fire at a nearby PIMS hostel in July.

Asked what is required after an incident like this, she does not hesitate.

“We should all have proper drills. If a fire starts, everyone needs to already know what to do.”

She lists what should follow: extinguishers within reach, cross-ventilation to clear smoke, and a rehearsed evacuation route for babies who cannot walk or call out for help.

Until the fire, almost nobody outside her own ward knew her name, Noreen says.

“I have almost no presence in the main hospital,” she said. “Nobody there knows who I am. I work in the nursery, in my own department. I never imagined that saving one baby would take me this far.”

She travelled on Thursday to meet the prime minister in a car the government sent.

During the meeting, Sharif called her “the nation’s daughter” and said her act would be remembered “in golden letters” in Pakistan’s history.

He confirmed Noreen will formally receive the country’s Sitara-i-Khidmat (Star of Service) award at a ceremony on March 23, and handed her a cheque for 10 million Pakistani rupees ($36,000).

She used the meeting to say what she had already told her own colleagues privately.

“My fellow nurses work with just as much dedication,” she said. “This was a very heartbreaking incident.”

Eight days on, Noreen is unwell. She has had a fever of 102 to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (38.9C to 39.4C) on and off, and a cough she says came from smoke she breathed in from the fire that morning — a morning she will never forget. She takes an antibiotic and sleeping tablets at night. Neither has worked as it should.

“I haven’t slept, not since that day,” she said. “I take the tablets, I drink the cough syrup, but sleep doesn’t come. I close my eyes, and I open them again.”

Asked whether the same dawn shift keeps replaying in her mind, she did not need the question finished.

“The whole incident. The same babies. The mothers’ screams, and the babies’ screams, how they must have screamed. Those are the things that don’t let me sleep.”

She was signed off on medical rest only the day before this interview. Colleagues have been steadying her since.

“I would just start crying, sitting there,” she said. “They supported me like I was a child.”

“It comes back to the same thing,” she said. “When I’m in the hostel, when I’m alone, it all comes back.”

The baby Noreen carried out — she hasn’t been named yet, according to the nurse — remains in the neonatal intensive care unit a week on.

Born preterm at just over a kilogramme (2 pounds, 3 ounces), the baby was already unwell before the fire. She remains critical.

Noreen met the baby’s parents for the first time the day before the meeting with the prime minister.

“She [the baby’s mother Asifa] hugged me and thanked me, and cried, and I cried with her,” Noreen said, “because for the rest of the children, my heart is still exactly where it was.”

She has told the mother the same thing she tells herself.

“I said, look, your child survived such a huge storm, she will survive what comes next, too. You pray, and I will pray.”

Asked what she would tell other nurses, Noreen urged them to work with honesty and without conditions.

“When you work somewhere with honesty, the reward comes eventually,” she said. “It came to me after 21 years. Work with the same loyalty. That is our real strength.”

Then, unprompted, she returned to the 14 babies who died.

“I do regret it,” she said. “I could not save the rest of the children. That, I regret.”

title: UN approves new map showing Africa’s true size
excerpt:
UN approves new map showing Africa’s true size

The UN General Assembly has backed a resolution to change to maps that more accurately show the true size of Africa. Supporters of the resolution say th...
body_text:
UN approves new map showing Africa’s true size

The UN General Assembly has backed a resolution to change to maps that more accurately show the true size of Africa. Supporters of the resolution say the widely used, and centuries-old, Mercator world map distorts the size of countries, thereby changing how they are seen.

title: LSU holds off on adding players with NFL ties as SEC lawsuit looms over program, Lane Kiffin
excerpt:
Will LSU be able to start former NFL players??

BATON ROUGE, La. - The ongoing battle between LSU and the SEC reached a tipping point Thursday when the conference filed a federal lawsuit against the s...
body_text:
Will LSU be able to start former NFL players??

BATON ROUGE, La. - The ongoing battle between LSU and the SEC reached a tipping point Thursday when the conference filed a federal lawsuit against the school over Lane Kiffin’s potential addition of players with NFL ties.

On Thursday, plaintiffs were granted a preliminary injunction by Judge William Jorden of the 19th District Court of Louisiana that allows them to be rostered by different schools for the upcoming season.

Because of this ruling, all eyes were on a Friday deadline in which schools are required to submit their rosters before their official season begins.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

But, lost in the arguments around this deadline was an exemption the SEC enacted this past April that allows a team to add players to their roster if they are currently enrolled in classes as a full-time student.

According to multiple sources, LSU did not add Dae'Quan Wright or Zxavian Harris to its roster on Friday, but have the option to add them at a later time. This could come at any point over the course of the season, but would most likely happen sooner rather than later, if they do at all.

There was also a number of intense conversations had on Friday surrounding this situation, with the SEC hellbent on punishing LSU if they were to have added the players to their official roster.

What began as a lawsuit filed by members of the 2022 recruiting class seeking an additional season of eligibility has now escalated into a legal battle involving five different parties.

The dispute stems from the NCAA’s new "five-for-five" eligibility rule, which stipulates that athletes have five years to play five seasons of college sports.

JUDGE GRANTS INJUNCTION AGAINST NCAA, SEC, ALLOWING ATHLETES WITH NFL TIES ELIGIBLE TO PLAY FOR LSU, OTHERS

LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin talks with SEC commissioner Greg Sankey during SEC Media Day 2026 at the JW Marriott Waterstreet in Tampa, Fla., on July 23, 2026. (University Images via Getty Images)

Some of those athletes granted protection by the court included former Ole Miss football players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who both told OutKick that they were under the impression that the Tigers would be adding them to the roster for the upcoming season.

This followed a highly contentious hearing that involved SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey, who testified that any school in the conference that rostered players with professional ties would be violating newly created rules pertaining to the eligibility of those with NFL experience.

In a shocking turn of events that started just three minutes after Sankey took the stand, the SEC had already filed a federal lawsuit in a North Alabama court against LSU, Lane Kiffin and other school administrators for violating the SEC's first amendment rights to enforce conference rules.

"We established our First Amendment right for freedom of association, so that our conference can make decisions and our members can make decisions about membership," Sankey said under oath when asked about the SEC filing the lawsuit.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

Now, with the conference making its stance clear, which came with SEC Presidents and Chancellors authorizing Sankey to enforce the rules with punishments that include a 50% suspension of the head coach, along with substantial fines to any school that violates the guidelines, it came down to the final hours on Friday.

This decision was not made by Lane Kiffin. Multiple sources told OutKick that school administrators, along with Governor Jeff Landry and President Wade Rousse were discussing the situation with LSU legal counsel throughout Thursday evening and all of Friday.

Head Coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers speaks at SEC Football Kickoff Media Day at Tampa Marriott Water Street in Tampa, Fla., on July 23, 2026. (Getty Images)

As the clock ticked on Friday, officials were still unsure as to what the Tigers football program would do as conversations between all parties involved continued.

Now, with court cases continuing to play out across the country, it will be interesting to see what other schools who were thinking of taking this route are going to do.

If LSU had added Wright and Harris to their roster and then taken them off down the road, attorney Ryan Downton told OutKick that he would have then returned to the same courthouse that was the epicenter of college football on Thursday to file a 'contempt of court' order against the Tigers.

Dae'quan Wright catches a touchdown pass for Ole Miss against Miami during the College Football Playoff semifinal at the Vrbo Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Jan. 8, 2026. Miami defeated Ole Miss 31-27. (Getty Images)

But now, with LSU deciding to not add them to the official list for the Clemson game, everyone can take a deep breath and regroup.

Conversations around this matter will continue, while the SEC still has its lawsuit against LSU sitting in a federal court.

Now, we can focus on the upcoming slate of college football this weekend, while lawyers for all parties involved figure out what to do next.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
excerpt:
The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers

When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital las...
body_text:
The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers

When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.

Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.

Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.

Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".

"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."

The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.

Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.

After the mutiny was put down, state television broadcast images of the arrest of some of the soliders

"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."

The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.

In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.

"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.

"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."

One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.

They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.

Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.

Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.

Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.

"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."

On Wednesday, soldiers appeared at a pro-junta rally in the capital, Niamey

Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.

Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.

"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.

Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.

But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.

Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.

"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.

"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."

Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.

"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.

Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.

All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.

Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.

"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.

"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."

Niger's Gen Abdourahamane Tiani (C), Mali's Gen Assimi Goïta (L) and Burkina Faso's Capt Ibrahim Traoré (R) came together for the first heads of state summit of the AES in 2024

An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".

France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.

"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."

Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.

The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.

"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.

"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."

But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.

This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.

Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.

"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.

"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."

Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

title: ‘Every girl now wants to be a boxer’: excitement in Katie Taylor’s home town for her valedictory bout
excerpt:
Irish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke Park

When Katie Taylor steps into the ring on Saturday night to defend her titles and once...
body_text:
Irish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke Park

When Katie Taylor steps into the ring on Saturday night to defend her titles and once again enthral Ireland, there will be a bittersweet tinge. After a singular career that pioneered women’s boxing, the super-lightweight champion and Olympic gold medallist is bowing out. She is 40 and it is to be her final bout.

“The end of an era, isn’t it?” said Trevor McMahon, her brother-in-law and founder of a gym where she trains. “It’ll be an amazing night but it’ll also be a little bit sad. Everything she did, it might not ever be achieved again.”

There is consolation in the manner of her farewell. Taylor will fight in front of an 80,000-strong roaring, pulsing crowd at Dublin’s Croke Park, the citadel of Irish sport, in a valedictory like no other.

Before tickets went on sale in June, some worried that a boxing match might not fill such a vast stadium. The event out in 17 minutes.

Westlife and other musical acts have joined the bill, adding to the sense of extravaganza. The national broadcaster, RTÉ, will broadcast proceedings free to air, so every home and pub can tune in for Price’s showdown with Flora Pili, an unbeaten French champion.

David Finnegan, 55, who was selling Taylor hats, flags and posters from a stall in her home town of Bray, County Wicklow, this week, said: “Business is tipping away. This is her farewell, everyone wants to be part of it.”

Catherine Hill, 45, had a precious ticket and wanted a Taylor T-shirt for the occasion. “It’s going to be amazing for Katie, the whole country and all women,” she said. “Every young girl now wants to be a boxer or an athlete. It wasn’t like that before.”

Another customer, Denise, 71, bought flags for a pub in Kerry where she planned to watch the bout. “What I love about Katie is that she’s not full of herself. She’s down to earth and still meets up with her friends here. She’s so good with the children.”

Even those with no interest in boxing have been swept up in excitement for an athlete who is adored for blazing a trail in female sports with talent, grit and humility.

Encouraged and trained by her father, Pete, Taylor began sparring as a young girl at a gym so rudimentary it was nicknamed the Tin Can. Women and girls were banned from the ring in Ireland and the UK, so she disguised herself as a boy and signed up to bouts as “K Taylor”.

Father and daughter helped to persuade Irish authorities to lift the ban in 2001, when she was 15, and were instrumental in having women’s boxing added to the Olympic Games. Taylor won gold at London 2012 and went on to headline Madison Square Garden and win an epic trilogy with Amanda Serrano.

McMahon, whose Liberty Boxing gym hosts Taylor during her return visits to Bray, said: “The talent was always there but it was more the dedication. She knew from the get-go what she was going to do. When she comes down to train in the club, the place is packed.”

The last time Croke Park hosted a boxing match was in 1972, when Muhammad Ali fought Alvin Lewis. McMahon said Taylor’s farewell promised to be even more special.

Pili, 29, has won all 12 of her professional fights and holds the IBO world super-lightweight title. She will be no pushover but McMahon said Taylor was determined to add another belt to her titles and go out on a high. “No matter how tough the fight is, Katie always seems to rise to the occasion. If she’s beaten, you’d have to carry her out of there in a box.”

Laney O’Connell, 28, who lives on the estate where Taylor grew up, said she had inspired girls to be fit and active. “When you meet her, she’s completely normal. I don’t think she realises just how big she is,” she said. “And it’s great to see the country represented by a woman instead of a man, especially not McGregor,” she added, referencing the mixed martial artist Conor McGregor.

Anne-Marie McHugh, 58, speaking below a supermarket’s Taylor mural, hoped that Bray’s most famous daughter will enjoy a restful post-boxing life. “It’s time for her to relax,” she said. “She’s earned it.”

title: Blasts at Bolivian military base kill at least 10, injure dozens
excerpt:
Two explosions at a military facility in the Bolivian city of Viacha have killed at least 10 people and injured dozens of others, authorities said.

The blasts occurred on Friday in an area used to st...
body_text:
Two explosions at a military facility in the Bolivian city of Viacha have killed at least 10 people and injured dozens of others, authorities said.

The blasts occurred on Friday in an area used to store pyrotechnic material, about 30km (18 miles) from the administrative capital, La Paz, Bolivia’s Ministry of Defence said.

Viacha health director Rita Nebraska told a local television station that between 10 and 15 people were believed to have been killed and 62 others were injured.

She said 14 of the wounded were transferred to hospitals in La Paz, including a girl with third-degree burns.

Fireworks were stored at the military facility, but the cause of the explosions remains under investigation, police spokesman Roger Roca said. He added that seven people were still missing.

Firefighters warned that a heat source remained at the site, Nebraska said, urging residents to stay at least 150 metres away because of the risk of another explosion.

Police said dozens of nearby homes were damaged and that many civilians were injured by shattered glass.

About 50 civilians and six military personnel injured in the explosions “have been treated … by the different medical centres of Viacha”, Deputy Minister of Defence Ernesto Justiniano Urenda said in a statement.

An investigation is under way to determine the cause of the explosions, how the pyrotechnic material was stored and whether anyone was responsible, he added.

Footage posted on social media showed one of the explosions shattering windows in nearby buildings and sending debris into the air as thick black smoke rose from the facility.

title: Malaysia declares emergency in Sarawak as haze from Indonesia worsens
excerpt:
Malaysia has declared a state of emergency in a district in Sarawak state after haze caused by wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia increased air pollution to “hazardous” levels.

King Sultan Ibrahim “...
body_text:
Malaysia has declared a state of emergency in a district in Sarawak state after haze caused by wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia increased air pollution to “hazardous” levels.

King Sultan Ibrahim “has consented to the declaration of emergency throughout Serian Division, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached air pollution levels hazardous to public health and safety”, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement on Thursday.

The declaration followed a formal request from the Sarawak Disaster Management Committee after the region’s Air Pollutant Index reached levels warranting consideration of a local emergency.

Under the order, 647 schools in Serian will close from Monday until at least the end of next week, alongside government and private offices, plantations, construction sites and quarries, with only essential services continuing to operate.

The state’s disaster management authorities said a three-day cloud-seeding operation launched on Thursday would be extended to at least Monday, citing forecasts of “more conducive cloud formations” during that period.

Sarawak State Disaster Management Committee chairman Douglas Uggah Embas, speaking at a news conference in Kuching, stressed that the emergency applied only to Serian, not the entire state, but urged residents there to take the situation seriously.

“Please minimise outdoor activities and avoid strenuous activities outdoors,” he said.

Sarawak, in the northern part of Borneo island, has been heavily affected by haze for weeks, as have the neighbouring states of Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia.

Other Southeast Asian countries like Brunei have also reported smoggy conditions. Singapore announced it would start providing daily haze advisories from Friday evening, after the 24-hour air quality readings entered the unhealthy range, the first since 2023.

It has also hit the Philippines, where President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered the suspension of classes in the capital region, Metro Manila, as well as more than a dozen provinces on Friday.

This year’s transboundary haze, which originates from fires burning across Indonesia, particularly the Kalimantan region and Sumatra island, is part of a wider seasonal wildfire crisis in the archipelago country.

Scientists say temperatures are expected to peak this month, potentially intensifying the fires by bringing hotter and drier conditions across the region.

title: Did Israel’s destruction of Gaza worsen its water crisis?

Scientists say Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s sewage system may have worsened the Mediterranean’s algae bloom crisis. The bloom has knocked o...
body_text:
Did Israel’s destruction of Gaza worsen its water crisis?

Scientists say Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s sewage system may have worsened the Mediterranean’s algae bloom crisis. The bloom has knocked out five of six Israeli desalination plants, which the arid nation relies on for water.

title: All eyes were on USC to see if the Trojans could bounce back from nightmare tiny crowd at season opener

Jayden Maiava found Trent Mosley for a 68-yard TD to extend the USC Trojans' lead over the Fresno State Bulldogs.

body_text:
Jayden Maiava found Trent Mosley for a 68-yard TD to extend the USC Trojans' lead over the Fresno State Bulldogs.

One of the big stories of Week 0 was the USC Trojans.

It’s not like they lost or anything; they beat San Jose State, 42-26. It was the turnout at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum that was getting a lot of attention.

And by that, I mean the measly crowd at kickoff was getting roasted all over social media.

USC FOOTBALL RIPPED FOR PATHETIC CROWD AT HOME OPENER: 'ABSOLUTELY EMBARRASSING'

USC Trojans head coach Lincoln Riley jogs onto the field before his team's game against Fresno State. (Photo by David Dennis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

So all eyes were on L.A. to see whether the Trojans could draw a crowd more befitting of a blue-blood Big Ten program currently ranked No. 14 in the nation.

The Trojans hosted the Fresno State Bulldogs on Friday night, a Pac-12 team that isn't one to overlook.

And sure, no one thought this was going to bring in a sellout crowd the way a big rivalry game would... but you'd think they could draw a little better than this:

LINCOLN RILEY DISMISSES EMPTY SEATS CONTROVERSY AS A 'FALSE NARRATIVE' AFTER LOW-ATTENDANCE USC HOME OPENER

Not as "ouch" as Week 0, but it's still not pretty.

Of course, as that post noted, it is a Friday before a holiday weekend in the traffic hellscape that is Los Angeles... but this is also USC football, and they look like they could have a solid year.

But nope. Still a lot of red stadium seats staring at everyone.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But hold the phone ... this is L.A.: Not only is traffic a nightmare, but it’s also the kind of place where it’s cool to be fashionably late.

You know who shows up for kickoff and is on time for stuff?

USC QB Jayden Maiava warms up before taking on the Fresno State Bulldogs. (Photo by David Dennis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images))

That's why, by the time the second quarter had rolled around, the stadium had filled out pretty well, considering it was a Week 1 non-conference tilt.

The Trojans' first home game against a Big Ten opponent will be on Sept. 26 when they host the Oregon Ducks.

title: After Pretoria peace deal, old enemies in Ethiopia’s Tigray find new ground
excerpt: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – When Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed the Pretoria Agreement in November 2022, it was meant to end two years of devastating ...
body_text:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – When Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed the Pretoria Agreement in November 2022, it was meant to end two years of devastating war.

The agreement called for a permanent cessation of hostilities, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of Tigrayan forces, political dialogue and the return of displaced people. Article 7 also required the TPLF to refrain from conscription, training, deployment and mobilisation of military forces, as well as preparations for renewed conflict.

Nearly four years later, the large-scale war has ended, but many of the disputes that fuelled it remain unresolved.

More significantly, the period since 2024 has seen the TPLF reposition itself politically and organisationally while retaining military leverage and developing new relationships.

The sequence is striking: TPLF contacts with Eritrean officials, including reported meetings in Dubai and Zalambessa; a renewed struggle over political control in Tigray; reports of recruitment and mobilisation; new clashes involving Tigrayan forces; and the emergence of Tsimdo, a loose convergence of groups opposed to the federal government.

Taken together, the developments raise a question over whether Pretoria became less a completed transition to peace than a period in which the TPLF could regroup and reposition itself while the underlying conflict remained unresolved.

There is no evidence that the TPLF entered the agreement with a predetermined plan to use it as a tactical pause. But the events since 2024 suggest that the movement has retained an organisational and security role that Pretoria was supposed to diminish.

Article 6 established the process for disarming, demobilising and reintegrating TPLF fighters. Tigrayan forces handed over heavy weapons after the agreement, and thousands of former combatants have entered demobilisation programmes.

But the process did not fully dismantle the region’s military structures.

In 2026, reports emerged of renewed recruitment and forced mobilisation in Tigray. If confirmed, such activity would go beyond the incomplete implementation of the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) process and directly challenge Article 7’s ban on conscription and mobilisation.

The distinction between organised mobilisation and the views of Tigray’s civilian population is important.

There is no basis for assuming that Tigrayans as a whole support a return to war. Many are still living with the consequences of the last conflict.

A civilian source in Tigray, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said: “The people of Tigray want peace; we don’t want a second war.”

For those civilians, reports of recruitment carry a simple implication: the possibility of being pulled back into a conflict they believed had ended.

From 2024, the TPLF was increasingly consumed by an internal struggle over its direction after the war. The internal meetings and political manoeuvring formed part of a wider contest over the movement’s future.

The struggle eventually reached Tigray’s political institutions.

Getachew Reda was removed as head of the interim administration in 2025 and replaced by Lieutenant General Tadesse Werede.

Then, in May 2026, the Tigray regional council was reinstated and elected Debretsion Gebremichael as president, strengthening the position of the faction around him.

The developments showed that the TPLF remained a powerful political force in Tigray. Instead of a settled post-war political order emerging, the region was again caught in a struggle over authority while the security question remained unresolved.

By early 2026, political tensions were accompanied by military developments.

Tigray Defence Forces-aligned troops crossed the Tekeze River into the disputed Tselemt district in January and clashed with Ethiopian federal forces. Later, TDF-aligned fighters took control of Alamata and Korem after a federal command post withdrew.

By August, fighting had again broken out in western Tigray near the Sudanese border, in another serious breach of the peace agreement.

The federal government and the TPLF blamed each other for the escalation, while responsibility for initiating the clashes remained disputed.

But the renewed fighting demonstrated that organised armed forces were still capable of mobilising and contesting territory.

The incomplete disarmament has therefore become more consequential as the political disputes left unresolved by Pretoria have begun to coincide with renewed military activity.

The repositioning has extended beyond Tigray.

Eritrea and the TPLF fought a devastating border war from 1998 to 2000. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-22 Tigray war.

Yet the post-Pretoria period has brought reports of closer contacts between Eritrea and elements of the TPLF.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and using it as a proxy. Eritrea rejects that characterisation.

A broader realignment is reflected in the emergence of Tsimdo, a loose convergence of groups opposed to the federal government.

Recent reporting has identified cooperation involving the TPLF, Fano, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and other armed groups. Fano leader Zemene Kassie has confirmed the existence of such a coalition while saying Eritrea is not currently part of it.

The significance of Tsimdo lies not simply in whether its members share the same political programme, but in what they appear willing to put aside to cooperate.

Major disputes remain unresolved: displaced people have yet to return to some contested areas, including Welkait, while territorial claims continue to divide Tigray and Amhara actors.

Yet groups that once fought on opposing sides now appear willing to set aside some of those differences when cooperation can increase pressure on the federal government.

That raises a further question about the TPLF’s post-Pretoria strategy. The organisation appears to be rebuilding its political influence while retaining links to military structures, even as many Tigrayans remain displaced and fear renewed mobilisation.

The emerging convergence points to a potentially widening gap between the strategic calculations of political and armed actors and the immediate interests of civilians still dealing with the consequences of war.

The groups have different histories and political ambitions, and their cooperation may not last. But their willingness to find common ground against Addis Ababa matters.

For the TPLF, Tsimdo offers another arena in which to build political and strategic relationships beyond Tigray.

The war displaced about 1.9 million people. Many remain unable to return, particularly to disputed areas including Welkait, Tsegede, Humera and Raya.

Those territorial disputes remain closely tied to the return of displaced Tigrayans, while the political relationship between Tigray and the federal government remains unsettled.

The federal government has also failed to deliver on important elements of the post-war settlement. But those failures do not erase the TPLF’s commitments under Pretoria.

Article 6 envisaged the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of its fighters. Article 7 banned conscription, mobilisation and preparations for renewed conflict.

The record since 2024 does not prove that Pretoria was deliberately used by the TPLF to buy time.

It does, however, show a movement that has remained politically organised, fought to regain control of Tigray’s institutions, retained links to armed structures and found new potential partners as the settlement stalled.

Pretoria ended the large-scale war. It did not settle the struggle over power, territory and security that lay beneath it.

For Tigrayans, however, the calculations are simpler.

A young man from Tigray, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said: “The fear of being drafted is what’s making many youth lose hope.”

title: At least two dead in blast at Bolivia military barracks
excerpt:
The explosion happened at a barracks in Viacha, about 30km from La Paz

At least two people have been killed after an explosion at a military barracks in Bolivia but authorities fear the toll could be...
body_text:
The explosion happened at a barracks in Viacha, about 30km from La Paz

At least two people have been killed after an explosion at a military barracks in Bolivia but authorities fear the toll could be higher.

Bolivian Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said at least 58 people had been injured when "pyrotechnic material" detonated at the barracks, where an artillery regiment is stationed, about 14:30 (18:30 GMT) on Friday.

Health official Rita Nebraska told local television between 10 and 15 people were believed to have died in the incident in Viacha, about 30km (19 miles) from La Paz, according to Reuters.

Police said dozens of homes had been damaged - largely windows shattered in the blast - and emergency workers are searching the rubble.

Nebraska said there was a risk of further explosion and urged people to stay at least 150m away from the military base.

Police spokesman Roger Roca told AFP news agency that fireworks had been stored at the barracks, and the cause of the blast remained under investigation.

Viacha's authorities have declared three days of mourning.

title: Venus and Serena Williams' highly anticipated US Open return ends in heartbreaking loss
excerpt:
Serena Williams called the anti-doping process 'unprofessional' ahead of her return at Wimbledon. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

For the first time in four years, Venus and Serena William...
body_text:
Serena Williams called the anti-doping process 'unprofessional' ahead of her return at Wimbledon. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

For the first time in four years, Venus and Serena Williams returned to the US Open court together Friday night in Queens.

The legendary sisters were set to reunite earlier this summer at Wimbledon; however, Serena — who, at 44, is in the midst of a comeback after several years away from the sport — was forced to withdraw due to injury.

Friday night, the two walked onto the court at Arthur Ashe Stadium to a massive ovation from the crowd.

GROUP OF INFLUENCERS FORCES PAUSE DURING US OPEN MATCH WITH CRINGEWORTHY PHOTOSHOOT IN SUITE

Serena's jacket listed her US Open titles, including the pair of doubles titles that she and Venus won in 1999 and 2009.

Their opponents were Taiwan’s Chan Hao-ching and Australian Maya Joint, who, at 20 years old, was just a toddler when the Williams sisters won the 2009 US Open.

Venus and Serena Williams walk onto the US Open court to a massive ovation. (Photo by Robert Prange/Getty Images)

The first set was fairly back and forth to start, but Chan and Joint pulled ahead to win it 6-3.

The Williams sisters responded and started the second set strong, but it went the distance, needing a seven-point tie-breaker to decide the winner.

In the tie-breaker, Venus and Serena had multiple opportunities to put Chan and Joint away, but they fought back. Finally, after the scare, the Williamses clinched the set to keep the match going.

While they were respectful throughout the match, there was no question that the overwhelming majority of the crowd was behind the sisters, erupting after every point.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The tennis greats battled back against an impressive pairing that is only in their fourth event together to force a decisive tie-breaker in the final set.

Venus and Serena Williams delivered a thriller against Chan Hao-ching and Maya Joint, but came up short in heartbreaking fashion. (Photo by KENA BETANCUR / AFP))

The Williamses took the first five points in a row to jump out to an early lead; however, Joint and Chan took the next three.

Joint and Chan battled back to take the lead, and in the end, they walked away with the win in the match that was just a shade over three hours.

In the end, it was a fantastic three-set thriller, 6–3, 6–7(6), 7–6(10), that showed the Williams sisters — already all-time greats of the sport — are still a force to be reckoned with.

title: ‘To challenge deadly blockade’: New flotilla mission sets sail for Gaza
excerpt:
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition (FFC) has announced that a new international mission is under way, with vessels stopping at European ports ahead of its attempt to reach Gaza’s shores in October.

The c...
body_text:
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition (FFC) has announced that a new international mission is under way, with vessels stopping at European ports ahead of its attempt to reach Gaza’s shores in October.

The coalition said in a statement that the mission to “challenge Israel’s illegal and deadly blockade of Gaza” would go ahead despite the violence Israeli forces inflicted on flotilla volunteers and activists, such as documented cases of severe beatings, repeated tasering and sexual assault.

It added that “action is needed now more than ever as much of the world has moved on from Gaza” since the announcement of a ceasefire in October 2025.

According to the statement, two vessels have already set out. Handala II sailed around Scandinavia in June and July, stopping in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, while the ship Kate departed Bristol, UK, earlier this month and has since called at ports in Ireland, Germany and France.

Stops in Spain, Portugal and Italy are planned before the flotilla continues towards Gaza, the mission added.

“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, an FFC Steering Committee member.

“At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity,” he added.

Human rights advocates, peace activists, elected representatives, journalists, medical professionals and advocates for Palestinian rights have joined the new flotilla.

The coalition is calling on governments to guarantee safe passage for the flotilla, press Israel to end its obstruction of food, water and medicine into Gaza, declare that any attack or seizure of the vessels will trigger diplomatic consequences and use diplomatic and economic measures to end the blockade.

“We know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks,” said Edward Digilio, an engineer from Maryland taking part in the mission. “But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world.”

The coalition traces its roots to 2010, when Israeli forces killed 10 activists on board the Mavi Marmara during a flotilla attempt, and to the Free Gaza Movement’s first voyages in 2008.

Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla twice within the past year, detaining more than 450 participants in October 2025 — including South African author Zukiswa Wanner and Nelson Mandela’s grandson, Mandla Mandela — and about 175 more in April 2026.

Amnesty International said it documented sleep deprivation, denial of water and medical care, and other ill-treatment of activists held by Israel after intercepting and storming the ships.

Two activists, Thiago Avila and Saif Abukeshek, were held incommunicado for days in April this year and had their detention extended partly on secret evidence before being deported.

The mission joins many other aid groups who have described Gaza’s humanitarian situation as reaching crisis levels despite the ceasefire.

UNICEF estimates that more than 82 percent of families remain water insecure and roughly 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure is destroyed.

Israel has continued to target hospitals, aid warehouses and medical supply sites in Gaza in recent weeks.

Gaza’s Health Ministry has recorded more than 1,300 deaths from Israeli fire since the truce took effect in October, alongside thousands still missing or believed trapped under rubble.

title: Tate brothers charged with further trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
excerpt:
Tristan and Andrew Tate pictured in April 2026 at Kaseya Center, Miami

Romanian prosecutors have charged social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate with further sex crimes.

They are accused of...
body_text:
Tristan and Andrew Tate pictured in April 2026 at Kaseya Center, Miami

Romanian prosecutors have charged social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate with further sex crimes.

They are accused of making more than $1.2m (£888,000) by coercing a girl to do sex acts on video chats, according to the Romanian Directorate for Investigating Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT).

Andrew, 39, is charged with trafficking minors, money laundering and sex with a minor. Tristan, 38, is charged with complicity in trafficking in minors and money laundering.

The Tates - currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges - deny all the allegations.

Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK?

The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.

They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.

Many of the new charges centre on a vulnerable woman investigators allege was recruited by Tristan when she was 15.

She is alleged to have been sheltered in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, for sexual exploitation by Andrew.

DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.

He is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.

Andrew is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.

Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 are confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.

It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US, and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can open.

The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.

Their lawyer Eugen Constantin Vidineac said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial.

"The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

title: Trump downplays war with Iran, in which 18 US service members have been killed so far, as ‘small potatoes’ – live
excerpt:
Thousands of Iranians have been killed and more than 750 US service members have been wounded during the ongoing conflict

Donald Trump minimized the war with Iran while speaking with reporters in the...
body_text:
Thousands of Iranians have been killed and more than 750 US service members have been wounded during the ongoing conflict

Donald Trump minimized the war with Iran while speaking with reporters in the Oval Office on Friday. When asked how he would describe the conflict, if not a war, the president called it “small potatoes”.

“A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” Trump said. “We did Venezuela and we did this. In Venezuela we lost nobody. In this we lost 18 people and in Vietnam we lost 100,000 people and in other conflicts you lost tens of thousands of people.”

When a reporter followed up, saying 18 service members have died and there are record-long deployments, Trump retorted: “Why is it record long? How long were we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam? We’re at five months now.”

The war with Iran started in late February, nearly seven months ago. During the conflict, thousands of Iranians have been killed and more than 750 US service members have been wounded. The war has also brought soaring gas prices and disrupted food supply chains worldwide, as the blockade over the Strait of Hormuz has stifled trade and oil supply.

Despite Trump saying Friday that the Iran war is not a “war”, he himself has repeatedly called it a war. Just on Monday, the president referred to it as “a relatively little war”.

Trump told reporters Friday that “there’s no fighting right now”, despite a sharp escalation in the war this week with US strikes on Iran. He also said “we’re taking out a lot of oil” and “we control the Hormuz Strait”, both of these statements are not accurate. The president added that the US could hit Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, where nuclear facilities are reportedly housed, “very soon”.

Donald Trump’s “Build the Wall” game is getting blowback from the game maker Tetris. The game, which is a near replica to the iconic falling blocks game, has the player build a structure to “protect the border from the coming horde.”

In a post on X, Tetris wrote that: “we take copyright infringement very seriously.”

The company added that it was not involved in the creation of the administration’s game and said, “at Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them”.

The White House launched an “arcade” on Thursday, that houses five 80s-style computer games that includes “Build the Wall”. Other games involve the player flying a bald eagle down the National Mall and acting as border patrol agent along the Rio Grande river.

Adam Telle said Friday that he is “honored” Donald Trump named him as the acting army secretary to replace Daniel Driscoll. He comes to the role, which is the army’s top civilian post, after serving as the assistant secretary of the army for civil works.

“My previous work in the Army focused on moving at Trump Speed to deliver on one of the Army’s original missions,” Telle wrote in a post on X. “I will apply that same relentless focus on efficiency to how the Army mans, trains, equips, and modernizes.”

Driscoll’s departure came after widespread reports of tensions with defense secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll gave no reason for leaving, but reportedly clashed with Hegseth after some of his allies had been ousted by Hegseth.

Telle said Hegseth’s leadership at the department of defense is “historic” and that working closely with the department “we will deliver a more ready and capable Army”.

On Truth Social, Trump called Telle: “A Great Patriot, who is respected by all.”

Donald Trump’s executive order to limit mail-in voting has been blocked again by a federal judge. US District Court Judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking Trump’s mandate and has now replaced that with a stronger preliminary injunction.

“Plaintiff States are required under state law to mail millions of ballots to voters on a prescribed timeframe. As detailed below, they are unable to pivot this late in the election cycle, nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters,” the judge wrote in her ruling.

Her injunction comes after Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters and compel the US Postal Service (USPS) to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. This would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists.

USPS has said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the order isn’t even available. Earlier this week, a USPS whistleblower came forward and warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try and carry out the order.

After Trump signed the order, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general joined together suing USPS to challenge the rule. They also filed a motion for the temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction as litigation was ongoing. Oral argument on the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction was held on Thursday.

“We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” said Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, which co-led the state coalition. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.”

Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday that his real estate background has helped guide his knowledge on data centers. He said that if he were in charge of a city or state, he’d try to get in as many data centers as possible.

“If you want your house to be more valuable and everything else, you’re going to want a data center,” Trump said. “If you want to go through poverty, crime, and squalor, I would say don’t approve data centers, you know, you have your choice.”

The president’s remarks come as a nationwide backlash to data centers is underway, which is likely to be a flashpoint for the midterm elections. Town meetings have filled with constituents angry about massive data centers moving into residential neighborhoods and small towns. They worry about pollution, loud humming noise and strains on the electrical grid and water supply.

The momentum has even caused some notable republicans, like Texas Governor Greg Abbot and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, to regulate data centers.

While speaking with reporters on Friday, Trump said that he’s letting companies build their own power plants so they don’t have to use the grid, which would mean lower energy costs for residents. He didn’t mention, however, that would also mean excess pollution and smog for communities that would have the additional power plants in their backyards.

“There’s a lot of places that want them, both in this country and in particular in China,” Trump said.

The president is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s president, later this month. He told reporters that he’s looking forward to it.

“He’s a great gentleman. We get along great. We have a very good trading relationship and you know they’re a competitor and all of that, but we have a very good relationship with President Xi,” Trump said. “He’s coming with his beautiful wife. She’s a beautiful woman and a great woman, respected all over the world.”
