How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran?

title: Nepal search teams rescue two workers from hydropower tunnel
excerpt:
Search teams have rescued two men from a hydropower tunnel buried by debris during the flash flood that devastated Nepal nine days ago.

The two workers were pulled alive from the main tunnel at the c...
body_text:
Search teams have rescued two men from a hydropower tunnel buried by debris during the flash flood that devastated Nepal nine days ago.

The two workers were pulled alive from the main tunnel at the construction site of the Trishuli 3A plant early on Friday. The rescue raises hope of recovering more of the hundreds of people believed to remain trapped in hydropower tunnels.

The cascade, believed to have been triggered by the partial collapse of a glacier, killed more than 1,200 people and devastated entire communities, as water, rock and mud raced down Himalayan valleys.

A video released by Nepal’s Ministry of Energy showed cheering as a man emerged through a small muddy opening. He was helped to his feet by rescuers and carried on the backs of emergency workers, raising his hand as they took him towards a helicopter.

A second man covered in mud pressed his hands together in prayer as he was carried away on a stretcher.

The rescued men were identified as Sanjay Shah, 30, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor, by the minister of home affairs of Nepal, Sudan Gurung.

“I am so happy, my heart is lighter,” Maharjan’s brother Amir told the AFP news agency.

The Nepali Army said the two men were receiving medical treatment and would be taken to a hospital in Kathmandu, while “search and rescue operations are ongoing.”

The pair are the first to be rescued from hydropower stations or construction projects in Nepal. At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A project. About 115 are believed to have been trapped in the main tunnel.

An army spokesperson reported that one of the survivors had told rescuers more people remain alive inside the tunnel.

Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued. “We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” he wrote on social media.

Rescuers have been desperately seeking survivors after the disaster on August 26 left more than 5,000 people missing in Nepal and Chinese-controlled Tibet.

Nepal has largely refused international help. However, Australia sent a team of drone specialists to the country on Friday.

The 15-member team, predominantly consisting of state emergency operatives, is joining the rescue operations on the request of Nepal’s government, authorities said. Thirty-six Australian citizens remain missing.

“We are still holding out hope that people might still be surviving in some sort of locations and hopefully this team can help locate any of those people,” Jeremy Fewtrell, the commissioner of Fire and Rescue New South Wales, told reporters at Sydney Airport.

At least 1,287 people have been confirmed to have been killed in the disaster in Nepal, and tens of thousands displaced. China has said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side.

title: Blue state school district accused of defying Supreme Court, hiding gender transitions from parents
excerpt: Thomas More Society attorney Christopher Ferrara says parents have a constitutional right to direct their children’s upbringing, while Moms for Liberty warns similar policies are spreading across New ...
body_text:
Thomas More Society attorney Christopher Ferrara says parents have a constitutional right to direct their children’s upbringing, while Moms for Liberty warns similar policies are spreading across New Jersey and the country.

A New Jersey school district is being sued over a policy allowing students to change their name and gender identity at school without notifying their parents.

Under the School District of the Chathams' policy, students are able to change their name in official school records, use the bathrooms and locker rooms that align with their gender identity, and the school guidance counselor decides "whether, and to what extent" parents are involved in the decision.

The school's policy flies in the face of the Supreme Court's ruling in Mirabelli v. Bonta in March, which granted an injunction against California over state policies that keep students' gender identities confidential from parents while the issue works its way through the lower courts, according to Christopher Ferrara, senior counsel for the Thomas More Society, who filed the lawsuit.

"Well, the court has made clear in the Mirabelli case, and the Third Circuit has a decision along the same lines, that parents have standing to challenge a policy like this, which would hide a gender transition from the parents, whether or not the child is actually transitioning," Ferrara told Fox News Digital. "And the Supreme Court indicated that the reason parents have standing is that the parents are the objects of this policy."

People supporting the right to opt their children out of classes containing LGBTQ-related content demonstrate outside the U.S. Supreme Court as the court hears oral arguments in the Mahmoud v. Taylor case in Washington, D.C., on April 22, 2025. Parents challenged a Maryland public school district after it ended opt-outs for classroom discussions involving LGBTQ-related books. (Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images)

"The policy provides that this information will be hidden from them, so they have the right to object to it, whether or not their particular child or children is at that moment being transitioned. And there's always a risk, of course, that the child under peer pressure, or the influence of teachers, or social media will go along with this ridiculous trend and decide that his gender is not the biological one that parents believe is God-given and immutable, but some other gender."

Ferrara noted that the policy could have major consequences for students who aren't seeking to transition their gender because they could be forced to share locker rooms and bathrooms with members of the opposite sex.

Moms for Liberty CEO and founder Tina Descovich, whose organization is one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, also alleged that students who refuse to use other students' preferred pronouns could face disciplinary action under the school's code of conduct.

"They have a policy in the school district that will actually punish children that don't use the demanded new gender identity pronoun and name of another student," Descovich told Fox News Digital. "They can do that just one time on accident and they can be punished up to suspension just for using the wrong pronoun or the wrong name of someone that is identifying as something other than they actually are."

Fox News Digital reached out to School District of the Chathams for comment.

Along with Moms for America, two anonymous parents of elementary school-aged daughters are plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which was filed Aug. 24. The plaintiffs accuse the school of violating the parents' and students' First Amendment rights to free speech and religious liberty, as well as the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment. The school district is also accused of violating parental rights that were affirmed in the Supreme Court's ruling in Mahmoud v. Taylor, which determined that parents can opt their children out of LGBT-centered lessons.

WASHINGTON MOTHER PULLS CHILDREN FROM SCHOOL AFTER PRIDE LESSON SHOWN IN MUSIC CLASS WITHOUT NOTICE

Moms for Liberty co-founder Tina Descovich speaks during the 2024 Joyful Warriors National Summit on Aug. 30, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"The Supreme Court has ruled twice on these issues," Descovich said. "We know that parents have to have a right to opt out of things that violate their religious beliefs."

The lawsuit follows a June 15, 2026, school board meeting in which Ann Ciccarelli, president of the Chatham School District Board of Education, said the district was not legally bound by the Mirabelli decision and instead was required to follow the New Jersey Department of Education's 2018 guidance on transgender students.

DAD OF THIRD-GRADE GIRL IN MASSACHUSETTS ALLEGEDLY BARGED IN ON BY TRANS STUDENT IN BATHROOM CALLS FOR ACTION

Parents from the Montgomery County Public Schools district speak out about parental rights issues impacting their school district outside the U.S. Supreme Court on April 22, 2025. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

But New Jersey Attorney General Matthew Platkin acknowledged that Policy 5756 is not mandatory, according to NJ Spotlight News.

"The guidance violates both Maribel and it violates Mahmood and so you know there's a lot of crossover and confusion here but what it comes down to is the school board the school has a duty and responsibility to protect constitutional rights of the citizens in its community of its employees of its students of its families and it is not doing that," Descovich said.

Ferrara told Fox News Digital that since parents began speaking out against the policy, they have been subjected to threats and intimidation. He said that one family has had a police security outside their homes.

"This is what happens when you oppose these policies," Ferrara told Fox News Digital. "You basically are going to be subjected to a vicious public backlash by ideologues who are totally intolerant of basically the normal point of view on this issue."

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: I'm Gen Z: If the GOP wants my vote, stop the speeches and fix the housing crisis
excerpt: Political commentators Brilyn Hollyhand and Brecca Stoll join 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze Gen Z voter priorities regarding the economy and inflation ahead of midterm elections. Hollyhand and Stol...
body_text:
Political commentators Brilyn Hollyhand and Brecca Stoll join 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze Gen Z voter priorities regarding the economy and inflation ahead of midterm elections. Hollyhand and Stoll also discuss a Resume.org survey indicating 54 percent of Gen Z applicants ghost employers following a job offer.

I’m going to Dallas next week to attend the 2026 Republican Midterm Convention. I'm not going for the merch and not for the parties. I’m going because Republicans are about to get two nights of primetime television, the first midterm political convention in American history, and if we waste that stage just talking to ourselves, we will deserve a Blue Wave on Election Day, November 3.

Let me say the quiet part at full volume: We are running against a Democratic Party that has stopped pretending. Democratic socialists are winning primaries, and their platform is not "more Medicaid." It is a new constitution, public ownership of the economy, and the end of the United States Senate.

President Trump has called members of the DSA communists, and he wasn’t being cute. If we lose Congress to that coalition, it will not be because America secretly wanted commissars. It will be because we could not look a 20-year-old like me in the eye and tell him why our side will let him buy a house, keep a paycheck, and speak without getting hurt.

REPUBLICAN PARTY TO HOST HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION IN DALLAS, TRUMP ANNOUNCES ON TRUTH SOCIAL

Gen Z is not a lost cause. Young men already moved toward the GOP in 2024. Housing is their number-one issue, and the cost of living is the country’s number-one issue. They do not care about our process stories. They care whether this country still works for people who were not born holding a down payment.

Here is what I want to hear from the stage at the American Airlines Center next week – highlight the wins that are real, and stop burying them under slogans.

So here is what I want to hear from that stage at American Airlines Center: Highlight the wins that are real, and stop burying them under slogans.

The border is not a vibe. Illegal crossings collapsed, catch-and-release is dead, and net migration went negative for the first time in half a century. Fentanyl deaths dropped more than 20 percent in a year. That is not "tough talk." That is fewer dead classmates.

REPUBLICANS CAN WIN THE MIDTERMS IF THEY JUST STOP UNDERSELLING SUCCESS

The Working Families Tax Cuts made the 2017 rates permanent, with no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security, Trump Accounts for kids, and a bigger Child Tax Credit. That is money that stays with a bartender, a welder or a nurse working a double. Do not assume young voters already know, because their algorithm has been feeding them the opposite story.

School choice is expanding, hostages came home, and factories are being announced again. And when we remember Charlie Kirk, who was killed on a campus last September for doing the one thing Gen Z actually respects—showing up and arguing in public—it should not be a 90-second tribute and a cut to commercial. His death is the argument. If a 31-year-old can be shot for debating college kids, free speech is not a branding exercise. It is a survival issue.

WHO WANTS THEIR CHILD TO BE A MILLIONAIRE? TRUMP HAS GIVEN YOU THAT CHANCE

Then make promises that sound like they were written by someone who has paid rent in this decade.

Promise a housing offensive that treats supply like a national emergency: Smash the zoning cartel, speed permits, and stop turning every starter home into a museum piece for people who already own one. Promise a first-time-buyer track that is not another 400-page bill named after a senator. Promise the next Congress will ban members from trading individual stocks. Young people think the game is rigged, and they are not crazy.

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH

Promise trade schools and apprenticeships with the same intensity we give tax rates. A generation drowning in degrees and debt does not need another lecture that college is the dream.

They need a path that does not require a $90,000 ticket to learn a job America actually needs. Promise energy abundance like you mean it, not as a culture-war prop but as a cost-of-living policy. Electricity, gas, groceries, and rent move together. If we cannot explain that chain on national television, we will lose affordability to people who will nationalize the grocery store and call it compassion.

Promise campuses will not be permission slips for political violence, that boys are not a problem to be managed, and that we will stop importing labor to undercut the kid who stayed and showed up for work.

That is the speech, not "our values" and not "the swamp": specific, measurable, and aimed at the cohort that can still flip.

Democrats want this convention to look like a circus, and that is fine, because circuses draw a crowd. The question is what the crowd hears when the lights hit. Vice President JD Vance opens Wednesday, and President Trump closes Thursday. Between those two nights, the country will decide whether Republicans are a governing party with a future or a nostalgia act with better production value.

I am tired of hearing that Gen Z is "too far gone." That is what losers say, so they don’t have to do the work. This generation is transactional, anti-incumbent, and allergic to being lied to. They voted against Trump, then they voted for him, and they will vote against us just as fast if we talk like consultants. Next week is the cleanest shot we will get before November: primetime in Dallas.

If we cannot win that argument, we don’t get to blame the media, the map, or the kids. We get to blame the people who had the microphone and used it to congratulate themselves.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM BRILYN HOLLYHAND

Brilyn Hollyhand is a 20-year-old political commentator and debater, bestselling author of "Make America Talk Again," and host of "The Brilyn Hollyhand Show." You can follow his hot takes on socials @Brilyn Hollyhand or learn more at BrilynHollyhand.com.

title: Gun control activists demanded better data. What they got surprised the heck out of them
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Georgetown professor just taught gun control activists an important lesson: When you criticize studies that don’t su...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Georgetown professor just taught gun control activists an important lesson: When you criticize studies that don’t support anti-gun talking points, be careful what you wish for — you just might get it. In this case, they got an unprecedented amount of new data that obliterates their narrative.

In 2021, Professor William English published the findings of his National Firearms Survey, by far the most comprehensive assessment of gun ownership ever conducted. The data demonstrated that defensive gun uses were commonplace, that ordinary Americans really like the weapons gun control activists hate most and that longstanding stereotypes about the "sort" of Americans who exercise their Second Amendment rights were misplaced.

Gun control activists predictably hated this. They attacked the report’s conclusions and author, blasting the survey over nitpicky concerns. English explained how the alleged problems wouldn’t have significantly impacted the results. Critics categorically dismissed the report anyway.

MAJOR APPEALS COURT DECLARES NEW JERSEY AR-15 BAN UNCONSTITUTIONAL IN LANDMARK SECOND AMENDMENT RULING

So, English humored them. He re-administered the survey, "fixing" its alleged "mistakes."

Bryan Zielinski displays a rifle in his gun store in Post Falls, Idaho. (Hannah Ray Lambert/Fox News Digital)

If gun control activists hated the 2021 conclusions, they will likely lose their minds over the new ones, which English just released online. The improved and redesigned 2026 survey fails to vindicate their criticisms and deals even mightier blows to anti-gun narratives.

Here are four of the most significant findings from the new report:

Anti-gun activists love to target so-called "assault weapons" and "high-capacity magazines" (magazines holding more than 10 rounds). They frame them as "weapons of war" with "no civilian purpose," claiming they’re not "in common use" for lawful purposes and therefore unprotected by the Second Amendment.

VIRGINIA GUN SALES SPIKE AHEAD OF JULY 1 ASSAULT WEAPONS BAN SIGNED BY GOV. SPANBERGER

The 2021 survey tore this argument to shreds, estimating that tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these rifles and magazines for lawful purposes like self-defense, hunting and sport shooting. Critics complained that the questions asked whether respondents had ever owned a magazine holding more than 10 rounds, or an AR-15 or "similarly styled rifle." They argued this language inflated numbers by including former (but not current) owners and semiautomatic rifles that aren’t technically "assault weapons."

The 2026 survey accordingly asked whether respondents currently own an AR-15 or a "similarly styled semiautomatic rifle with a pistol grip" — a feature universally cited in "assault weapon" definitions.

The new data vindicates English. Despite five years of efforts to "get weapons of war off our streets," an estimated 26.4 million American adults now own an AR-15 or its equivalent, up from the 24.6 million Americans estimated by the 2021 survey to have ever owned one.

The same trajectory holds for magazines. In 2021, 48% of gun owners — roughly 39 million Americans — were estimated to have ever owned one capable of holding more than 10 rounds. Five years later, an estimated 44.5 million currently own one, and gun owners are now even slightly more likely to own one (50.5%) than to not own one.

English’s original survey estimated that American adults use firearms to defend themselves, their property or others 1.67 million times annually, excluding military, police and security work.

The new data vindicates English. Despite five years of efforts to "get weapons of war off our streets," an estimated 26.4 million American adults now own an AR-15 or its equivalent, up from the 24.6 million Americans estimated by the 2021 survey to have ever owned one.

Critics called that estimate "implausible," arguing that the broad definition — which included incidents where a gun was mentioned but not displayed — and allegedly "leading" questions meant many reported uses may have been "imagined."

DOJ TARGETS SPANBERGER, NEWSOM GUN LAWS WITH TWIN LAWSUITS AFTER SCOTUS AFFIRMS SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS

Ironically, critics were right that the numbers were off, but wrong about the direction: the 2021 survey may have actually undercounted defensive gun uses.

The new dataset yielded an annual average of 2.2 million defensive gun uses. Part of the increase likely came from asking about protection against animal attacks, which accounted for over 8% of reported uses.

Gun control advocates are losing the public-carry culture war. Seventy percent of gun owners now report at least "some circumstances in which they carry a handgun for self-defense," up from 56% in the original survey.

That doesn’t necessarily reflect public carry, since some may carry only on private property. Still, the new report estimates that 33.6 million Americans are "public carriers" — that is, they have a concealed carry permit and carry for self-defense "at least sometimes." That’s a remarkable 60% increase in five years.

The original survey ran from Feb. 17 to March 23, 2021. Much has changed in the public-carry landscape over the last five years.

Since July 1, 2021, 12 states with over 117 million people have enacted permitless carry laws, making it easier for law-abiding gun owners to arm themselves in public. Montana’s law took effect during the original survey. The Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in "New York State Rifle & Pistol Association" also opened the door for tens of millions of Americans to finally engage in some manner of public carry, even if the 10 states whose public carry laws were implicated still make it incredibly difficult, expensive and time-consuming to get a concealed carry permit.

This increased access to public carry, combined with historically unprecedented violent crime spikes, seems to have facilitated something of a nationwide "come to Jesus" moment about the importance of armed self-defense in public spaces. And it’s fundamentally changing societal perceptions regarding the right to bear arms and not in the direction that gun control activists favor.

Finally, the 2026 survey indicates that more Americans from all walks of life are recognizing the importance of their Second Amendment rights. An even greater proportion of gun owners now hail from demographic groups that historically owned guns at much lower rates. It’s a consequential cultural shift that undermines some of anti-gun activists’ favorite tropes about gun owners.

Importantly, the new report puts to rest conjectures by anti-gun activists that the original survey found surprisingly high rates of female gun ownership only because women reported their husbands’ "household" guns as their own. The 2026 design explicitly told respondents to count only firearms that they personally own and not to include their spouse’s guns. Even with this change, the estimated proportion of gun owners who are female increased by 3.5% compared to 2021. It tuns out that women weren’t confused by the original question, after all.

In the end, gun control advocates might’ve fared better by just quietly licking their wounds when the original survey shredded their narrative. Instead, they doubled down and dared English to run the play again. He called their bluff and ran up the score.

Amy Swearer is a Senior Legal Fellow in the Edwin Meese III Center for the Rule of Law at Advancing American Freedom.

title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Talarico brings a touch of Trotsky to the Texas Senate race
excerpt:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott discusses Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico’s claim that I.C.E. kidnapped a 5-year-old on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico app...
body_text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott discusses Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico’s claim that I.C.E. kidnapped a 5-year-old on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico appears ready to bring a touch of Trotsky to Texas. In a video from a climate forum, Talarico is shown declaring capitalism an "oppressive system" linked with White supremacy and saying that it must be "dismantled" to achieve a better world. It is reminiscent of Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky, who denounced the "fundamental evil of the capitalist system" and called on citizens to free themselves from its oppression. The Democratic Socialists of America and radical sites have long called "to dismantle the capitalist state."

As a state representative, Talarico addressed the 2020 climate conference by the Austin chapter of the Sierra Club with other Texas House candidates. However, it was Talarico who roused the crowd with an attack on capitalism:

"I’m so thankful that you asked this question and also thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country ... And I think only ending the ways that all three of those oppressive systems work together are we gonna be able to begin the process of dismantling them."

TALARICO’S ‘PROUD CAPITALIST’ ABOUT-FACE COLLIDES WITH RESURFACED CALL TO ‘DISMANTLE’ CAPITALISM

Talarico added criticism of Texas’s oil and gas industry, which he mocked as a dying industry "like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s." He predicted with obvious satisfaction, "That industry is not gonna last."

Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally on Sept. 9, 2025, in Round Rock, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Ironically, given his earlier promise of running a meatless, vegan campaign, opposing both beef and energy markets in Texas could well achieve the dismantling of the economy by default in Texas.

WATCH: UNEARTHED VIDEO SHOWS LEFTIST SENATE HOPEFUL CELEBRATING ANTI-FOSSIL FUEL GROUP'S ARRIVAL IN TEXAS

Talarico's views closely parallel socialist and communist talking points online. The Democratic Socialists of America has challenged people to "imagine the end of capitalism." Those words in The Democratic Socialists of America manifesto offer Americans a world without landlords, debt, mandatory work hours, and "food, education, energy, medicine, and transportation … are common goods and utilities."

The DSA is premised on the same stated objective of Talarico, declaring that there has to be "a revolutionary transformation to replace the capitalist social order based on exploitation and oppression."

JONATHAN TURLEY: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS WANT TO REMAKE AMERICA IN THEIR IMAGE. THAT’S TERRIFYING

Other candidates have sought to pander to this radical mob. Recently, California Democrat Gov. Gavin Newsom thrilled the mob by declaring that "nostalgia is not working," adding that "capitalism as we know it doesn’t work either."

In "Rage and the Republic," I discuss the rise of socialism and the coalition of politicians, pundits and professors in attacking capitalism as well as core institutions such as the Supreme Court. It is a crisis of faith on the 250th anniversary of the oldest and most successful republic in history.

SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM

It is the 250th anniversary not only of the Declaration of Independence but of Adam Smith’s "Wealth of Nations." Smith's free-market theories were immediately embraced by the Founders as the perfect economic theory to match their political theory. They had declared the first Enlightenment Revolution based on a belief in natural rights that came from God, not governments.

However, those rights mean little without economic freedom. Capitalism offered citizens the ability to transcend class and social barriers, to advance as far as their skills and labor would take them.

MODERN CAPITALISM IS TURNING 250, TOO. WE NEED TO REMIND AMERICANS WHY IT’S IMPORTANT

Together, those political and economic theories created the most prosperous and stable democratic system in the world. That system is now under attack on both sides. Radicals are calling for the trashing of the U.S. Constitution and the discarding of our core constitutional values.

The DSA is premised on the same stated objective of Talarico, declaring that there has to be "a revolutionary transformation to replace the capitalist social order based on exploitation and oppression."

Even establishment figures from former Vice President Kamala Harris to Newsom now dismiss faith in core institutions as mere "nostalgia." Those of us who support the Madisonian democracy are derisively called "institutionalists" and constitutional "cultists."

JONATHAN TURLEY: DEM SOCIALIST RIPS ‘INSTITUTIONALISTS’ AS FAR LEFT TURNS UP HEAT ON DEFENDERS OF CONSTITUTION

The New York Times ran a column, "The Constitution Is Broken and Should Not Be Reclaimed," by Ryan D. Doerfler of Harvard and Samuel Moyn of Yale, calling upon citizens to "reclaim America from constitutionalism."

As these attacks on our constitutional system mount, a similar attack on capitalism is unfolding. In New York, Mayor Democrat Zohran Mamdani promised to show citizens the "warmth of collectivism" from free childcare to free buses to state-run grocery stores. Across the country, Mamdani allies are joining him in calling for the de-commodification of private property and the seizing of the means of production.

DSA CO-CHAIR MOCKED FOR PROUDLY CONFIRMING SOCIALISTS WANT TO ABOLISH THE SENATE, NATIONAL BORDERS, PRISONS

Polls show that these candidates are being propelled not by the working class, but by young, college-educated voters fresh out of the ideological echo chamber of higher education. They are armchair revolutionaries like Talarico, repeating socialist slogans with the same robotic rote delivery of a Young Pioneer camp.

As these videos surface, radical candidates from Michigan Democrat Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to Talarico brush off their earlier comments as media allies attack any reporting on prior statements. New York Democrat Socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is considering a run for president, recently called her own extremist statements "Woke 1."

SOCIALIST CANDIDATES CAN DELETE OLD POSTS, BUT THEY CAN'T ERASE THEIR RADICALISM

The transparent insincerity does not matter to their base. These figures have already shown their bona fides with extremist statements in the past. Talarico's desire to dismantle capitalism was not some slip of the tongue but a planned speech to fellow activists. To pivot now is considered to be mere packaging for uneducated and malleable dupes.

Indeed, the Talarico campaign responded by simply declaring that Talarico is a "proud capitalist," though one staffer admitted that the comments were a bit "cringey." Being a "proud capitalist" who wants to "dismantle" capitalism is a bit like being an avid meat-eater who denounces meat consumption as killing the world and banning meat from his campaign."

Accordingly, when asked about past radical positions, these figures immediately deny or dismiss them. If you want to dismantle the constitutional or economic systems of the United States, a few white lies hardly seem of much consequence. After all, as Trotsky explained, "The end may justify the means as long as there is something that justifies the end." For these radicals, there is no greater justification than their own election.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JONATHAN TURLEY

Jonathan Turley is a Fox News Media contributor and the Shapiro Professor of Public Interest Law at George Washington University.

He is the author of the new book "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution" (Simon & Schuster, Feb 3, 2026), on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.

He is a nationally recognized legal scholar who has written extensively in areas ranging from constitutional law to legal history to the Supreme Court. He has written over three dozen academic articles that have appeared in a variety of leading law journals.

Professor Turley also served as counsel in some of the most notable cases in the last two decades including the representation of whistleblowers, military personnel, former cabinet members, judges, members of Congress, and a wide range of other clients.

Professor Turley testified more than 50 times before the House and Senate on constitutional and statutory issues, including the Senate confirmation hearings of cabinet members and jurists such as Justice Neil Gorsuch. He also appeared as an expert witness in both the impeachment hearings of President Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.

Professor Turley received his B.A. at the University of Chicago and his J.D. at Northwestern. In 2008, he was given an honorary Doctorate of Law from John Marshall Law School for his contributions to civil liberties and the public interest.

title: ‘Astronomical’ fuel price surge hits farmers in UK and US
excerpt:
Intensification of Middle East conflict and ongoing Russian export ban sees diesel prices rise 10% in less than a week

Farmers are facing an “astronomical” jump in the price of fuel needed to operate...
body_text:
Intensification of Middle East conflict and ongoing Russian export ban sees diesel prices rise 10% in less than a week

Farmers are facing an “astronomical” jump in the price of fuel needed to operate their vehicles and machinery after a surge in diesel costs in the UK and US.

Renewed fighting between the US and Iran has driven up the price of crude oil, while last week Russia extended a ban on diesel exports, further pushing up market prices.

An intensification of Middle East hostilities over the weekend pushed fuel costs even higher for farmers, said Alex Harrison, a fuel buyer at Fram Farmers, a not-for-profit farmer-owned co-operative. The price of all fuels had gone up by “an astronomical amount in just a few days”, she said, rising by between 10p and 14p a litre since Monday.

This represents about a 10% increase in the cost of red diesel – fuel used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate to standard diesel – which currently costs about £1.10 a litre.

The average price of diesel for UK motorists had climbed to 183.5p a litre on Thursday, according to government data, up from 164.5p in mid-July.

The volatility in oil wholesale markets has left farmers struggling to decide how much fuel to buy and when, with many calling for advice from Fram Farmers, which represents more than 1,400 farm businesses across the UK.

While the harvest peak demand for red diesel and other fuels has passed, many growers traditionally buy more fuel at this time of year as they begin to prepare their land for winter.

“This latest spike has really caught everybody by surprise and hit them quite hard because it’s been such a large spike and because of the time of year,” Harrison said. Farmers are “trying to decide what’s best to do, how to order for [managing their] cashflow”.

The co-operative’s members have changed their buying patterns since the outbreak of war in Iran sent oil prices soaring. Harrison said: “A lot of people have ordered in much smaller increments and more often, as they are trying to hedge their bets a little.”

The rise in diesel prices comes amid a squeeze on global refining capacity. Russia, which normally supplies about 10% of the world’s diesel despite western sanctions, has been hit by Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries in August, prompting the export ban extension.

That has been compounded by a wider increase in the price of crude oil. The international benchmark Brent crude was trading at close to $97 a barrel on Thursday, its highest point in about six weeks.

There was a major flare-up in attacks in the Middle East last weekend, the first US strikes since July. Two Saudi supertankers were hit in the strait of Hormuz late on Monday, fuelling concerns of a longer-term return to hostilities.

Tehran warned ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the Iranian strikes.

US diesel prices have climbed to their highest level in about four years. The average price reached $5.78 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motoring organisation, up 54% since the war began. Diesel last traded close to this level in 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Small businesses and larger companies that rely on vehicle fleets, such as delivery firms and construction companies, will also face higher running costs as a result.

Back in the UK, the price of paraffin, or heating oil – widely used on farms to heat buildings including farmhouses and barns – is also higher, at a time of year when many households, mostly in rural communities that are not connected to the gas network, would usually be starting to think about filling their tanks ahead of the winter.

The current price for paraffin is close to £1 a litre, compared with prices of about 60p a litre just before the Iran war.

title: News live: Two more Australians confirmed safe in Nepal-Tibet floods; Bowen calls joint statement on China ‘strong’
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Two more Australians have been confirmed safe in the aftermath of the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods.

The pair, who were previously uncont...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Two more Australians have been confirmed safe in the aftermath of the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods.

The pair, who were previously uncontactable, have been found safe and do not require consular assistance.

It brings the total number of Australians missing in the floods down to 36.

Fifteen people in the Australian disaster assistance response team are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later today, while seven AFP disaster victim identification specialists are to arrive on Saturday morning.

More than 1,200 people have been confirmed dead in the disaster, with more than 5,500 people missing.

‘She’s a hero to all women’: Remembering Gloria Steinem

In case you missed the news overnight, we have an obituary for the late, great Gloria Steinem.

Steinem was a groundbreaking campaigner for women everywhere who brought the feminist perspective to the mainstream. She was 92.

Public trust in politicians drops amid voter cynicism

Four in five Australians believe governments should deliver social services directly but a majority no longer think politicians serve their interests, AAP reports.

A new report from the Centre for Policy Development comes amid a surge in support for One Nation as voters vent anger at the two major parties.

The research found more than 80% of people surveyed want governments to maintain the capability to deliver social services directly and believe health, education and childcare must be universally affordable.

But almost six in 10 people believe their elected representatives do not serve their interests, a figure that has steadily increased.

Almost 70% of people surveyed viewed modern politics as far more concerned with short-term political gains than addressing long-term challenges.

The research also found 65% of people want ordinary citizens to have a much greater say in setting core policy priorities.

Chris Bowen said he would meet members of the Nepali Australian community later today.

The minister said news two other Australians were safe was a welcome development but for other families of the 36 still missing or unaccounted for, the reality is just “gut-wrenching”:

double quotation markEvery person who’s been rescued or found is a relief to their family and to the broader Australian community. But of course, we still have 36 Australians who are missing and unaccounted for, which is just gut-wrenching for all Australians and for the Nepalese Australian community in particular, whom I’m spending time with later today.

But all I can say is that we’re continuing to send any support that the Nepalese government asked for.

Chris Bowen has called a joint statement about China’s missile test “strong” despite it not referring to the nation by name.

One of the biggest talking points of this week’s Pacific Islands Forum been the lack of a regional response to China’s nuclear-capable inter-continental ballistic missile test in July, as AAP reports.

The communique includes a reference to the Fiji-led Ocean of Peace declaration made last year, which states that the region should be free from coercion and militarisation. It doesn’t name China.

Speaking to ABC’s Radio National, the climate change and energy minister said:

double quotation markI think that leaders in the Pacific were deeply concerned: one, that a missile test was done without permission of the countries whose airspace it had travelled through, and two, that there was no notice of the said missile test. So I think it’s both. It is a concern about sovereignty and safety, and one that Australia fully backs. 
  It’s a pretty strong statement, Sally, and one that Australia played a role in crafting.

‘Serious concerns’ for missing Australians, Jim Chalmers says

The Albanese government still has “serious concerns” for the Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, Jim Chalmers says.

Speaking to ABC’s News Breakfast, the treasurer said it was “good news that two Australians have been located overnight:

double quotation markThat would be a huge relief to the loved ones of these two Australians who’ve been located, but we still have very serious concerns for the 36 Australians that we haven’t been able to be located yet.

Chalmers said about 40 of Australia’s “best” personnel were either on the ground or en route to assist in recovery and humanitarian efforts. Unicef warned overnight that at least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water and better sanitation.

Coalition says main focus of tobacco excise cut is tackling organised crime

Anne Ruston, the shadow minister for health and aged care, spoke this morning to tout the Coalition’s plans to slash the tobacco excise by 80%, saying the effort was designed to “break the business model” of organised crime.

Ruston spoke to RN Breakfast this morning, saying that after the government wrested control back of the cigarette market with a lower excise, it could step in to “put in place the things to try and make sure that, first of all, we encourage Australians not to smoke, not to use nicotine products”.

Ruston was asked if cheaper tobacco products would lead to an uptick in smoking rates. She had this to say:

double quotation markThis is very much designed to try and get the government back in control of the nicotine market, not organised crime gangs.

We are hoping that the combined package of what we’re proposing here, not just the dropping of the excise, but the regulation of the market and making it certainly more difficult for children to access these products. In the enforcement surge and the anti-smoking and anti-vaping campaigns, we are hoping to put downward pressure on smoking rates.

She went on to say the purpose of the policy was to shut down the black market and, while the Coalition wanted to see smoking rates decline, “the absolute focus of this is to get this market out of the hands of organised crime”.

Good morning, Nick Visser here to take over the blog and see us through Friday. Let’s get to it.

Two more Australians have been confirmed safe in the aftermath of the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods.

The pair, who were previously uncontactable, have been found safe and do not require consular assistance.

It brings the total number of Australians missing in the floods down to 36.

Fifteen people in the Australian disaster assistance response team are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later today, while seven AFP disaster victim identification specialists are to arrive on Saturday morning.

More than 1,200 people have been confirmed dead in the disaster, with more than 5,500 people missing.

Pauline Hanson to make cost of living ‘worse’, union boss warns

Asked if she saw her role as one of countering One Nation on the cost of living, Melissa Donnelly said Pauline Hanson’s party “says one thing and does another”:

double quotation markThe reality is that Pauline Hanson’s track record is voting against penalty rates, voting against rights for casual and gig workers.

She’s opposed the minimum wage. She’s most recently suggested it should be easier to sack workers.

Our job, as the union movement, is to make sure our members and workers understand that is what she stands for. And if you’re worried about cost of living, Pauline Hanson is going to make it worse.

The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, Melissa Donnelly, has said cost-of-living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role.

Donnelly told ABC’s 7.30 program workers “absolutely deserve” a say on AI in their workplaces but it would not amount to a veto.

She said unions would test the existing laws demanding workers are consulted about significant impacts of new technology before suggesting the laws need to be strengthened for AI:

double quotation markThere are a whole range of workplace issues, and workers’ rights issues, that arise with the advent of AI.

The stronger guardrails, Donnelly said, would include the capacity of workers to have a say on “when it’s used and how it’s used”:

double quotation markThere’s a broader conversation that we should be having as a nation about what AI means and how we regulate it. It’s not a tropical cyclone bearing down on the coast. It is technology. We’ve seen governments step in on issues like social media and set some guardrails.

We have all sorts of commentators from Bill Gates to others saying that we’ve got to have some rules around how this works, we’ve got to have protections, because we need to protect workers into there future. We need to make sure there are meaningful and quality jobs going forward.

Labor says it will shut down a management course amid fears it is being “misused by shonks” and providing a back door into Australia.

As the government faces increased pressure to curb overseas migration, Labor says the graduate diploma of management (learning) which is registered at 452 institutions, showed students either were enrolled but weren’t even starting the course, weren’t completing the course or were transferring out of it.

It’s the first time the government will use powers to shut down courses due to concerns over their integrity – though students now completing the course will be able to finish it.

The assistant minister in charge, Julian Hill, pinned the blame on the Coalition:

double quotation markThe Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks.

Australia continues to welcome genuine international students seeking a premium education and must maintain a ruthless focus on quality, integrity and a great student experience.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.

The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, Melissa Donnelly, has said cost-of-living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role. More coming up.

title: California girls’ sports advocates vow fight after judge tosses trans athlete case: 'Far from over'
excerpt: The 'Outnumbered' panel analyzes the Trump DOJ's legal challenge over biological males on girls' teams. They also evaluate comments from Gov. Gavin Newsom regarding athletic fairness and discuss Title...
body_text:
The 'Outnumbered' panel analyzes the Trump DOJ's legal challenge over biological males on girls' teams. They also evaluate comments from Gov. Gavin Newsom regarding athletic fairness and discuss Title IX implications for biological female athletes.

Advocates for girls' sports vowed to keep fighting after a federal judge dismissed a Department of Justice lawsuit  challenging California policies that allow biological male athletes to compete on girls' school sports teams.

A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital the administration remains committed to enforcing President Donald Trump’s policy barring biological males from girls’ sports despite the setback and is considering an appeal.

"We are disappointed by the Court’s order, and remain committed to enforcing President Trump’s agenda preventing boys from playing in girls’ sports," the spokesperson said. "We are evaluating our options for appeal."

Sophia Lorey, California Family Council outreach director and a former college soccer player who organized "Save Girls' Sports" demonstrations in California, told Fox News Digital that the ruling did not resolve what she called the central Title IX dispute.

A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit challenging California policies allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls’ sports. (AP Photo/Jae C. Hong)

NEWSOM FACES CRITICISM FOR STATE'S STANCE ON TRANS ATHLETES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AFTER SCOTUS RULING

"California should not mistake a courtroom technicality for a victory," she said. "The judge did not rule that allowing males into girls’ sports is fair, lawful, or consistent with Title IX. This case was dismissed on a technical issue without ever deciding the fundamental question at the heart of this fight."

The court avoided the underlying debate over biological fairness entirely. Instead, U.S. District Judge Cynthia Valenzuela grounded her decision in administrative funding rules, finding that the federal government failed to give California explicit prior notice before threatening to pull $44 billion in education funds.

The Justice Department sued the California Department of Education (CADOE) and California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) in July 2025, alleging their transgender athlete policies discriminated against female athletes.

"I hope to see this decision appealed, but regardless, this fight is far from over," Lorey continued. "California lawmakers have the power right now to protect female athletes. A courtroom technicality does not erase biological sex, and it does not make discrimination against girls acceptable. We will not stop until CA girls are protected…California girls are still paying the price, losing medals, opportunities, roster spots, and privacy while state leaders prioritize gender identity over biological reality."

The Justice Department told Fox News Digital it is "evaluating our options for appeal" after the California transgender sports case was dismissed. (Courtesy of Sophia Lorey)

NEWSOM'S OFFICE RESPONDS TO SCOTUS RULING ON WOMEN'S SPORTS AS CALIFORNIA FACES ONGOING TRANS ATHLETE WAVE

Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California superintendent of public instruction who has been involved in filing federal civil rights complaints over transgender athlete policies, also sharply criticized the dismissal.

"Parents in California are no strangers to this fight, or to these underhanded tactics. We stood up to Gavin Newsom and the CIF when they decided girls’ sports and girls’ locker rooms were political fodder," she said. "A Biden-appointed judge just tossed out a case that should have protected female athletes, and she did it after the Supreme Court already ruled that states can keep women’s teams as a safe space for biological females. That is a political choice dressed up as law, and it is the girls who get robbed."

"This fight is not going away, and neither am I," Shaw continued. "I am not backing down because an activist judge in a kangaroo court dismissed a case. This is a hill we are willing to die on. We will keep fighting for fairness, safety, privacy and the future of female athletes. California parents have been told 'no' before, and we refused to quit then. We’re not quitting now. We will keep standing, we will keep fighting, and we will keep protecting our girls."

California superintendent candidate Sonja Shaw and California Family Council’s Sophia Lorey criticized the ruling and vowed to keep fighting the state’s transgender athlete policies. (San Francisco Chronicle via Getty)

SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

The California Interscholastic Federation declined to weigh in on the court’s dismissal when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

"The CIF does not comment on legal matters," CIF Director of Media Rebecca Brutlag said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The California Department of Education also declined to address the substance of the ruling when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday, citing the ongoing legal proceedings.

"The California Department of Education cannot comment on pending litigation," a CDE spokesperson said.

The legal fight intensified after transgender Jurupa Valley High School athlete AB Hernandez won girls’ events at California’s state track championships, prompting federal scrutiny and changes by the CIF intended to preserve qualifying and podium positions for biological female athletes.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

OutKick's Alejandro Avila contributed to this report.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

title: Trump administration asks supreme court to intervene over judge’s ban on USPS mail-in voting restrictions – live
excerpt:
Justice department files emergency request seeking to have court lift Judge Indira Talwani’s order temporarily blocking postal service from implementing plan

As a federal judge is deciding whether to...
body_text:
Justice department files emergency request seeking to have court lift Judge Indira Talwani’s order temporarily blocking postal service from implementing plan

As a federal judge is deciding whether to extend a ban on the USPS’s new mail-in voting restrictions, Donald Trump has asked the US supreme court to step in.

The Justice ‌Department filed an emergency request seeking to have the court lift ​Judge Indira Talwani’s order that temporarily blocks the ⁠postal service from implementing the plan, which includes an online portal that would track millions of mail ballots.

The new system to regulate mail ballots, which came about following an executive order by Trump, has drawn fierce criticism. A whistleblower told Congress that the requirements could result in scores of mail ballots never being sent.

Donald Trump announced an interim replacement for army secretary, Dan Driscoll, who suddenly resigned earlier this week amid reports of tension between him and defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

The president said on Thursday that Adam Telle, who currently serves as the assistant secretary of the army office for civil works, will become the acting army secretary.

“He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all,” Trump said.

Congressman Don Beyer, whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery, described Trump’s arch project as “illegal, gridlock-increasing [and] narcissistic” and criticized the administration for moving ahead with it.

The representative pointed to a report from the the National Park Service – which supports the project – that found it would have adverse effects on multiple landmarks.

“This project is not even close to being ready for prime time. The Administration has not won the legal battle over the proposal, which is plainly illegal without congressional authorization,” Beyer said in a statement.

“The only study they have completed and released, from the National Park Service, confirms my admonition that the arch would be a massive, unnecessary disruption to iconic and historic sites across the region.”

Excavation work on Donald Trump’s “Great Triumphal Arch” project in Washington is set to begin in the coming weeks, interior secretary Doug Burgum said on Thursday.

The 250ft tall gilded structure will be built in between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

“This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World,” Burgum said.

But critics say the arch will interfere with historic sightlines and that it has not received congressional authorization. Three veterans and an architectural historian filed a lawsuit over the project.

“We believe that construction cannot and should not proceed apace, and we are prepared to inform the court that it needs to, at this juncture, needs to step in,” said Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with Public Citizen Litigation Group, who is representing the plaintiffs.

As a federal judge is deciding whether to extend a ban on the USPS’s new mail-in voting restrictions, Donald Trump has asked the US supreme court to step in.

The Justice ‌Department filed an emergency request seeking to have the court lift ​Judge Indira Talwani’s order that temporarily blocks the ⁠postal service from implementing the plan, which includes an online portal that would track millions of mail ballots.

The new system to regulate mail ballots, which came about following an executive order by Trump, has drawn fierce criticism. A whistleblower told Congress that the requirements could result in scores of mail ballots never being sent.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency appears to be downplaying $168 million in winter storm damage across New York City, Long Island, and Mid-Hudson region.

In response to a query about New York Gov Kathy Hochul’s claim that federal authorities denied her request for disaster relief because of “political games,” FEMA said: “No new information was provided by New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island for FEMA to consider; they only repeated their requests for federal reimbursement of costs to plow snow.”

“Winter weather is not new to the Northeast and neither is snow removal,” FEMA also said in its statement to The Guardian. “Federal disaster aid is not a backstop for routine state and local budgeting.”

JD Vance’s comment about the US-Iran conflict that he “wouldn’t call it a war right now” has sparked criticism.

Rep Ro Khanna, referring to this comment, said it was made “as if Americans can’t see what’s going on on their own phones, with their own eyes.”

“It’s unbelievable gaslighting,” the California Democrat also said in a video posted to X.

“This is war. You know who understands it’s a war? Donald Trump. He claims that we’re winning the war.”

Former US pardon attorney Elizabeth Oyer on Thursday sued the department of justice and attorney general Todd Blanche, alleging that they “unlawfully” fired her last year after she said she rejected a recommendation to restore actor Mel Gibson’s gun rights.

The Guardian’s Anna Betts reports that Oyer’s Washington DC federal court complaint maintains that in early 2025 she was asked to “disregard her duties and facilitate a political favor” for the embattled actor because of his “relationship with President Trump”.

Oyer alleges that she was “asked to make it seem like an independent review had concluded that Mr Gibson, who was convicted of a domestic violence offense, should have his gun rights restored”. After Oyer declined, “she was fired by then deputy attorney general Todd Blanche”, her suit alleges.

Read more of Betts’ reporting on Oyer’s lawsuit here.

Moments before Vance’s presser ended, the vice president was asked an unexpected question: Did he and Trump know about Milo Yiannopoulos’s deportation?

“So on Milo, I won’t speak for the president, but I found out, I think, like so many others found out.”

“I found out about it publicly,” he also said of the rightwing provocateur’s deportation. “I’m not sure if the president knew about it beforehand, but I’m sure we can follow up with the president and get you an answer to that question.”

Yiannopoulos recently broke his silence about being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, stating “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”.

During an appearance on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Yiannopoulos said it was a “humiliating and disorientating” experience, as well as “physically degrading” and “frightening”.

Yiannopoulos also said he was “ashamed” of his prior support for Trump and the mass deportation agenda.

“I wouldn’t call it a war right now,” Vance said of the ongoing US-Iran conflict. “There is no active shooting.”

“I recognize there is there have been places where this is flared up [but] major combat operations again, major combat operations lasted for about six weeks and since then, we destroyed, of course, their nuclear facilities…”

JD Vance downplayed the disconnect between widespread opposition to data centers and Trump’s artificial intelligence fervor.

Asked if a Democrat-held Congress would disadvantage US AI development, Vance agreed.

He said there’s a “very good chance” that the US could be bested by China in the AI race if Democrats held Congress.

“On the data center question, you asked how do how do you split the difference, or how do you bridge the gap?” Vance said. “The simple answer is the way that you bridge the gap is by following the president of the United States.”

Vance said a lot of data center opposition – which is increasingly a bipartisan sentiment – stemmed from people worrying their neighborhood would get worse, that their power bills would go up. Vance said that Trump has pushed for ratepayer protection and insisted that data centers must return power back into the grid.

“The way to bridge that gap is for people to do what the president United States has enabled. He’s made it easier to build a nuclear power plant, or any other power plant, next to a data center. He’s made it easier for people to put power back into the grid as opposed to take it out.”

The vice president rebuffed Iran’s claims that US strikes hit a wedding party, saying that country’s state-run media has not been a “very good scribe” about covering the conflict.

“I’m extremely skeptical of this. What I can say with 100% confidence is that unlike [Iran], the United States never targets civilians in combat. We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen,” Vance said in a response to a question about Iran’s claim. “But in this particular case, I don’t think that we have any information one way or the other. We’re investigating because obviously we care.”

“We want to know, and if we do make mistakes – again, this is a big difference between us and Iran – when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them. “So we’re investigating it very quickly.”

Vance also described Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – whose leadership of the military has come under immense scrutiny – as a “very good friend of mine.”

And, Vance said, “I think he’s an amazing secretary of war. And, you know, fundamentally where I look, there are a lot of issues where I agree with Pete on the issue. Where I’m in the most strident agreement with Pete is that we needed to have a culture shift at the Department of War.”

“What Pete came in wanting to do was revive the warrior spirit in the United States of America,” Vance said.

Vance was asked: Why shouldn’t the American people blame Republicans for inflation?

The vice president started to answer by saying things were worse under Joe Biden – and that higher prices during that administration set the stage for “damage” that Donald Trump is trying to reverse.

“When prices get baked in like that, it takes a little bit of time for us to undo some of the damage,” Vance said.

“My point is that because America’s inflation problem wasn’t created in a day, it was created by very bad policies in the Biden administration, trillions of dollars of new spending that was going more to fraudsters than it was to the American people,” he also claimed. “It takes a little bit of time to rebuild the foundation of America’s middle class economy.”

JD Vance claimed during his presser that agreements to develop oil in Venezuela would be used to bolster the US’s strategic petroleum reserve and lower gas prices.

“Now we’re using, of course, the successful Venezuela operation and some of the friendships and some of the relationships that developed in the wake of that operation, to create what is effectively a new 65 billion barrel of oil reserve for the United States of America,” Vance said. “The way that that’s going to work is that private companies, American companies, can go in there, generate a lot of oil revenue.”

“That’s going to mean world oil markets get only more suppl[y], that will lower costs for Americans,” Vance claimed, also saying, “It’s good for Venezuelans, it’s good for anybody who’s buying gas, and it’s good for the American taxpayer as well.”

Vance’s announcement about the oil reserve comes before a round of midterm elections where Democrats have hammered Republicans on increased cost-of-living – including gas prices.

Vice President JD Vance has just started his press conference at the White House.

The Pentagon has stepped back from its recently posted clinical guidelines for its new, mandatory testosterone deficiency testing policy for US armed service members age 30 and above, Reuters reported Thursday.

The Pentagon published a “Clinical ⁠Guidance for Health ​and Human Performance Optimization” Wednesday on its website. But by Thursday, Reuters said, this memorandum and a press statement were taken down.

“The draft (document) published on September 2, 2026, has been temporarily rescinded to allow for updates,” an official told Reuters, saying temporary guidance was still in effect.

The testosterone deficiency testing guidelines set forth different assessment paths for men and women that are supposed to take place during yearly health checks.

This guidance was poised to start right away. The Pentagon has claimed this testing was intended on strengthening military readiness by mitigating potential hormone problems and associated symptoms such as low energy.

Defense secretary Pete Hegseth announced the new testosterone deficiency screening program in July. In a video to X, Hegseth said he wanted to make sure service members had “the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best.”

“As we know, the modern battlefield is brutal and unrelenting,” Hegseth also said. “It requires and demands maximum psychological and mental readiness, and by addressing these health markers early, we’re keeping you on the leading edge of lethality, and giving you the same level of support that you give this nation – the absolute best.”

Those with low testosterone--a condition which has become a frequent topic of conversation in conservative circles--can get treatment for “restoring and optimizing”, Hegseth said. This treatment would be voluntary.

title: Missouri supreme court throws out new congressional maps backed by Trump
excerpt:
Setback for Republicans in redistricting battle as court orders forbids maps from being used in November elections

The Missouri supreme court has unanimously blocked new congressional districts backe...
body_text:
Setback for Republicans in redistricting battle as court orders forbids maps from being used in November elections

The Missouri supreme court has unanimously blocked new congressional districts backed by Donald Trump from being used in the November election and ordered a statewide vote on whether to uphold or reject the new map.

The decision Thursday marks a rare setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle. Republicans had hoped Missouri’s new congressional boundaries could help them win an additional seat and hold onto their slim House majority in the midterms. The ruling still could be appealed to the US supreme court.

Missouri’s new districts were used in the August primaries. But the state supreme court said they cannot be used in the November general election – or ever again, unless voters first uphold the new districts passed by the Republican-led legislature.

The court placed the new districts on hold because citizens submitted petition signatures seeking a referendum.

“The referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, and the secretary incorrectly concluded otherwise,” the court said in its ruling. The legislation containing the new districts “did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters.” As as result, the congressional map adopted after the 2020 census “remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election”.

The Missouri constitution does not specifically say a referendum petition can be used for a congressional redistricting law passed by the legislature. But the supreme court ruled that a constitutional provision allowing a referendum on “any act” of the Legislature encompasses congressional redistricting.

The ruling capped a year of political maneuvering and legal wrangling over the new districts.

After Trump urged Republicans to redraw congressional districts to their advantage, Missouri governor Mike Kehoe called lawmakers into a special session last year to dramatically reconfigure the fifth congressional district, held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver.

Opponents submitted over 300,000 petition signatures in December seeking to put the map to a vote of the people. But Republican secretary of state Denny Hoskins waited until primary election day in August to reject the petition. He asserted that the referendum process cannot be used for congressional redistricting. A lower court agreed , resulting in an appeal to the state’s highest court, which overturned Hoskins’ decision.

Attorneys representing Hoskins and Republican party committees had argued it was too close to the general election to revert to the prior districts without causing confusion and chaos.

Missouri currently has six Republicans and two Democrats in the US House.

Cleaver, who was unopposed in the August primary, has carried the Kansas City-based district with at least 60% of the vote in each of the past two elections.

Republican state senator Rick Brattin won an August primary in the reshaped fifth congressional district, which had been stretched eastward to include rural Republican areas. About 59% of the district’s voters were new under the revised map, according to an Associated Press estimate.

Cleaver had not posted campaign signs in many of the new rural areas, explaining that he was waiting for the Missouri supreme court’s decision. But he had vowed to continue his re-election campaign regardless of the outcome.

Congressional districts typically are redrawn at the start of each decade, based on new census data. But Trump’s quest for a midterm election advantage triggered an unusual mid-decade redistricting battle that spread to more than a dozen states — and triggered a dozen lawsuits in Missouri alone. All told, Republicans had hoped to net as many as 10 additional seats nationally.

The Missouri supreme court ruling was one of only a few nationally to go against Republicans’ redistricting plans.

Prior to its latest ruling, Missouri’s top court already had rejected claims that the special session was illegal, mid-decade redistricting isn’t allowed and the new districts aren’t compact enough .

title: Marijuana users may face hidden driving danger that standard tests can miss
excerpt: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail a new study linking marijuana use to heart disease and discuss data suggesting diet and exercise could help cancer patie...
body_text:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail a new study linking marijuana use to heart disease and discuss data suggesting diet and exercise could help cancer patients.

A new study warns that driving after eating cannabis edibles can significantly impair road performance and reaction times, even if blood tests show THC levels far below the legal limit.

The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, highlight a potential challenge for impaired-driving enforcement in Canada and some U.S. jurisdictions.

Most previous cannabis-driving studies have involved smoked or inhaled marijuana, which more rapidly spikes levels of THC (tetrahydrocannabinol, the main psychoactive compound in cannabis) in the bloodstream.

AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING

Edibles are absorbed more slowly and can produce driving impairment even when blood THC concentrations remain relatively low.

Researchers found that drivers who consumed higher doses of edible THC struggled with lane control, had slower reaction times and experienced greater speed fluctuations. Yet, their blood tests stayed below the standard legal cutoff used to prove impairment at roadside traffic stops.

Researchers measured how well drivers stayed in their lane, how quickly they reacted to road events and how consistently they maintained their speed. (iStock)

To assess how oral cannabis impacts driving, researchers at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto conducted a trial with 40 healthy adult volunteers who regularly use cannabis.

Each participant attended four separate sessions in which they consumed soft-chew gummies containing either 0, 2, 10 or 20 milligrams of THC.

CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS

The researchers then tested the drivers using a driving simulator at two, five and 24 hours after consumption, tracking how well drivers stayed in their lane, how quickly they reacted to road events and how consistently they maintained their speed.

Blood samples and self-reported ratings of intoxication were also collected.

Participants recognized their own limitations, reporting a lower willingness to drive and reduced confidence in their driving skills after taking the gummies. (iStock)

The results showed driving impairment at two and five hours after consuming 10- and 20-milligram gummies. Compared with placebo, participants who consumed those doses had greater variability in lane position, while the 20-milligram dose was also linked to slower reaction times and less consistent speed control.

Participants also recognized their own limitations, reporting a lower willingness to drive and reduced confidence in their driving skills after taking the gummies.

The highest blood THC concentrations averaged 1.6 nanograms per milliliter after the 10-milligram dose and 3.4 nanograms per milliliter after the 20-milligram dose. Those levels were below the commonly used 5-ng/mL threshold, although THC limits vary by jurisdiction and some individual samples exceeded 5 ng/mL.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

By comparison, participants in the team’s previous smoked-cannabis study showed similar levels of impairment while reaching an average peak blood THC concentration of 30.3 nanograms per milliliter, nearly 10 times higher than the 20-milligram edible group.

The study did have some limitations. Tests were conducted on virtual simulators rather than actual roads, meaning drivers faced no real physical risk during the experiments. It also focused on regular cannabis users, so it is unclear how occasional users might react to similar doses.

When the research team previously tested smoked marijuana, drivers with similar impairment levels registered blood THC concentrations averaging 30.3 nanograms per milliliter, nearly 10 times higher. (iStock)

Additionally, minimal residual effects were detected after 24 hours. While maximum speed remained slightly higher among participants on the 10-milligram and 20-milligram doses, subjective feelings of intoxication had completely faded.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In an accompanying commentary, Dr. José Ignacio Nazif-Munoz of the Université de Sherbrooke noted that these biological differences pose a challenge for law enforcement.

Because edibles are absorbed slowly through the digestive system, standard blood tests may fail to identify unsafe drivers, leaving policymakers searching for more reliable roadside tools.

"The delayed absorption and prolonged duration of effects of edible cannabis distinguish it from smoked or inhaled cannabis, complicating the interpretation of biological measures," he wrote.

Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months
excerpt:
Organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the US

A genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidn...
body_text:
Organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the US

A genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure alive for a record nine months and successfully acted as a “bridge” to a human transplant in a world first.

Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list.

Kidney transplantation provides the best survival and quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease, but global demand for human organs far exceeds supply.

Surgeons in the US successfully transplanted a kidney from Wilma, a Yucatan miniature pig, into Andrews, after genetically engineering it to be compatible with his immune system.

The kidney kept Andrews free of dialysis for a record nine months, the longest period ever recorded, before it began failing and he received one from a dead human donor. It was also the first time a pig’s kidney had been used as a temporary “bridge” to a human transplant.

Details of the breakthrough, which offers hope to millions of people whose kidneys have failed, were published in the Lancet medical journal.

Andrews, from New Hampshire, described the pig kidney transplant as a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” He was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog, Cupcake, he said.

Transplanting genetically engineered pig organs has long been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. But the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days when the patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft survival beyond two months, according to the Lancet.
