In response to the US assault on Larak Island late on Sunday, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.

In the interview with Fox News on Monday, Trump said all of the missiles were intercepted by American air defence systems, except one which was allowed to pass through the airspace because it was identified as not on course to hit anything “significant”, according to Yingst.

Scott Bessent, US secretary of the treasury, has said that Tehran is taking Washington’s sanctions seriously, arguing that Iran is resorting to kinetic military responses only because it is losing economically.

Reuters reports Bessent added that the US will maintain its economic pressure on the country, claiming that Iran’s economy does not need to collapse, but rather, he said, the Iranian government needs to come to its senses.

Reuters has a quick snap that US Central Command (Centcom) has denied claims made by Iran state ⁠TV and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that a ship had struck mines in the strait of Hormuz.

In a statement posted to social media, Centcom said “Iran’s claim that a supertanker passing through strait of hormuz struck two mines and was brought to a complete stop is false.”

The denial followed reports in state media earlier today that Iran had said an oil tanker caught fire in the strait after it hit two naval mines.

“A rogue supertanker attempting to pass through the illegal route south of the strait of Hormuz caught fire in massive fires after striking two naval mines and was brought to a complete stop,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in an earlier statement.

Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece on Monday, the largest between the two countries, AP reports.

Israel’s defence ministry said the $3.5bn (€3bn / £2.6bn) export deal, dubbed Achilles Shield, is one of the country’s largest and includes a multilayered air defence system for Greece using Israeli technology.

The Greek defence ministry said in was part of “the greatest reform of its armed forces in its history”, as the Nato member looked to ramp up defence spending.

The deal was signed in Tel Aviv by Israeli defence ministry director general, Maj Gen Amir Baram, and Maj Gen Ioannis Bouras of Greece.

We have a statement from the Iranian presidency detailing what Pezeshkian said during the meeting with Modi on the sidelines of the summit. The statement read:

double quotation markWe continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region.

We believe that the solution to the existing problems is dialogue and cooperation, and all capacities must be used to prevent the spread of insecurity and conflict.

The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is attending a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Kyrgyzstan where he will hold talks with numerous officials and world leaders.

Pezeshkian, seen as a relative moderate in Iran, has already met with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi ‌on the sidelines of the summit and told him that Tehran ⁠still seeks a negotiated solution to ⁠end the war with the US, despite the flare up in hostilities over the last 24 hours.

According to the Tasnim news agency, the Iranian president told Modi that fighting was in ​no one’s ​interest and that ​dialogue and ​cooperation ‌were ​the ​way to resolve existing problems.

But, according to Fars news agency, Pezeshkian said the US has “not fulfilled its commitments”, which he presumably means the US continuing a blockade of Iranian ports and holding on to frozen Iranian assets. He also said “there are currents within America that see their interests in the continuation of war”, without eleaborating.

There are sharp disagreements within Iran on how to proceed in the conflict, with the new hardline leadership reportedly favouring confrontation with the US, wanting to squeeze reparations out of Washington and a right to toll the strategic strait of Hormuz.

Medics ⁠said two ⁠people ​were killed and several others injured when an Israeli airstrike hit ⁠a crowd of people near the municipal public park in Gaza ⁠City on Monday, an area densely populated with ​families displaced by Israel’s assault.

Gaza’s health ministry says at least 1,320 people have been killed by Israeli attacks since a ‘ceasefire’ was signed between Israel and Hamas last October.

Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan ​by the US to end the war on Gaza.

Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said earlier this month that there can be no progress on the stalled Gaza ceasefire deal or an Israeli withdrawal from the territory until Hamas first disarms.

In its latest update, Gaza’s health ministry said that 73,456 people, mostly women and children, have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since October 2023, when Isreal launched its assault on the territory following the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

A number of legal and rights experts have concluded that Israel has committed genocide – considered the most serious international crime – against the Palestinian population of Gaza. Israel denies the charge, despite the widespread evidence that supports the conclusion.

title: The Scottie vs Tiger comparison, Michael Block's party gets shut down, and a final word on YouTube golf drama
excerpt:
Dan Dakich calls out the massive corporate meltdown over Good Good Golf’s controversial Callaway ad as cancel culture has officially hit the golf world.

Remember that narrative about Scottie Scheffle...
body_text:
Dan Dakich calls out the massive corporate meltdown over Good Good Golf’s controversial Callaway ad as cancel culture has officially hit the golf world.

Remember that narrative about Scottie Scheffler suddenly forgetting how to win golf tournaments and putting together a disappointing 2026 campaign? It was a popular one for much of the year, but that storyline is now dead with Scheffler winning the Tour Championship on Sunday, two weeks after dominating the first FedEx Cup Playoff event to wrap up his season with three wins and earning just shy of $31 million, a sum that excludes bonuses.

While the final round of the Tour Championship lacked any sort of juice down the stretch, it did mark the 30-year-old's 18th win over the last three seasons. A player by the name of Tiger Woods also picked up exactly 18 wins during the same time frame by the age of 30, which leads us into our favorite exercise: making comparisons.

Scheffler winning the Tour Championship by three shots and ultimately cruising down the stretch was the culprit of creating little excitement, but Michael Block doing Michael Block things over on the senior circuit was admittedly taking attention away from the proceedings at East Lake as well. The man is his own content factory.

Lastly, the week-long drama in the YouTube Golf world with Good Good's terrible ad, the blowback, and Grant Horvat peddling kids' clubs at an obscene price tag, there is one final analysis of the situation that must be brought forward.

Welcome to Par Talk, a weekly read to get you caught up on all the happenings that took place in professional golf that you need to know. You can follow Mark on X @itismarkharris and email him at mark.harris@outkick.com.

BACKLASH OVER GOOD GOOD GOLF AD GOES TOO FAR AS STORES PULL MERCHANDISE, PGA TOUR EVENT POTENTIALLY CANCELED

Scottie Scheffler of the USA holds the FedEx Cup Trophy after the final round of the TOUR Championship 2026 at East Lake Golf Club on August 30, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Andrew J. Clark/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) (Andrew J. Clark/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images)

There isn't much to recap from the Tour Championship. The best player in the world, who played the most consistent golf all season, earned the crown as FedEx Cup champion at East Lake. Scheffler, far and away, had the best iron play for the week, and when he's in control of his irons, as he was in Atlanta, he's untouchable and capable of sizable victories, which is exactly what unfolded.

Now, let's get into the fun stuff. Kyle Port of Normal Sport fired off a post on X after Scheffler's win, comparing his age 28-30 age season to Tiger Woods' age 28-30, and they're alarmingly similar.

SCOTTIE SCHEFFLER TURNS HOT-MIC F-BOMB INTO MOTIVATION, RALLIES FOR TOUR CHAMPIONSHIP WIN

Strictly looking at the numbers, the resumes are nearly identical, but Woods winning four majors compared to Scheffler's three, and Scheffler edging out Woods in the strokes gained category, is where things open up for a discussion. Strokes gained, remember, is a statistic relative to tournament fields and how a player performs against other players, not just the golf course, such as greens hit or fairways hit.

If we stick to the golden rule that majors trump all things, that version of Woods beats out this version of Scheffler. There is no fun in that scenario, but where there is fun is claiming which era of the PGA Tour was deeper.

Woods, battling with the likes of Phil Mickelson, Ernie Els, Vijay Singh, Retief Goosen, Jim Furyk, and other greats during his 28–30 run, may make that era more top-heavy than what Scheffler is dealing with at the moment. Does that also mean Woods' era was deeper overall, though?

I'm not sure it does. Technology has played a huge role in professional golf, which has helped with the result that the PGA Tour is filled with more elite talent than ever before, but that shouldn't mean it should be cast aside as if it doesn't matter. Just because the times have changed doesn't automatically mean the times have gotten worse or less meaningful.

Tiger Woods of The United States out on the course watching Scottie Scheffler of The United States on the 16th hole during the pro-am prior to the Hero World Challenge 2025 at Albany Golf Course on December 03, 2025 in Nassau, Bahamas. (Photo by David Cannon/Getty Images) (David Cannon/Getty Images)

Nobody is comparing Woods' overall career to Scheffler's, but over a three-year stretch, this version of Scheffler is (at the very least) on par with that version of Tiger. It may not be as flashy, it may not be as exciting, and you can call Scheffler 'boring' all you want, but that doesn't make the previous statement untrue.

Michael Block turned 50 in June, making him eligible to compete on the PGA Tour Champions, and he's not-so-quietly made the most of his sponsor's exemptions on the senior circuit.

Playing on another sponsor's invite in this past weekend's Ally Challenge, the PGA professional had not missed a cut in his four previous starts and earned a pair of Top 10 finishes along the way. The guy has simply been playing great golf, has brought juice to the senior tour, and has suddenly become one of the better players – for at least a stretch – on a 50-and-up circuit that is absolutely filled with legends of the game.

Block began Sunday's final round at the Ally Challenge atop the leader board, and while he posted a 2-over 74 to finish T-3 and four shots back of eventual winner Steven Alker, he still stole the show, just as you'd expect him to.

Michael Block smiles during the PGA Championship Practice Round at Aronimink Golf Club on Tuesday, May 12, 2026 in Newtown Square, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/PGA of America via Getty Images)

JUSTIN ROSE SLAM DUNKS HOLE-IN-ONE DURING FINAL ROUND OF TOUR CHAMPIONSHIP ON EXTREMELY DIFFICULT PAR 3

On the Par 3 eighth hole, one of the most absurd things ever witnessed in a professional golf tournament unfolded courtesy of Mr. Block.

After hitting his tee shot on the 200-yard hole to about 15 feet, Block decided that this was the perfect opportunity to put on a show for the fans. Not only did he launch his club back to his caddie to catch and rip his putter out of his hand, he began walking backwards to share some fist bumps and high fives with the volunteers surrounding the tee box.

Again, this all took place on the eighth hole after he hit a pretty standard shot onto the green. You would have thought he knocked it to eight inches and was about to tap in for the win, but no, the man hadn't even made the turn yet.

If this were anyone else on planet Earth doing this, they'd be criticized until the end of days, but since it's Michael Block, it's just another day.

Love the guy, hate the guy, don't care about the guy, whatever the case may be, one thing is for sure, and that is that you can't ignore him or escape him.

Everyone, including myself, has an opinion about the Good Good and Callaway ad, the complete fallout that has taken place after the fact, and Grant Horvat jumping into the fray by creating a set of kids' clubs and selling them for the cool price of $200.

It was a week to forget for the YouTube golf universe and the millions of fans who occupy it, and while there was no shortage of knee-jerk reactions to it all, one overarching analysis I saw simply has to be mentioned courtesy of Tweeth Mitchell on X.

We live in this strange time when everything moves at a pace no one can keep up with, and analytics in the form of likes, shares, and engagement rule all. Good Good, and Grant Horvat, are the prime examples of a group and, frankly, a generation who know nothing else. It's not their fault; one doesn't choose when they are born, but it's just the fact of the matter.

YouTube golf personality Grant Horvat looks on after his shot on the second tee during the second round of the BMW Charity Pro-Am presented by TD SYNNEX 2025 at Thornblade Club on June 06, 2025 in Greer, South Carolina. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) (Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images)

Horvat, who does not have children, diving headfirst into the kids' golf space and selling clubs that very much appear to be made of plastic for two hundred American dollars is strange and presents the image of a guy looking to get rich in what he sees as an opportune, never-ending market with humans continuing to create little humans looking to get into golf.

You can't fault someone for taking a chance in business, but in Horvat's case, it's not taking a chance given he's at the top of the Golf YouTube pyramid, and that's why it comes across as a money grab. As Mitchell noted on X, there is no north star.

title: Jim Clyburn regrets supporting Clarence Thomas' SCOTUS appointment, calling it a 'mistake'
excerpt:
Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., told "Meet the Press" that his support for Clarence Thomas during his 1991 confirmation hearing a "mistake" given Thomas' record.

Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., told NBC News...
body_text:
Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., told "Meet the Press" that his support for Clarence Thomas during his 1991 confirmation hearing a "mistake" given Thomas' record.

Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., told NBC News' "Meet the Press" on Sunday that he regretted supporting Clarence Thomas during his 1991 Supreme Court confirmation hearing, calling it a "mistake."

During the show, host Kristen Welker remarked that Clyburn had previously testified in favor of Thomas' appointment to the Supreme Court during his contentious 1991 hearing. Since his appointment, Thomas has been considered a prominent conservative justice.

Welker asked Clyburn whether he stood by his decision to support Thomas as the Democratic Party increasingly supports court-packing and enforcing term limits for justices.

CLARENCE THOMAS PRAISED AFTER RARE TELEVISED ADDRESS WARNING OF PROGRESSIVISM GOES VIRAL

South Carolina Rep. James Clyburn previously supported Clarence Thomas during his 1991 confirmation hearing. (Ting Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Absolutely not. I have made mistakes in my life," Clyburn said. "And that’s one that I made, and I will own up to that mistake. The fact of the matter is, I had faith and confidence in the fact that his background and experiences would instruct him in his professionalism, especially sitting on the bench. We had worked together when he was chair of the Equal [Employment] Opportunity Commission and, of course, I was running the state agency here in South Carolina."

Clyburn said that, despite their political differences, he believed that Thomas would be "upholding those precedents" set by the Voting Rights Act and Civil Rights Act.

"I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences. He was raised by his grandfather, and he has shown very little sensitivity to the environment his grandfather grew up in Pin Point, Georgia," Clyburn said.

During the 1991 hearing, Clyburn referred to Thomas as "a personal and professional friend, in spite of the fact that he shares a conservative Republican philosophy."

By Sunday, however, he referred to Thomas as a "very angry rightist."

'LOOK AT ME!' JUSTICE FIRES BACK AT CRITICS WHO DARE QUESTION HIS BLACKNESS

Rep. James Clyburn, left, told "Meet the Press" that he regrets his past support for Clarence Thomas, right. (Rebecca Cook/Reuters; Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

"I had hoped that Clarence Thomas would follow the modern underpinnings of that Constitution of ours, but he has not done so," Clyburn said. "In fact, he decided to go all the way from an angry leftist to a very angry rightist."

During a rare interview with Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz last week, Thomas rejected the idea that being a Black man requires him to subscribe to Democratic beliefs.

"We had this saying [that there are] only two things I have to do: stay Black and die," Thomas said. "That was a retort to people who had these sort of requirements for us, these mandates for us because of our skin color… But at any rate, they think that here's the way you're supposed to think. Again, here's your skin color. There's this kind of deterministic view that you're supposed to think this because we say so."

CONSERVATIVES HAIL JUSTICE THOMAS FOR 'TRUTH BOMB' ABOUT RULING PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas has spoken out against Democratic critics attacking him for his conservative views. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

He added, "And I, of course, declined that invitation. And so now that means something, that I'm a walking contradiction because I've deviated from their perception of what I should think."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Supreme Court for comment.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

title: Germany poised to identify suspect in Leipzig drone attack on Ukrainian plane
excerpt:
Berlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by Russia

The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a s...
body_text:
Berlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by Russia

The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a suspected drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane earlier this month and to outline its response to the incident in coordination with its European and Nato partners.

The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told the public broadcaster ARD in an interview on Sunday evening: “We are in the process of concluding the investigations; we have reached a broad agreement within the federal government on how we will respond, and we will make this clear in the coming days. It won’t take much longer.”

The government has so far declined to say officially who it thinks was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. There has been widespread speculation that it was coordinated by Moscow.

A drone containing explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. The drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate, according to a report last week referencing the investigation.

About 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted.

Days later, a third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen.

This explosive also failed to detonate but according to media reports, the investigators’ report stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”

Merz indicated that the information the government was due to release was being closely communicated with Berlin’s partners, and any response would also be carried out in cooperation with them.

“It will be a response from Germany, but our partners in the European Union and Nato will not be taken by surprise,” he said.

It has been speculated in Berlin that meetings this week of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, could be used to make the announcement.

Last week Merz stopped short of naming a suspect but said: “They will pay for this.” He underscored the necessity for a decisive response due to the lengths he said those behind the Leipzig plot and other acts of sabotage had been prepared to go.

“Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said.

The daily Die Welt and the news website Politico have reported, citing sources, that the government will blame Russia for the attack and that its retaliatory measures are likely to include a new, extensive package of sanctions coordinated with Brussels to hinder it financially, as well as more forceful measures against Russia’s shadow fleet, the Russian ships illegally transporting oil.

The closure of Russian House, an institution representing Russia’s cultural interests that has a large presence in the centre of Berlin, is also said to be on the cards. In return, Russia would be expected to close Germany’s cultural body in Russia, the Goethe Institute.

The political dimensions of the government’s response are potentially considerable owing to the timing. A heated election campaign in eastern German states culminates in a vote this Sunday in which the anti-immigrant, populist AfD is expected to do well. The debate over relations with Russia and whether and how Germany should continue to support Ukraine are playing an important role in the campaign.

The AfD’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, said he believed “without a doubt” Germany faced hybrid threats but said he would not speculate over who was behind them, calling on the government to “first establish transparency and provide information about the current state of knowledge”.

title: A pediatrician is running for Senate. Can doctors change the political debate over health and science?
excerpt:
After Lindsey Graham’s death, Democrat Annie Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race as she seeks to flip his Republican seat

Annie Andrews was a dark horse Democrat challenging a five-term R...
body_text:
After Lindsey Graham’s death, Democrat Annie Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race as she seeks to flip his Republican seat

Annie Andrews was a dark horse Democrat challenging a five-term Republican in the US Senate when 314 Action, a political action fund devoted to electing scientists and doctors, first backed her.

Now, after the unexpected death of Senator Lindsey Graham, Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race. Donald Trump persuaded South Carolina voters last week to select Graham’s sister, Darline, as the new Republican candidate. They will face off in November in an election still heavily favored to remain in Republican hands in the conservative state.

Andrews, a pediatrician for 20 years, has made public health and science a central part of her campaign, highlighting the importance of vaccines as measles spread through South Carolina – and so have the other candidates supported by 314 Action.

Last year, 314 laid out an ambitious goal: elect at least 100 doctors to state and federal office by 2030. The group had an initial fundraising target of $25m, which it reached in August, to help establish Democratic doctors in state legislatures, governorships, and federal offices – “building that pipeline of talent to higher office”, said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action.

Headlines in 2026 have been dominated by outbreaks of infectious diseases and foodborne illnesses, the biggest cuts to Medicaid in its history, the gutting of scientific research, immigration raids in hospitals, and more, making health and science salient issues in the US midterm elections.

Doctors and experts are “on the frontlines of this”, Andrews said. “I don’t think there’s ever been a more important time to elect scientists and medical doctors to all levels of our government.”

In the 2018 midterm elections, record numbers of people – nearly 200 – with backgrounds in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem) ran for House and Senate seats. But only about 12% of the candidates won, according to research by Matthew Motta, assistant professor at Boston University’s School of Public Health.

“So to say that you want to get 100 physicians to not just run but to actually be elected to public office is quite a tall order,” he said.

Endorsement and financial support from 314 Action do increase the likelihood that Stem candidates will win, according to his research. But the goal of 100 wins in the next four years is ambitious, Motta said.

In fact, candidates with Stem backgrounds were less likely to win than non-Stem peers in 2018, according to an analysis coauthored by Meredith Conroy, political science professor at California State University, San Bernardino. They probably didn’t lose because of their science background, Conroy said, adding: “I just don’t think it was a salient enough identity at the time to suggest it made or broke their campaign.”

But recent events are changing that, making health and science a top-of-mind concern for voters, Conroy and Motta pointed out.

“It’s really important then, if we want to defend science from politicized attacks on its daily operation, that those who actually do science and who do medicine are elected to Congress,” Motta said.

State-level leadership on health will also be key as national health agencies falter and as states consider restrictive laws on issues like vaccination and reproductive health, Motta said.

Josh Green, the governor of Hawaii and an emergency physician, is the only doctor-governor in the United States right now. But he wants to feel less alone.

“We want to create a bench of people” who are better-qualified and could be appointed to positions like these, Green said. He is mentoring candidates through 314 on how to engage with constituents and “how to message in a way that political people have to master”.

There are 20 physicians in the House and Senate right now, but only six of the House representatives are Democrats, and there are no Democratic doctors in the Senate. Running for office takes deep pockets, which means doctors who are already wealthy – a group that tends to skew conservative – are more likely to be elected. Some of these doctors, like Rand Paul, have contributed to misinformation on vaccines and other health issues.

That partisan divide is increasingly evident when it comes to health, Motta noted: “Just because somebody has a scientific background does not necessarily mean that they’re going to fight for science.”

Yet electing more physicians could help repair trust in science, Naughton said, as “most people do trust their physicians and they bring a lot of credibility.” Doctor-politicians aren’t just important for opposing harmful laws or misinformation, Naughton added. They also have a fact-based approach to problem solving.

Scientists and doctors frequently go into debt for their education, making it difficult for them to leave their fields for politics, Green pointed out. He was only able to do it because he qualified for student loan forgiveness through the National Health Service Corps.

“Had I had $300,000 or $400,000 of debt, like a lot of my colleagues from medical school, I could never have run for the state house. There’s no way,” he said. “If we can seed their campaigns with enough money to get off the ground,” Green said of new candidates, “they’ll stand a chance.”

When Barbara Bollier, an anesthesiologist and a Republican-turned-Democratic state lawmaker in Kansas, decided to run for the Senate in 2020, she knew the odds were long. Kansas hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

Even though Bollier lost that race, she still feels victorious. “I moved the ball down the field,” she said. She received more votes than any Democrat in the history of the state, she said, and when the next big health issue arose in Kansas, the state shocked the country by voting to protect abortion rights.

There’s a persistent belief that medicine and science are above politics, Naughton said, pointing out “that approach has failed us … We need folks to go beyond just signing polite letters and waiting to be tapped as scientific advisers, and actually step up and claim the seat at the table.”

And the stakes are high: “The hard truth of it is, people are going to die if we don’t follow science,” Green said.

Running for office “was not something I ever, in a million years, thought I would be doing with my life”, Andrews said. At age 4, she told her preschool teacher she would be a doctor one day, and she never wavered from that plan. But “it became clear to me that the most effective and efficient way to solve the problems my patients and their families were facing was through politics, by changing who actually has the power, by electing people who inherently care about America’s children,” she said.

It’s going to take decades to counter the misinformation and damage from officials currently in power, Andrews said. But she is in it for the long haul. “I’m just so happy to be a part of this movement of physicians all across the country raising their hands, stepping up to run for office,” she said.

title: BT on track for estimated £2bn windfall from selling old copper amid AI boom
excerpt:
Telecoms company to benefit from soaring prices for recycled metal recovered from full-fibre broadband rollout

BT is on track for an estimated £2bn-plus windfall over the next decade from selling off...
body_text:
Telecoms company to benefit from soaring prices for recycled metal recovered from full-fibre broadband rollout

BT is on track for an estimated £2bn-plus windfall over the next decade from selling off old copper cabling, as it cashes in on soaring prices amid the AI market frenzy and switches the UK’s network to full-fibre broadband.

Copper is one of the main beneficiaries of the “electrification of everything”, essential for the rapid growth of AI datacentres, electronics and the fast-growing renewable energy industry.

The metal hit its highest-ever closing price of $14,294 a metric tonne on Friday, close to the record intraday high of $14,500 reached earlier this year amid global shortage fears.

BT has a recycling deal with EMR, the UK’s largest cable granulation company, and has now received £99m upfront for thousands of tonnes of surplus stripped copper.

It is the second such payment received by the telecoms company, which is rolling out full-fibre broadband to 30m homes by the end of the decade through its Openreach subsidiary, after £105m in 2024.

The forward sale agreements, which are understood to cover the delivery of about 20,000 tonnes of copper over a four-year period each, do not include any revenue BT makes each year if it chooses to sell recycled copper on the spot market.

BT recovered a record nearly 10,000 tonnes in the year to the end of March, almost three times the amount it managed in the year to the end of March 2024, and a total of 22,347 tonnes since the telecoms company began stripping and selling the cabling in 2023.

The record haul, which is 63% more than the 5,600 tonnes reported in BT’s 2025 results, comes at a time of soaring prices which could handsomely benefit BT.

In the year that BT reported its first copper haul the average price for the metal was about $8,500 a tonne.

“We recovered even more copper cabling,” said Mike McTighe, the chair of Openreach, acknowledging the potential financial benefit of the market surge, in BT’s latest annual report. “Removing 9,147 tonnes from our network for recycling at a time when global demand has never been higher.”

Howeer, the jump in value has also made the metal a target of thieves across Britain’s telephone network, railways and even windfarms.

Openreach has said it expects to be able to recover up to 200,000 tonnes, with telecoms cabling producing high-grade recycled copper, as the programme runs through the 2030s in line with moving customers on to full-fibre connections.

While the precise details of BT’s contract with EMR, which initially runs until 2028, are not known, the market value of the copper it expects to be able to extract had previously been estimated at £1.5bn.

However, the soaring price of copper and a future supply crunch – the rating agency S&P Global expects demand to grow from 25m metric tonnes now to about 50m by 2035 – means at current market prices BT’s entire copper tonnage could be valued at £2bn-plus.

“Copper has become one of the most strategic materials in the modern economy,” said Abby Chicken, the head of sustainability at Openreach. “As we connect the nation to more reliable full fibre, we’re able to retire parts of the legacy network that are no longer needed.

“Recovering and recycling that copper is the right thing to do. It reduces waste, supports the UK’s energy transition towards renewables and helps keep a critical resource in circulation at a time when growing demand is putting pressure on global supply chains.”

Amid the soaring prices, Openreach has acted to prevent copper theft. Last year, thieves struck in St Neots, Cambridgeshire, twice in a month, resulting in nearly a mile of underground cables being damaged.

In 2024, Openreach suffered copper thefts in the New Forest, affecting 128 premises, and County Tyrone, Northern Ireland, leaving hundreds of homes and businesses with connectivity issues.

Openreach is using a wide range of anti-theft measures including coating miles of underground cables with a synthetic DNA and UV tracer, called SelectaDNA.

This is widely used across the Openreach network and the tracer easily transfers to hands and clothing.

Openreach reported a 30% fall in copper phone and broadband cable theft in 2024, which it attributed to the deployment of the new technology.

However, this technology cannot be applied to cables that are already underground, meaning thieves continue to target copper cables.

title: Sleeping in on weekends is good for the heart: What research has shown
excerpt:
Sleeping an extra hour or two on the weekends can reduce the risk of high blood pressure, a study shows.

Scientists have largely asserted that people should keep regular bedtimes and wake-up times, m...
body_text:
Sleeping an extra hour or two on the weekends can reduce the risk of high blood pressure, a study shows.

Scientists have largely asserted that people should keep regular bedtimes and wake-up times, maintaining a consistent sleep schedule across the week, including weekends.

But the new study questions that view, building on other recent research that suggests weekend lie-ins – and extra sleep more broadly – are good for the heart and overall health.

The findings, presented on Sunday at the European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress in Munich, Germany, were based on a seven‑year study of 40,727 adults in South Korea. These were adults from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, studied from 2016 to 2023.

The researchers examined how many extra hours participants slept at weekends compared with weekdays.

The latest study found that catching up on sleep at the weekend after a long workweek lowers the prevalence of high blood pressure.

However, this was only the case when lie-ins were kept at a moderate length – about one to two hours of extra sleep with an optimal increase of about one hour and 37 minutes.

In all, weekend catch-up sleep was associated with a 6 percent decrease in the chances of high blood pressure. This decrease was larger for physically inactive people, who saw a 6.9 percent decrease in chances of hypertension. The study found that someone getting one hour and 37 minutes of extra sleep at weekends could reduce their chances of hypertension by 9 percent.

As of 2024, 1.4 billion adults aged 30-79 worldwide have hypertension, accounting for 33 percent of the world population in this age range, according to the World Health Organization. High blood pressure is a major cause of premature death worldwide, the United Nations agency added.

The findings of this study have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The author of the study, Nawon Lee from Korea University in Seoul, said in remarks reported by several news outlets on Monday that not sleeping enough places extra stress on the body, forcing the heart and blood vessels to work harder, which can increase blood pressure.

She added that people should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer at the weekend if they have not been able to get enough sleep during the week. Sleeping in during the weekend could be the body’s way of recovering from that sleep loss.

However, she warned that when weekend catch-up sleep becomes excessive, the degree of sleep irregularity and circadian disruption may increase, which could offset that benefit.

In the 2024 European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress in London, researchers presented a study of more than 90,000 individuals.

The study found that people with the most weekend catch-up sleep had about a 20 percent lower risk of developing heart disease than those with the least.

A large body of modern medical research supports a strong association between adequate sleep and better heart health.

For decades, the medical consensus has been that too little sleep can harm cardiovascular health, that seven to nine hours a night is generally optimal for adults and regularly sleeping much more than that may sometimes point to an underlying health problem.

However, scientists have previously suggested that weekend lie-ins could be harmful by disrupting the body’s natural circadian rhythm, a built-in biological clock running on an approximately 24-hour cycle that regulates sleep, hormone release and body temperature.

In 2019, researchers studied 36 adults, dividing them into three groups. One group had their sleep restricted to five hours a night over nine nights, including weekends, another was restricted to five hours a night but was allowed to catch up unrestricted at weekends and one group was allowed nine hours of sleep over nine nights.

Both the groups with restricted sleep snacked more in the evening and saw a decline in metabolic health. The study found that the people who slept more at the weekend partly improved while they were actually sleeping more.

However, once they went back to short sleep, the benefits disappeared and overall metabolic health was still worse than in people who consistently slept more every night.

title: Greece signs $3.5bn air defence deal with Israel
excerpt:
Greece has signed a $3.5bn defence deal with Israel to provide its first integrated “multi-layered” air defence network.

Israel said the agreement, negotiated over three years, is one of the largest ...
body_text:
Greece has signed a $3.5bn defence deal with Israel to provide its first integrated “multi-layered” air defence network.

Israel said the agreement, negotiated over three years, is one of the largest in the country’s history..

Engineers will set up an aerial defence shield for the Greeks, integrating three Israeli systems, including the SPYDER system, produced by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, the BARAK MX system, made by Israel Aerospace Industries and David’s Sling air defence technology, an Israeli defence ministry statement said on Monday.

The agreement comes as Israeli weapons’ exports are soaring, despite widespread criticism over its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza and other wars in Lebanon and Iran.

Israeli weapons exports reached record highs with more than $19bn last year, a 30 percent increase from 2024, according to official data.

“Modern conflicts have already altered the parameters of military defence and deterrence,” Greece’s Defence Minister, Nikos Dendias, said in a statement after the agreement was signed.

“Technology, ballistic missiles, satellite communications, unmanned systems, cyber threats, hybrid forms of warfare and the interconnection of fields of operations have long rendered pre-existing defence doctrines completely unrealistic,” he said.

Reporting from Athens, Al Jazeera’s John Psaropoulos said the systems could counter a range of aerial threats.

“The SPYDER and David’s Sling are short-to-medium-range air defence missile systems. They fire missiles to intercept incoming aircraft, cruise missiles and large drones. The BARAK can do all these things, but it also intercepts incoming ballistics,” he said.

Separately, Greece signed a $30m deal with Israel for Rafael’s Drone Dome system, “to defend strategic sites against UAVs and drones and to reinforce existing defences”.

Greece is the second European Union member to agree to buy the David’s Sling system, after Finland.

“This is Greece interpreting the lessons from the war in Ukraine, which has changed the nature of armed conflict and realising that it needs much stronger air defences to intercept whatever might come in from the East.” Psaropoulos said.

“Now that the war in the Gulf has reawakened Iranian animosity towards US allies in Europe, there is a perceived threat from there as well as from other countries in the East,” Psaropoulos added.

Greece spends nearly 3.5 percent of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than ⁠many NATO allies due to its long-standing dispute with neighbouring Turkiye.

title: Why is piracy picking up off Somalia’s coast again?
excerpt: The Federal Government of Somalia announced on August 29 that the Turkish navy, working with Somali forces, had freed the cargo ship MV Lutuf after a 10-day pursuit, killing 14 pirates and destroying ...
body_text:
The Federal Government of Somalia announced on August 29 that the Turkish navy, working with Somali forces, had freed the cargo ship MV Lutuf after a 10-day pursuit, killing 14 pirates and destroying four of their boats.

The vessel had been seized on August 17 off Jifle, on the coast of Puntland, Somalia’s semi-autonomous northeastern region. Mogadishu’s Defence Ministry credited its release to a 2024 defence pact between Somalia and Turkiye.

Puntland has disputed that account. Its Ministry of Security said no military rescue had taken place and accused federal officials of securing the vessel’s release through a ransom payment to the pirates.

The conflicting accounts have not been independently verified. But the seizure and the military response around it mark the most dramatic episode yet in a series of pirate attacks off Somalia this year, raising fresh questions about how far a resurgence that began in the spring could go.

Piracy incidents in Somali waters and the Gulf of Aden have risen sharply since the spring, after several years in which the crime had all but disappeared from the region.

An AFP analysis of International Maritime Organization data found at least 15 attacks since the start of the year, including eight in the Gulf of Aden since May.

One tanker seized off Yemen in May was later directed towards Somalia by pirates demanding $10m. Another vessel, the MV Honour 25, has been held for more than two months.

In May, a separate pirate group abandoned a hijacked Emirati dhow after running short of supplies while using it as a mother ship to attack other ships, Puntland security officials told AFP.

The Joint Maritime Information Center, which monitors threats to shipping in the region, raised its piracy threat assessment to “severe” in response to the surge in attacks during April and May.

The increase is significant, but still far below the scale of the crisis in the early 2010s, when the International Maritime Organization, the United Nations agency responsible for shipping safety and security, recorded around 200 attacks a year.

Afyare Elmi, a Somali academic at City University in Mogadishu, told Al Jazeera there had “been an uptick, but compared with the levels seen in the early 2010s, the number of attacks is not that high”.

Mostafa Elbanna of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime said piracy remains well below its historic peak. Speaking at a security meeting in Nairobi last week, he said countries in the region are better equipped to respond than they were last time.

Between 2005 and 2012, pirates carried out more than 1,000 attacks off Somalia, according to a World Bank study. They successfully hijacked 218 vessels and collected an estimated $315m to $385m in ransom payments.

At the peak in 2011, Somalia accounted for well over half of all piracy attacks recorded worldwide.

One Earth Future’s Oceans Beyond Piracy programme, a maritime security initiative set up during the Somali piracy crisis, estimated that piracy off Somalia’s coast cost the global economy between $6.6bn and $6.9bn in 2011, largely through security measures, higher fuel use, insurance and naval operations.

The crisis was eventually brought under control by a vast international security effort. NATO’s Operation Ocean Shield, the European Union’s Operation Atalanta and the US-led Combined Task Force 151 increased naval patrols, while shipping companies hardened vessels and changed procedures.

Between 2013 and 2023, barely a handful of hijackings succeeded off Somalia.

NATO ended its counter-piracy mission in 2016.

But the long period of relative calm did not mean the conditions that sustained piracy had disappeared. International patrols and better-protected ships made hijackings far harder and more expensive, while weak coastal governance, illegal fishing and criminal networks persisted onshore.

As early as 2013, a report by the UN secretary-general said the persistence of pirate networks reflected “the onshore rule of law and governance vacuum in which they operate”, and cautioned that attacks could rise again if naval patrols were reduced or commercial vessels relaxed their defences.

The resurgence is now testing how durable that earlier success was.

No single factor explains the resurgence, Abdullahi Mohamed Kulmiye, a former ports and maritime transport minister in Galmudug, a state neighbouring Puntland, told Al Jazeera. Several conditions, he said, appear to have aligned at once.

One is a shift in naval attention elsewhere in the region. The United States and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and Iran has at times controlled passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

Naval forces that might otherwise patrol waters closer to Somalia have been drawn towards that crisis.

Abdurrahim Muhammad Ali of the Djibouti Maritime Authority told a regional security meeting in Nairobi this week that pirates were exploiting the diversion of naval forces elsewhere.

“They use this opportunity and the distraction of maritime forces globally to carry out more attacks in this area, because they know everyone is busy [looking in another direction],” he said.

Economic pressure onshore has intensified at the same time. Inflation in Somalia reached 9.2 percent in March, its highest level in years, as fuel and food prices surged.

The International Monetary Fund ranks Somalia among a handful of countries, including Sudan, Yemen and Afghanistan, with almost no financial buffer against such shocks.

Cuts to aid from the US and United Kingdom, two of Somalia’s most important humanitarian funding sources, have further deepened the country’s economic pressures.

Seasonal conditions may also play a part. According to analysis from the Institute for Security Studies, a Johannesburg-based think tank, attacks typically fall during the winter monsoon, when rough seas keep small boats close to shore, before rising again as the waters calm in spring.

Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa, while its exclusive economic zone covers an area larger than its landmass.

The country is still rebuilding after decades of civil war, with law enforcement stretched thin on land and no effective coastguard to patrol its waters.

The African Development Bank estimates Somalia loses about $300m a year to fishing fleets operating illegally in its waters.

Coastal communities have long accused foreign trawlers of depleting stocks on which local fishermen depend.

That grievance helped shape the first major wave of piracy attacks in the 2000s, when some fishermen took up arms to defend the waters that nobody else was protecting.

But piracy has since developed far beyond that origin story. Andrew Mwangura, a maritime security consultant who spent three decades at sea and later helped negotiate hostage releases during the earlier crisis, told Al Jazeera that the motive had changed.

“Before, the people were vigilantes mainly driven to sea because of illegal fishing in Somali waters and the dumping of toxic chemicals. Now it is more about seizing ships for ransom,” he said.

Recent attacks suggest both dynamics may still be present. According to the French navy’s Maritime Information Cooperation and Awareness Center (MICA Center), pirate groups operating far offshore typically use dhows disguised as fishing boats as floating bases.

From them, crews launch fast skiffs capable of striking vessels as far as 600 nautical miles (1,111km) from the Somali coast.

Mwangura believes at least some of those involved are trained seamen, pointing to their use of GPS navigation and long-range vessel-tracking systems.

Closer to shore, the MICA Center has identified a different pattern, with attacks launched directly from the coast and aimed at foreign fishing boats accused of stealing Somali fish rather than commercial vessels.

Recent piracy operations also appear more organised than the image of impoverished fishermen taking opportunistically to sea might suggest, according to experts and Somali officials tracking the resurgence.

A former pirate speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera said that today’s operations are financed by investors, often businesspeople in Yemen and Somalia, who supply crews with satellite phones, navigation equipment, weapons and provisions to head to sea.

A joint study by Interpol, the United Nations and the World Bank found that during the earlier piracy crisis, financiers behind attacks typically took 30 to 50 percent of ransom payments. The men who actually boarded ships generally received a much smaller fee.

The study found that small groups in communities near pirate anchorages also supplied crews with food, repairs and khat, a stimulant leaf widely chewed in the region.

Abdifatah Mohamed Abdinur, a state minister in Puntland’s government, said the pirates were also linked to criminal networks operating across Somalia and Yemen, allowing some groups to operate closer to the Yemeni coast and with a greater hijacking success rate.

“There is definitely a connection,” Abdinur told Al Jazeera, “but we have to put the pieces together to make the big picture clearer.”

The security landscape around Somalia has changed considerably since the last crisis.

The international response to piracy helped turn nearby Djibouti, which sits on the narrow Bab al-Mandeb Strait between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, into a hub for foreign military forces. The area is now one of the world’s most crowded strategic arenas.

There are signs that another response is beginning to take shape, though its scope and prospects for success remain uncertain.

The European Union’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, signed a new basing agreement with Djibouti in July, preserving access for Operation Atalanta and a second EU mission patrolling the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia has assembled a maritime task force for the Red Sea that a growing number of countries, including Somalia, have joined.

In early August, Puntland’s president also signed an agreement with a visiting US military delegation to deepen maritime security cooperation around Bosaso, its main port.

Officials from Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia and Yemen met in Nairobi this week under a UN-backed programme aimed at strengthening intelligence-sharing on piracy and other maritime crime.

These measures could make hijackings more difficult. But the conditions that allowed piracy to survive the last international crackdown have not disappeared.

Elmi, the Somali academic, argues that naval patrols alone cannot prevent piracy from repeatedly resurfacing. “Onshore-based solutions are more sustainable when it comes to dealing with piracy in the Somali coast,” he told Al Jazeera.

title: FIFA president Infantino ‘must go’, says former UEFA boss Platini
excerpt:
French football great Michel Platini says FIFA president Gianni Infantino “must go” following the scandals that have surrounded football’s governing body and rocked the sport globally.

“Economic affa...
body_text:
French football great Michel Platini says FIFA president Gianni Infantino “must go” following the scandals that have surrounded football’s governing body and rocked the sport globally.

“Economic affairs are one thing, but Infantino has failed because he is the guarantor of the rules of the game and he didn’t respect them,” former UEFA president Platini told a French media outlet on Sunday.

The 56-year-old Infantino has been under fire since his aborted plan to bring private investment into FIFA events, such as the World Cup. He was also lambasted over a number of controversies during the recently concluded World Cup in North America.

Platini hit out at the so-called hydration breaks at the World Cup, which often lasted as much as four minutes and were used by the host broadcaster for advertisements.

He also pointed to the half-time show during the final, which largely overran the required maximum of 15 minutes, and the furore around FIFA suspending the red card ban given to American forward Folarin Balogun following a phone call made by United States President Donald Trump to Infantino.

“The ad breaks are not in the rules, the 30-minute half-time break in the final is not in the rules, and the red card, that’s the worst,” said Platini.

“He’s the guarantor [of the rules], he doesn’t respect them, he must go,” added Platini, who was UEFA’s secretary-general under the Frenchman’s leadership.

Since the World Cup, UEFA threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments until Infantino scrapped the FIFA Forward Enterprises plan to bring in private investment.

European football’s governing body UEFA has also accused Infantino of “criminal mismanagement” over the private financing.

FIFA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for a comment.

Other regional bodies – the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) – have joined UEFA in putting pressure on Infantino, who is hoping to run for re-election in March.

“It won’t be sporting institutions that sort this out and bring him down,” Platini said.

“If UEFA want to bring down Infantino, it will be through the courts.”

“I always knew that he loved money and power,” Platini added about the Swiss-Italian.

Platini was himself accused of fraud in 2015 when he was UEFA president and eyeing the top job at FIFA to replace Sepp Blatter, who was likewise accused of giving an illegal payment of $2m to the Frenchman.

Platini was eventually acquitted of any wrongdoing in 2025 but was forced to step down at the time, with Infantino leaping on the opportunity to be elected FIFA president in his stead in 2016.

“He didn’t bring me down, he benefitted from it,” said Platini.

“But now that there are lots of investigations into him all over the world, there is some noise about how he knew about certain things — let’s see what happens next.”

Platini is suing Infantino, and former FIFA officials Marco Villiger and Domenico Scala, in France “to seek compensation for all the damages he has suffered as a result of the tactics used to prevent him from being elected FIFA president in 2015”.

He accuses the trio of a “criminal conspiracy to commit false accusation … influence peddling … and aiding and abetting influence peddling”.

title: Australians missing in Nepal targeted by ‘heartbreaking’ and ‘abhorrent’ racist slurs
excerpt:
As families await news after the catastrophe, community members appeal for compassion in the face of hateful rhetoric

A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards Australians missing...
body_text:
As families await news after the catastrophe, community members appeal for compassion in the face of hateful rhetoric

A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards Australians missing in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods, prompting calls for greater accountability of major platforms to remove hateful rhetoric.

On Monday, the total number of Australians missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas rose to 43, and the overall death toll was at least 810 people.

The majority of the missing Australians were on pilgrimages, including to Mount Kailash in Tibet, which is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon faith. Fourteen are Sydney-based members of the Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj community.

As families and friends face an agonising wait to learn the fate of their loved ones, mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians in Nepal.

Some outlets, including Guardian Australia, have limited who can comment on posts about the missing tourists after receiving strings of racist replies on social media.

One Daily Telegraph article received dozens of comments on Facebook from people claiming that missing citizens who were not white weren’t Australian, which were later deleted. One said: “Hoping we have new vacancies in Australia that Aussies can fill.”

The outlet’s editor, Ben English, said the comments on the post were “abhorrent” and “have no place on our platforms”.

“We are responsible for the comment threads on our pages and we take that responsibility seriously … But no automated filter reliably catches racism expressed in coded language,” he said.

“Where we cannot actively moderate a thread on a sensitive story, we will close it - and we have moved to do that here.”

The comments have also proliferated on X. One post by conservative commentator, Kobie Thatcher, who wrote “Aussie family” alongside an image of an identified missing couple, was viewed 3.2m times.

Associate Prof at QUT’s Digital Media Research Centre, Tim Graham, said hateful rhetoric had been increasing on social media platforms for the past decade.

“The design architecture of these websites, the algorithms that they use to curate content and put it into feeds, rewards this kind of stuff,” he said.

“It brings out the worst in people, but it also plays into the political economy of these platforms where rage bait, extreme content or borderline content … attracts so much attention.”

He said platforms had the technical infrastructure and the resources to push back against harmful content, including generative AI models that could detect “nuanced content at scale”, but weren’t using it for moderation.

“I really don’t understand why that can’t be applied in special circumstances to a really terrible humanitarian catastrophe like this,” he said. “It’s a bit mind-boggling.”

The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said he wasn’t surprised by the comments, which he connected to Australia’s current debate on migrants.

“They’re saying, you don’t deserve to … be seen as Australian. And that’s amplified by the rhetoric of far-right populist parties,” he said.

“We should be very concerned because it’s indicative of a real rise in white supremacy ideology … Words have consequences … It’s heartbreaking.”

Sivaraman said racism was “profitable” for social media companies, and the notion they were attempting to stop hate speech on their platforms was “fanciful”.

“This is just more evidence as to why we need a digital duty of care for all social media platforms that operate in Australia,” he said.

Hindu Council of Australia vice-president Surinder Jain said it was “saddening” to see people making use of a tragedy to “express their displeasure with the government”.
 “I … ask them to show some dignity to those who have perished and the families of those who are mourning their loss: give them a fair go,” he told Guardian Australia.

Australia’s Indian diaspora, which includes Hindus, has been the target of racist comments from far-right movements including March for Australia as immigration has emerged as a hot-button issue.

Nepalese Australian Welfare Society president, Chiran Tiwari, said Australians needed to look past nationalities and have humanity.
 “It is very hurtful and the families who are impacted feel really, really bad,” he told Guardian Australia. “All of us are human.”

title: Goodbye to Babylon Berlin, the 1920s TV drama that has eerily foreshadowed real-life politics
excerpt:
The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day

It’s the global hit TV series ...
body_text:
The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day

It’s the global hit TV series that pulled audiences straight into the chaotic hedonism of 1920s Germany, dramatising the brilliance and brittleness of a newly built democratic system with unprecedented ambition.

But in the 13 years that the German makers of Babylon Berlin have worked on the show, modern democracies from the US to Hungary to South Korea have come under pressure in ways the creators say they could never have imagined when they started.

Now they are preparing to unveil the fifth and final season, culminating in Adolf Hitler’s rise to power, the same week that Germany will face one of the biggest tests of its postwar order in a watershed state election.

The timing, they insist, is pure coincidence, but is fitting for an ambitious programme set a century ago during the Weimar republic that has always felt eerily prescient.

As the team gets ready to sign off, the inexorable end of the story is now upon the familiar characters of the noirish police procedural, with its lush period sets and frisson of impending doom.

“It’s no longer a dance on the rim of the volcano,” said lead actor Liv Lisa Fries, using a German idiom for the explosion of avant garde culture and sexual liberation in the 1920s before the descent into fascism. “We’re in the volcano itself.”

Fries plays the series’ intrepid working-class heroine Charlotte Ritter, who works her way up from secretarial duties and underworld sex work to become the first female detective on the Berlin police force.

Her co-star Volker Bruch is Gereon Rath, a shellshocked first world war veteran whose eventful odyssey through the trauma of his era bears a resemblance to Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster, The Odyssey.

But the more striking parallel is Germany in 2026.

The far-right Alternative für Deutschland, an extremist, anti-constitutional party founded around the same time that work on the series began, is now leading national opinion polls.

On Sunday 6 September, it could win its first absolute majority in a state election, in Saxony-Anhalt, and two weeks later may beat its opponents in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. In Berlin, it is polling close to the far-left party Die Linke.

With German democracy facing such a stress test, Bruch said the political “parallels” jumped out. But he resisted overly simplistic comparisons, citing an old adage: “History doesn’t repeat itself that way – it rhymes.”

The blurred lines between life and art took on sometimes surreal dimensions during the course of the production.

Series three was filmed in part at the neo-baroque Villa Adlon, which in November 2023 served as the real-life venue for a secret meeting of AfD officials and neo-Nazis to discuss a “remigration” plan for mass deportations if the party came to power.

Series five sees Hitler’s appointment as Reich chancellor, just as an medical file goes missing that casts new light on his time as a soldier in the first world war.

Although it was always clear how the series would end, watching Babylon Berlin has meant hoping to the last that history would take another turn.

That poignancy transformed a sophisticated crime show into something more affecting, and perhaps more enduring.

Across 50-odd hours, the show, based partly on a series of novels by Volker Kutscher, helped expand the scale and ambition of European television drama.

“It was almost impossible even then when they started,” said Scott Roxborough, the European bureau chief of entertainment trade magazine the Hollywood Reporter.

It was the product of a “pioneer time”, he said, when Germany was willing to throw massive resources at a chance to catch up with splashy shows from the US and Britain like Breaking Bad and The Crown.

“I think it would be almost impossible to do it nowadays unless an Apple TV or a Netflix decided to finance everything,” something he said was increasingly unlikely as the global streaming companies take a more cautious, profits-first approach.

Babylon Berlin has reached audiences around the world – 140 countries at last count – with its cautionary tale of a vibrant civilisation’s inherent fragility.

“The secret to the series’s success in capturing the zeitgeist is definitely not that it mirrors the present. I don’t believe that,” one of its three creators, Tom Tykwer, said.

Rather, audiences have been drawn to the “transformative force” of Berlin in the 1920s, when a weak government and a churning society left room for women, gay people and new immigrants to rewrite the rules.

“That brings forth an incredible number of wonderful, positive, beautiful blossoms, but because it’s so experimental, they’re also destroyed again almost immediately,” he said.

“We’ve tried to explore the universal themes that stem from the fact that political systems are people-centred so are always under threat. It will always be that way.”

Tykwer also co-composed much of the original music for the series, including the haunting theme song To Ashes, to Dust. The fifth season features a plot excursion to Paris and an on-screen rendition of the tune by French neo-chanson star Zaho de Sagazan.

In series five, Tykwer and his team have also revived the 1920 queer anthem Das Lila Lied with its rousing chorus “Wir sind nun einmal anders als die andern” (We’re just different from the others) for the series.

It is rousingly sung in a nightclub frequented by cross-dressing patrons and uniformed, gay SA officers – a startling melange the producers say was not uncommon before the brutal Nazi crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community.

While Tykwer bristles at the notion that the series should deliver any sort of “message” to Germans about their choices at the ballot box this month, fellow creator Henk Handloegten said he was proud to have “struck a nerve” with audiences around the world who find themselves at a political crossroads.

“I believe that we’ve taken a clear political stand, even now in the final series, and I find it very necessary,” he said.

For Handloegten, the pressure on democracy in many countries where the show is watched, “has really motivated me”.

“It’s given me the justification to engage with [this era] for so long and so deeply, because I felt there was a relevance to it in today’s world. And for me, in a strange way, that’s political work – something we’ve been doing here for 13 years now.”

title: Icac lawyer tells Charles Perrottet the key to lying is ‘you have to be really good at remembering it’
excerpt:
Perrottet disagrees when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC claims brother of former NSW premier is not truthful and ‘constructing evidence’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get ...
body_text:
Perrottet disagrees when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC claims brother of former NSW premier is not truthful and ‘constructing evidence’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A brother of former New South Wales premier Dominic Perrottet has told Icac he would lie to a property developer about delivering political outcomes “to keep him on side”, but Charles Perrottet has denied lying to the state’s anti-corruption watchdog.

Charles Perrottet, who is among three Liberal figures alleged to have anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited political donations from Jean Nassif, told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Monday that he “made up” updates for the property developer.

Perrottet said he provided advice with a “political flavour” when chasing payments for genuine services provided to Nassif’s company, Toplace, by lobbying company Beckington, which was controlled by Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, also named in Icac’s allegations.

Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest nor is he accused of wrongdoing.

Charles Perrottet, a member of the NSW Liberals’ conservative right faction, said he advised Nassif in the hope the developer would a sign a statutory declaration about allegations that the rival centre-right faction was circumventing electoral funding laws which prevent property developers from donating.

Under questioning from counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, he rejected the suggestion that his arrangement with Nassif was similar to the one he sought to expose.

“So you were doing that by promising Jean Nassif that you could achieve political outcomes for him if he gave money, correct?” Dwyer asked on Monday.

Perrottet replied: “They’re very separate issues.” He has insisted payments from Nassif were not political donations.

Dwyer read a message about the allegations against the centre-right – for which the commission heard Nassif never provided a statutory declaration – that Charles Perrottet sent to Ellis in February 2020: “It’s the money train. They cannot donate, but they get around that in two ways: cash and monthly government affairs retainers … the going rate is $50,000 per month.”

Dwyer suggested that Perrottet had been trying to set up “the same sort of arrangement to help the right”.

“You wanted to get on board the money train, didn’t you?” she said. Charles Perrottet denied this.

Earlier on Monday, Charles Perrottet was asked about a message he sent to Nassif in January 2021, in which he provided a “short summary” on actions he had taken in relation to three Toplace developments, including the reference “189 spoke to my PDU contact”.

The commission heard that “189” referred to a Toplace development in Parramatta and “PDU” referred to the NSW Planning Delivery Unit. Perrottet said he did not have a PDU contact and made no call.

“Ultimately, I made it up,” Perrottet told the Icac hearing. He said under questioning he would lie to Nassif by “regularly mislead[ing]” him about his own involvement in lobbying work by Beckington for Toplace.

“At times, I would add my own political flavour to it to keep him on side,” he said. He said this included “many messages of me providing political updates to encourage him to make those payments [to Beckington]”.

He was asked about at a meeting he attended at a Sydney pub in January 2021 with Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran, named in another of Icac’s allegations, at which messages suggested Charles Perrottet had collected a cheque for $148,500 for Beckington.

Charles Perrottet accepted he had told Nassif the money was for “assistance for the upcoming preselections”, but told the commission it was in fact for genuine lobbying work by Beckington.

After Dwyer said his evidence contradicted a private examination in June in which he said he was there to pick up Nassif’s statutory declaration, Charles Perrottet said: “It could be both.” Dwyer accused him of lying to the commission.

“The great truism about telling a lie, Mr Perrottet, is you have to be really good at remembering it,” she said.

“And when you gave evidence in June this year that you were picking up a statutory declaration that was a lie, and when you gave evidence this morning that you didn’t know what you were picking up, that was a lie.

“And you, when confronted with the truth about it being a cheque, you’re constructing your evidence around that. That’s what’s going on here.”

The commission heard evidence about an arrangement under which Beckington would receive 1% of the total Nassif made from any developments they were successful in fast-tracking.

“His example of the 1% for any project that could get through, and he gave an example of if you made $100m, you’d get 1%,” Charles Perrottet said.

Perrottet repeatedly insisted that he provided “advice”, rather than work, to Nassif. Perrottet told the inquiry he had agreed that his wife, Anita Perrottet, would receive money for advice he provided to Nassif through her business Macquarie Consulting from Beckington, controlled by Ellis and Greenwood, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.

The watchdog has evidence the payments to Anita Perrottet totalled $660,999 over two-and-a-half years. She has told the commission this was for “strategic and marketing advice” that she provided.

Under questioning from the presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, Charles Perrottet said it was his understanding at the time that this was not income he had to disclose in his tax return.

He said he had met with Ellis and Anita Perrottet to discuss the invoice arrangement, but Dwyer said this directly contradicted Anita Perrottet’s evidence to the commission last week, in which she said she had only spoken with Greenwood about payments.

“My recollection is the invoicing conversations that I had, and I believe Anita was present, were with Christian,” Charles Perrottet said.

Nassif, who fled Australia in 2022, is expected to appear by video link from Lebanon on Friday. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.
