title: New York City to increase cooling tower inspections after legionnaires’ outbreaks
excerpt:
State and city lawmakers push to boost regulations after two outbreaks of the disease over the last two summers

New York lawmakers are now trying to better protect residents from the deadly legionnai...
body_text:
State and city lawmakers push to boost regulations after two outbreaks of the disease over the last two summers

New York lawmakers are now trying to better protect residents from the deadly legionnaires’ disease by increasing regulations and inspections of cooling towers after two outbreaks of the infection over the last two summers and a raft of new lawsuits.

Legionnaires’ disease is a serious pneumonia caused by a bacterium called legionella. It often comes from large air-conditioning systems, like those used in hotels, hospitals and high-rise buildings, because the cooling towers contain water to remove heat. If not well maintained, the liquid can foster the bacteria, which can then be swept into fans and circulated through the air.

“The thing about a cooling tower is that it’s not just the people in your building that are affected,” said Amy Pruden, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Virginia Tech University. “You can just be walking by this hotel or hospital or apartment building and happen to linger having a conversation or something and then you get exposed.”

Scientists argue that deaths from legionnaires’ are preventable if people dedicate enough time and money to conduct routine maintenance of cooling towers and if government officials conduct regular inspections and penalize negligent building owners.

The upkeep to stop legionnaires’ could become especially important as global temperatures rise due to the climate crisis, causing greater reliance on air conditioning, experts say.

“We can all do better in preventing legionnaires’ disease,” said Dr William Schaffner, an infectious diseases expert at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine. “We have the tools in hand. They have to be done rigorously all the time. Will it be perfect? No. Can you substantially reduce the risk of outbreaks and even individual disease illnesses? Yes.”

In August 2025 in New York’s Harlem neighborhood, seven people died and more than 100 became ill during a legionnaires’ outbreak. This summer, the Upper East Side saw 92 cases of legionnaires’ disease, 79 hospitalizations and seven deaths. The city’s health department staff collected samples from more than 180 cooling towers and found that 59 tested positive for the bacterium, according to the city. Sites included the Guggenheim Museum, apartment buildings, a Whole Foods market and a private school.

Toronto and central Ohio also recently experienced legionnaires’ outbreaks.

Victims of the 2025 Harlem outbreak and their family members recently filed four lawsuits against the city, NYC Health + hospitals and contractors responsible for maintaining the cooling towers.

“We love New York City,” attorney Jared Scotto said at a press conference alongside plaintiffs; his co-counsel, the civil rights attorney Ben Crump; and the Rev Al Sharpton. “We love being close to our neighbors, but that presents an inherent risk that companies and building owners need to take into account, and they didn’t do that here.”

To prevent legionnaires, workers must regularly clean and disinfect cooling towers, test the water for the bacteria, and if it produces a positive result, report it to the local health department, Pruden said.

In New York City, the health department’s testing for legionella in water in cooling towers decreased dramatically before the 2025 outbreak, according to the Gothamist.

During the first six months of 2017, the first year of inspections, the agency inspected 3,190 towers; during the same period in 2025, the city inspected 1,167 towers.

A health department spokesperson told the Gothamist that the decrease happened because of a staffing shortage.

In May, the city announced it would allocate an additional $13m in fiscal year 2027 for cooling tower inspections – which includes funding to hire 23 water ecologists – and require building owners to test for the bacterium every 31 days in which the cooling towers are operating, the strictest requirement in the country, according to the city.

After the latest outbreak, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, approved legislation that requires biannual cooling tower certifications and increased penalties from $10,000 to $12,500 for any violations that result in a serious illness or death. Virginia Maloney, a city council member, also introduced legislation to require building owners to clean their cooling towers at least three times annually, rather than just two.

“With any regulation, there is a carrot and a stick,” Pruden said. “The carrot is we hope that building owners and operators understand that they are saving lives by maintaining these systems as they should be. The stick is there are penalties if they don’t.

“I don’t know if that [additional penalty] is high enough,” Pruden added.

Dedicating additional funding to inspections could also be difficult for a city that is projected to face an $8.8bn budget gap in fiscal year 2028, according to the city comptroller.

The effort to increase vigilance against legionella comes as global temperatures are increasing and people turn on air conditioning more, which could lead to increased risk of the disease.

As people use the machines more, they become less efficient, and as temperatures rise outside, the harder they must work to reject heat, said Jeffrey Siegel, a professor of civil and mineral engineering at University of Toronto.

“The more heat it’s trying to reject, the warmer that water gets and the greater likelihood you have of legionella,” Siegel said.

Despite the budget constraints, Siegel sees legionella prevention measures as a wise public investment.

“It’s easy to say: ‘Well, that’s a lot of money,’” Siegel said. “But if it stops outbreaks, I’m all for it.”

title: Flooding devastated swathes of Indiana but response is hampered by politics
excerpt:
Record inundations wrecked homes and took seven lives but Trump has not approved emergency aid and the state has cut funds for environmental agencies

It’s been 10 days since the floodwater receded fr...
body_text:
Record inundations wrecked homes and took seven lives but Trump has not approved emergency aid and the state has cut funds for environmental agencies

It’s been 10 days since the floodwater receded from Cambridge City’s main street and yet signs of disaster are all around.

Abandoned cars, toilets and bathtubs are strewn across parks and side streets on a recent visit to the city. Garages have been lifted from their foundations and moved by the rushing water. Dumpsters up and down the street are overflowing with people’s belongings, with red paint sprayed on homes indicating which houses have been cleared by water rescue teams.

Flooding from the Creitz Creek, a tributary of the Whitewater River, has damaged one-third, or about 250, of all houses in this quiet town of 1,700 people in south-east Indiana. About 175 of those homes have experienced significant damage.

“At first, earlier in the morning the water was coming into the basement from the west, and we were fighting it with a pump. We were good. But then, as the river swelled, it started to come back up the opposite direction,” recalls Rick Keasling of what happened on the morning of 12 August.

By the time about 10 inches of rain had fallen by mid-morning – three times the average amount for the entire month of August for the town – the flood waters had risen almost five feet inside his home. He, his wife and dog fled shortly before.

“The dog had to swim to the truck. We’ve lost everything on the first floor and in the basement. All the big appliances,” he says. “We’ve had some water in the basement [in the past] but nothing like this; not even close.”

Record flooding across swathes of central and eastern Indiana have destroyed critical infrastructure, made more than 1,000 people homeless and taken seven lives. In the north-west part of Indiana, hundreds of thousands of people in Gary, the only majority-Black city in the state, were left without electricity for more than two weeks following a derecho storm that pummeled the region on 11 August.

A section of Interstate-70, one of the most important regional highways connecting the populated eastern US with the midwest, was washed away a few miles north of Cambridge City.

All the while, Indiana’s state legislature, where Republicans hold a supermajority, have repeatedly refused to fund climate-related initiatives in the state. While Indiana cut state funding for state environmental agencies by 19% between 2010 and 2024, neighboring Ohio and Michigan increased resources in their states by 19% and 78% respectively.

Twice in recent years Indiana’s senate environmental affairs committee has refused to consider legislation for a climate solutions taskforce for the state. The state’s disaster relief fund stood at just $2m before the flooding (it has since been raised to $5m) and, according to the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, Indiana is one of 18 states with no climate action plan.

“Climate change played a role in the intensity of the event since the warmer atmosphere would have allowed for more vapor to ultimately condense and fall as rain,” says Beth Hall, director of the Indiana state climate office.

“Additionally, the warmer temperatures may have caused the heat dome to be the large size it was and to stick around longer than normal.”

Donald Trump has approved Federal Emergency Management Agency disaster aid for more than 50 counties around Indiana, but with that capped at just $5m, many say it doesn’t go far enough: the cost of this month’s storms and flooding is estimated by state leaders at about $5bn.

Fema, too, has come in for criticism. Indiana’s governor, Mike Braun, submitted a disaster declaration to the federal agency on 21 August, which would allow for the release of millions of dollars in federal support to flood victims, but no response has been received. Fema under the current Trump administration has turned down more than 30 disaster declarations and is taking longer to approve requests when it grants approval.

Meanwhile, Cambridge City has only a moderate risk from flooding, according to First Street, a flood risk non-profit.

But nearly all the properties affected by flooding in the town are located in a Fema flood zone AE, which signifies a high-risk flood area where there is a 1% or greater chance of flooding in a particular year. According to Fema mapping, many buildings, including a former elementary school, are located in a “regulatory floodway”.

In a town where the median household income is about 60% of the national level, many residents have been forced to go without flood insurance due to prohibitively high premiums and deductible charges.

In the aftermath of the flooding, while small businesses can apply for a county grant of up to $5,000, the few that have been able to open their doors are struggling.

“We’ve had some people [come in] but it’s not normal,” says Tami Hall, who runs Vinton House Antiques on Cambridge City’s main street, and which lost most of its basement equipment, including its HVAC system in the flooding.

“I think people think that everything’s closed.”

Sitting on a bench inside the antiques store, Tom Saunders, who serves on the town board in the neighboring community of Lewisville, which was also hit by flooding, says that smaller villages in particular are struggling in the flood’s aftermath.

“I have a gentleman, he’s 69 years old, he lost his mobile home, his four cars, everything. He’s living with me right now. We’re past a week of this and we still don’t know anything,” he says.

Ten days since disaster struck Cambridge City, volunteers are staffing a food truck that serves hotdogs, chips and drinks to about 70 people each day.

Residents have had to deal with looting and Keasling says that while he had some flood insurance coverage, it won’t come close to covering the damage incurred.

“There’s so many people displaced,” he says, as the sound of industrial dehumidifiers whirl through the ground floor of his home, where nothing but the wooden structural studs and floor are left.

“Down in Connersville, they’re tearing down houses today.”

title: Alleged tomb-raiding trio arrested in cross-country cemetery spree 'to steal from the dead,' police say
excerpt: The Orange County Sheriff’s Office in Central Florida say this trio traveled to cemeteries around the country to break into mausoleum niches and empty them of their valuables. (Orange County Sheriff’s...
body_text:
The Orange County Sheriff’s Office in Central Florida say this trio traveled to cemeteries around the country to break into mausoleum niches and empty them of their valuables. (Orange County Sheriff’s Office)

Three alleged tomb raiders from Indiana have been arrested for "disturbing thefts from cemetery niches containing cremated remains" across the "eastern half of the United States," authorities say.

Now law enforcement agencies are urging people to check the cemeteries where their loved ones are interred.

Twenty cases have been identified in Florida alone.

"But detectives believe there could be many more," who just don’t realize they’ve been victimized yet, the Orange County Sheriff’s Office in Florida wrote in a post on X.

MORE THAN 50 BODIES FOUND DECOMPOSING INSIDE CHICAGO FUNERAL HOME AFTER NEIGHBORS COMPLAINED OF 'STENCH'

Angela Christine Garret, left, Drake Lee Milam, center, and Porsche Roschell Bancroft, right, are accused of breaking into mausoleum niches across the country and stealing jewelry left inside as memorials to the dead. (Orange County Sheriff’s Office)

"What a horrible person you are if you decide to steal from the dead," a sheriff’s office spokesman said in a video asking for help identifying the thieves.

"These three people are going to cemeteries, breaking into deceased people's niches, and stealing their family heirlooms."

Within days, Drake Lee Milam, 33, and Angela Garrett, 52, were arrested in Indiana, court records show. And Porsche Bancroft, 32, turned herself in at Florida’s Seminole County Jail.

In court records, Bancroft was identified as the girlfriend of Milam and the daughter of Garrett. Her arraignment is scheduled for Sept. 22 in Sanford, Florida. And a trial has been set for Feb. 8.

Milam and Garrett will be extradited to Florida to face charges, according to the Orange County Sheriff’s Office. But their court documents were not accessible, a representative with the Seminole County Clerk of Court told Fox News Digital.

"All three face a variety of charges, including injuring or removing a tomb or monument; disturbing the contents of a grave or tomb; and grand theft over $20,000," according to a spokesperson for the Orange County Sheriff’s Office in Florida.

PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF STEALING OVER 100 SETS OF HUMAN REMAINS APPEARS IN COURT IN ‘HORROR MOVIE’ CASE

Drake Lee Milam is accused of teaming up with his girlfriend, Porsche Roschell Bancroft, and her mother, Angela Christine Garrett, to crack open mausoleum niches across the country and steal the jewelry and valuables left inside. (Orange County Sheriff’s Office)

A slew of mausoleum surveillance videos appear to show the trio breaking into glass-front niches, where urns of cremated remains and mementos are displayed, then removing items and strolling out, according to authorities.

"They've been everywhere from Oklahoma City to Minnesota to Texas [and] here in Florida," the Orange County Sheriff’s Office spokesman said. "They visited Georgia, Iowa, North Carolina, even so far northeast as to Buffalo, New York."

The accused grave robbers allegedly traveled through Illinois and New Jersey, too, the sheriff’s office said in an email to Fox News Digital.

"Imagine losing your wife or husband and placing their wedding ring, and yours, in the niche – only to have them stolen by thieves looking for an easy payday," the agency spokesman said. "This will not stand. Not in Florida."

Florida police reports list a variety of items missing from cemeteries holding great sentimental and monetary value:

A husband reported his late wife’s niche as missing their his-and-hers gold wedding rings and her Class of 1992 ring from Miami Southridge Senior High School. It was silver with a blue stone.

A wife reported as missing a ring given to her late husband for his 25th anniversary of working for The Walt Disney Co.

A father reported the theft of his daughter’s 1972 class ring with a blue stone.

A wife reported the theft of a 22-inch gold chain with a gold anchor from her late husband’s niche. It had been his wish to be interred with the jewelry, she told police.

‘LEGO BANDIT’ ACCUSED IN BIZARRE $34K SCHEME REPLACING MINIFIGURES WITH PASTA

Surveillance video appears to show suspects breaking into glass-front cemetery niches and removing valuables left with the remains of loved ones. (Orange County Sheriff’s Office)

A family reported missing jewelry they’d left with the remains of a beloved wife and mother, including a gold wedding band, two gold earrings, two gold rings and a gold bracelet.

A husband reported the theft of his wife’s platinum-and-diamond wedding ring and a diamond solitaire he’d given her for their engagement.

The wife of the late Charles Taaffe, former offensive coordinator for the University of Central Florida football team, reported his two gold championship rings had been taken from where his remains were interred.

The sheriff’s office is urging people nationwide to check their loved ones’ burial sites to be sure "cherished items" are still there.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

In Florida, valuables worth a total of $35,000 have been discovered as being swiped from cemeteries in Orange, Seminole and Hillsborough counties, the spokesperson said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"But the dollar amount is not what's important," a sheriff’s office spokesperson told Fox News Digital in an email.

"Having a loved one’s final resting place disturbed and cherished family heirlooms taken is deeply painful, and we recognize that no arrest can undo what these families have experienced."

Detectives are working to identify more victims.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"If you have a family member resting at a cemetery, take a moment to check their niche and make sure the items you placed with them are still there," the sheriff’s office wrote on X.

"And if you have information about this case or believe you may be a victim, please contact Central Florida Crimeline at 800-423-TIPS (8477)."

Fox News Digital attempted to contact all three defendants. Bancroft said her attorney would provide a statement but it was not received before publication. Garrett and Milam did not respond before publication.

title: Silicon Valley exec ignites firestorm after accusing JD Vance of bringing DEI back
excerpt:
Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson highlights efforts to ensure the H-1B program serves its intended purpose of bringing in specialized labor on ‘America’s Newsroom.’

Ankit Gupta, a ge...
body_text:
Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson highlights efforts to ensure the H-1B program serves its intended purpose of bringing in specialized labor on ‘America’s Newsroom.’

Ankit Gupta, a general partner at Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator, is facing backlash after describing Vice President JD Vance’s call for American companies to "hire and train Americans" as a return of "DEI."

"In a win for the woke left DEI is back," Gupta wrote on X.

"No, Ankit. It’s called putting your own citizens first," Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito wrote, arguing that American companies should prioritize American jobs and workers. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon, and Nalin Haley, the son of former South Carolina Gov. and U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley, also publicly pushed back on Gupta’s framing.

Gupta’s X post came in response to Vance’s call for American corporations to hire and train American workers when they need employees.

TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE

Vice President JD Vance listens as a reporter asks a question in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, on Thursday, June 18, 2026, in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

"Y Combinator is a supposed champion of 'Little Tech' but perhaps they’re nothing more than a front for the far left," Ferguson wrote in response to Gupta's post, which has since become private after the CEO changed his social media settings, according to X. "I’m deeply uncomfortable with wealthy investors attacking American workers like this. I’m afraid it’s increasingly obvious to many people that individuals such as this guy do not have the best interests of America and her citizens in mind. The purpose of the American economy is to promote the general welfare of American workers, not provide jobs for the rest of the world."

Ferguson subsequently posted a screenshot of his X account, showing Gupta had blocked him amid the criticism.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY

"It’s now DEI to train and hire Americans? Plenty of data to show that Americans are more than qualified, but corporate greed refuses to pay them respectable wages," Haley added on X following Gupta's post. "You can have a meritocracy in AMERICA but it has to apply to AMERICANS. Otherwise we’re just a globalist entity and not even a country anymore. Ban the H-1B Visa now!"

Fox News Digital reached out repeatedly to Y Combinator and Gupta for comment on his characterization but did not receive a response.

CEO UNDER FIRE FOR MASS LAYOFFS AMID FOREIGN WORKER HIRING SPREE NOW APPOINTED TO FED'S TASK FORCE ON JOBS

Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Andrew Ferguson speaks during the Semafor World Economy Summit 2025 at Conrad Washington on April 23, 2025. (Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)

Dhillon, meanwhile, accused some technology companies and other employers of exploiting visa programs and hiring practices to obtain cheaper foreign labor for jobs she said Americans could perform, including by failing to advertise openings through regular channels and relying on staffing pipelines.

"These are not good business practices; they are not patriotic economic practices; and they are illegal labor practices," Dhillon wrote, adding that the Trump administration "will not allow American employers to discriminate against American workers."

FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

Dhillon added that the Justice Department, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and Labor Department were working together to "level the playing field for U.S. workers."

Harmeet Dhillon speaks at the National Conservative Convention in Washington D.C., Sept. 2, 2025.  (Dominic Gwinn / Middle East Images via AFP) (Photo by DOMINIC GWINN/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

The clash comes as the Trump administration pursues an overhaul of the H-1B visa program, which allows U.S. employers to hire temporary foreign workers in specialty occupations. The Trump administration’s 2025 effort to impose a $100,000 payment on new H-1B petitions through a presidential proclamation was blocked by a federal judge. The administration is now trying a different route, with the Department of Homeland Security proposing a formal rule that would establish a $103,265 fee for cap-subject petitions.

Construction workers juxtaposed beyond an image of an American flag. (Mark Wilson/Getty Images)

The Labor Department has separately proposed changing how wages are calculated in H-1B and related visa programs. The department said the proposal is intended to curb incentives to hire foreign workers at below-market pay and to protect the wages and job opportunities of American workers.

Fox News Digital's Landon Mion contributed to this report.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: West Virginia looks to AI data center boom to help eliminate state income tax
excerpt: NetChoice director of policy Patrick Hedger warns that data center development has become a major flashpoint in key midterm races. He argues that local moratoriums will hurt communities in 5 to 10 yea...
body_text:
NetChoice director of policy Patrick Hedger warns that data center development has become a major flashpoint in key midterm races. He argues that local moratoriums will hurt communities in 5 to 10 years when they realize they missed out on critical tech investments, high-paying jobs, and lower taxes.

West Virginia leaders are escalating the debate over data centers, with Gov. Patrick Morrisey unveiling a seven-point plan developed with lawmakers to reduce and eventually eliminate the state income tax while addressing concerns about natural resources and infrastructure.

The plan comes as data centers are becoming a political flashpoint nationwide, with states looking to cash in on billions of dollars in investment and new jobs while communities raise concerns about utility costs, water use and local control. The massive facilities needed to power the artificial intelligence boom are also driving electricity demand higher, putting new pressure on power grids across the country.

Under the plan, West Virginia would dedicate 50% of revenue generated by approved hyperscale data center projects to reducing and eventually eliminating the state personal income tax, while directing some remaining revenue to counties and infrastructure projects.

"Today, as the world stands on the cusp of a new digital and economic frontier, West Virginia is stepping forward once again to lead, not by repeating the mistakes of other states, but by implementing a proactive, 20-year development strategy on our terms," Morrisey said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

‘BACKYARD BRAWL’ IGNITES AS WEST VIRGINIA'S MORRISEY MOVES TO POACH BLUE STATE RIVAL SPANBERGER'S JOBS

Country roads take West Virginians home across the Virginia state line near Charles Town, where the data center debate has intensified. (Charlie Creitz/Fox News)

The second listed "principle" in Morrisey’s plan says all West Virginians should benefit from data center projects approved through Charleston’s "High Impact Data Center Designation (HIDC)" process and the revenue they generate. The process was established under a separate 2025 state law.

Morrisey’s plan includes "direct tax relief for citizens," with none of the HIDC revenue entering the state general fund.

AN OVERLOOKED RED STATE QUIETLY BUILT ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST COMPETITIVE TAX SYSTEMS

"By law, 50 percent of project revenue is dedicated directly to reducing and ultimately eliminating the State Personal Income Tax," the plan reads.

Counties hosting data centers would receive 30% of the revenue for schools and local government, while 10% would be distributed to all 55 counties and another 10% would fund infrastructure upgrades, including public water systems. Water infrastructure has become a flashpoint across parts of southern West Virginia that have struggled since the coal industry’s decline.

ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY: DATA

State Capitol of West Virginia features Kanawha River. (Visions of America/Joseph Sohm/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"This shared framework gives us the exact blueprint we need to attract billions in private investment, create thousands of high-paying construction and technology jobs, lower taxes for our citizens, and revitalize economically distressed regions, all while preserving the wild and wonderful state we call home," Morrisey said.

But the promise of tax relief comes as some West Virginians are raising concerns about who could bear the costs of the state’s data center expansion.

The bipartisan bill underpinning the governor’s plan also sought to protect utility customers from added costs — a major concern across the Eastern Panhandle, which borders the Washington, D.C. metro area.

MARXIST ORGANIZER LEADS CAMPAIGN AGAINST VIRGINIA AI DATA CENTER AS FOREIGN INFLUENCE CONCERNS MOUNT

A West Virginia welcome sign greets travelers leaving the East River Mountain Tunnel on Interstate 77 near Princeton, W.V. (Fox News/Charles Creitz)

"No Data Centers" signs are becoming common along roads in Jefferson and Berkeley counties and neighboring Clarke County, Virginia, as residents point to nearby Loudoun County, Virginia, where sprawling data center development has increasingly pushed up against residential subdivisions and commercial centers.

"We are a cautionary tale for the rest of the country," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., of Ashburn said in recent remarks critical of the data center explosion. "[I]f my district were a country, it would have more data centers than almost every other country in the world."

TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION

Back in West Virginia, some state lawmakers are pushing for additional safeguards as data center development accelerates.

West Virginia House Minority Leader Sean Hornbuckle, D-Huntington, was listed as a sponsor of the 2025 bill that helped set the plan in motion but recently said the law should be amended to allow some local control over data center development.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

"We are not going to allow a hostile takeover in our communities. It’s not going to happen on our watch," Hornbuckle said in June, according to the Steubenville Herald-Star.

"We all know what House Bill 2014 did, and it’s setting a very dangerous precedent in the state of West Virginia, [where] we all know we love our property rights," he added.

But Morrisey emphasized in comments to Fox News Digital that "all West Virginians must directly benefit from data center revenue."

"By statute, 50% of the proceeds … will be dedicated to directly reducing and ultimately eliminating the state income tax."

"[It’s] very powerful [and] it’s going to benefit many, many West Virginians."

West Virginia income taxes have already been falling. Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.V., signed a record 21% cut while serving as governor, and Morrisey followed with another 5% reduction this year. The top marginal rate stands at 4.58%.

A spokesperson for West Virginia House Speaker Roger Hanshaw said the plan came from the governor’s office but echoes what the legislature enacted in the 2025 law.

An Amazon Web Services data center in Stone Ridge, Virginia, on July 28, 2024. Data center developers in Northern Virginia are asking utility Dominion Energy Inc. for as much power as several nuclear reactors can generate as artificial intelligence helps drive up electricity demand. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)

Hanshaw has supported data center development in West Virginia, previously telling the Warren Tribune-Chronicle that Charleston is "not only working with industrial partners as friends and allies to grow and diversify an economy, but also to regulate appropriately industries that are important to the communities in which they're situated to the people of West Virginia and to the residents that we all collectively represent."

Morrisey’s plan also focuses on power grid reliability, requiring data center developers to work directly with PJM and other interstate grid operators. The plan also casts data centers in West Virginia as strategic infrastructure with national security implications in the nation’s competition with China.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Jimi Hendrix’s final words to roadie revealed after violent Hells Angels clash
excerpt:
Carlos Santana recalls the moment he impressed Jimi Hendrix

It was supposed to be another stop on the road for Jimi Hendrix — but a festival marred by violence and chaos would become the rock legend'...
body_text:
Carlos Santana recalls the moment he impressed Jimi Hendrix

It was supposed to be another stop on the road for Jimi Hendrix — but a festival marred by violence and chaos would become the rock legend's final official concert performance.

Eric Barrett, who was Hendrix's roadie and confidant from 1968 to 1970, has written a memoir, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." Barrett went on to spend nearly five decades working behind the scenes with other iconic artists, including Madonna, David Bowie and Aerosmith.

"We were playing on the Isle of Fehmarn, and the Hells Angels had taken over," Barrett recalled to Fox News Digital. "There was no control. It was a scary place to be. We had two cars there waiting to get us off the island and go back to London. But the Hells Angels didn't want us to get off the island. They wanted the boys to stay and party. And then it got violent."

PAUL MCCARTNEY REVEALS HOW A 'HAPPY' TEEN HITCHHIKING TRIP WITH GEORGE HARRISON DELIVERED A SHOCK

Jimi Hendrix is the subject of a new book by his roadie and tour manager, Eric Barrett, titled, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." (David Redfern/Redferns)

According to Barrett's book, hundreds of Hells Angels descended on the island and took over the venue. He wrote that many fans who had been camping out were "beaten and robbed" as festival security was chased off. Hendrix, he said, took one look at the mayhem and retreated to his room "alone, sober." The outlaw motorcycle club had taken over.

The next day, Hendrix took the stage and was met with boos. He told the hostile audience, "I don't give a f--- if you boo, as long as you boo in key, you mothers," before chuckling. When he was done, Hendrix told the audience, "Thank you, goodbye. Peace!"

"Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond" by Eric Barrett is out now. (Diversion Books)

Barrett ushered Hendrix and the band off the stage toward the waiting cars. Barrett was eager to get out. But then the bikers surrounded them.

WATCH: CARLOS SANTANA RECALLS THE MOMENT HE IMPRESSED JIMI HENDRIX: ‘I’LL TAKE IT’

"I saw a Hells Angel about to hit [tour manager] Gerry Stickells over the head with this baton," said Barrett. "I put my arm up to take the blow. I nearly passed out from the pain, but imagine if it had landed on Gerry's skull? We managed to get inside the car. Jimi kept looking at me because he saw me take the blow. He just said to me, 'Are you OK, Eric? Are you OK?' He kept asking me if I was OK. That's just the kind of man he was. And... that was the last thing he ever said to me."

Eric Barrett was Jimi Hendrix's roadie from 1968 to 1970. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)

On Sept. 18, 1970, paramedics arrived at Monika Dannemann's apartment at the Samarkand Hotel in London and found Hendrix unresponsive. He was 27.

An exterior view of the former Samarkand Hotel in London, where Jimi Hendrix died in 1970. (Future Publishing via Getty Images)

"I couldn't believe it," said Barrett. "I remember walking around London in a fog. It was a stupid, tragic accident. He took too many of [girlfriend] Monika Dannemann's sleeping pills. She supposedly had these incredibly powerful German tranquilizers. And she said he took nine of them. She couldn't wake him. She called Eric Burdon of The Animals, who was a good friend of Jimi's. He screamed at her, 'Call the f-----g ambulance!'"

From left: Friends Jimi Hendrix, Eric Burdon and Noel Redding. (Sygma via Getty Images)

"What I'm being told was the ambulance guys ... laid him on his back, and he threw up," said Barrett. "He asphyxiated. That was the accident. The pills were the accident. Tragedy was him dying."

Jimi Hendrix performs at the Isle of Wight festival on August 29, 1970. (Jean-Pierre Leloir)

In the book, Barrett wrote, "The paramedics arrived but couldn't revive Jimi. They carried him out on a stretcher to the ambulance, assuring Monika that he was going to be all right. Either lying in bed on his back or on the way to the hospital, Jimi threw up on himself. The post-mortem concluded that Jimi had died of asphyxia while intoxicated with barbiturates."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Monika Dannemann is seen here outside the building where Jimi Hendrix died. (Brian Aris/Mirrorpix)

"... I flashed back to the time I took too much Mandrax, and my girlfriend couldn't wake me up," he wrote. "It was easily done and could've happened to any of us in Jimi's group of friends. That it happened to Jimi himself was heartbreaking. But I've never heard anything to make me think Jimi's death was anything other than what it appeared."

Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix is seen here with Eric Barrett at Heathrow Airport after flying in from New York on his way to the Isle of Wight pop festival. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Barrett firmly rejected the rumors and conspiracy theories that have surrounded Hendrix's death for decades. Among them was an allegation by former roadie James "Tappy" Wright, who wrote in his 2009 memoir, "Rock Roadie," that Hendrix’s manager, Mike Jeffery, confessed to killing Hendrix, The Guardian reported.

Barrett strongly disputes Wright's account and rejects any suggestion that Hendrix was murdered.

Manager Michael "Mike" Jeffery is seen outside Marylebone Register Office in June 1965. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

"I don't believe for a second that Mike Jeffery was the cause of Jimi's death," he said. "I just don't believe it. The circumstances don't add up. And I was told by so many people that Tappy only wrote that to try and sell books. But I've never believed it. I will never believe it. I was there, and right now I'm probably the last man standing. All the lads are passing. So no, I wouldn't believe that for a second."

Jeffery died in a plane crash near Nantes, France, in 1973.

Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett are seen here at the Hollywood Bowl. (Chris Boyd)

Dannemann died in an apparent suicide in 1996, two days after she was found guilty of contempt of court in a long-running legal dispute with Kathy Etchingham, another former girlfriend of Hendrix's. She was 50.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

German painter and former figure skater Monika Dannemann holds a palette and brush as she works on one of her paintings in London, England, circa 1970. (Getty Images)

Barrett said that shortly after Hendrix's death, he lied to reporters about Hendrix's drug use.

"I was, what, 24 when he passed?" said Barrett. "I didn't want to besmirch his memory. So I lied. I just wanted people to see him in a good light. But I came to realize as I got older that I didn't have to lie. Yes, he took drugs. Did he take heroin? I've never seen heroin anywhere near him. I've worked on many backstages for almost 50 years. I know it's a drug that has killed a lot of musicians. But I don't believe Jimi was taking it. He smoked pot. He took a lot of LSD. He took pills. But I don't believe he was into heroin."

Eric Barrett watches over Jimi Hendrix as he performs in Zurich. (Johannes Bruell courtesy of the Marcel Aeby Collection)

Looking back, Barrett described Hendrix as "a wild man" on stage. The musician was famous for playing the guitar behind his head and with his teeth. He would also smash guitars and amps during encores and, on occasion, set his guitar on fire. But when the shows were over and audiences had long since left, Hendrix was a "quiet, mild-mannered, polite young man."

Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix plays his Fender Stratocaster with his teeth at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"He talked to everyone," he said. "He was very charming. And he was shy. People were in awe of Jimi. And when he had his guitar around his neck, over his shoulder, he was comfortable. That was his crutch. But I also remember Paul McCartney walking towards him, and he's gasping, 'It's Paul McCartney!' He was just a shy man who didn't know how to take the accolades of his talent."

"At the Shokan House before Woodstock, trying to teach a very stoned Jimi to ride," said Eric Barrett. (Willis Hogan Jr./David Pearcy Collection)

"I have so many memories of that wonderful man," Barrett continued. "I remember we were all staying in Benedict Canyon and it was my birthday. We were all hanging out by the pool, and Jimi came out in no shirt, just velvet pants. He goes, 'Eric, Eric!' I responded, 'Hey Jimi, what do you need?' He smiled and went, 'Happy birthday, man. Here's some money. Go and buy yourself something you really want.' He gave me $500, which was a huge amount back then."

Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett at Benedict Canyon. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)

"I went to North Beach Leathers, a place I'd seen Jimi had bought some clothes from. I bought myself this long leather coat, spent all my money on it. It was the best gift I ever bought. When I came back, he loved it. He went, 'Wow, that's a coat! I wish I had seen that before you.'"

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix performs onstage with his Fender Stratocaster electric guitar at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Barrett said he carries "beautiful memories" of Hendrix. One in particular has never left him.

"With Jimi at TTG Studios in Los Angeles," said Eric Barrett. "He replaced my tambourine with a beer." (Michael Ochs)

"I was on a plane with him after a show," he said. "Jimi looked at me and said, 'Eric, what do you think, will they remember me?' I was flabbergasted. I went, 'Will they remember you? You're huge over here.' But he was so insecure. 'Are you sure, Eric? What if the kids don't come?' I just told him, 'When it comes to success, you have nothing to worry about.' That was Jimi, a gift to the Earth from the Lord. And I miss him."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: JD Vance's new chicken coop puts spotlight on growing American backyard trend that family has 'loved'
excerpt: Matt DuBoise, founder and CEO of Carolina Coops in North Carolina, tells Fox News Digital how the pandemic sparked interest in producing meals at home and why raising chickens provides health, educati...
body_text:
Matt DuBoise, founder and CEO of Carolina Coops in North Carolina, tells Fox News Digital how the pandemic sparked interest in producing meals at home and why raising chickens provides health, educational and lifestyle benefits for families.

Matt DuBoise has built chicken coops for many well-known people, including Mike Tyson and four-time World's Strongest Man Brian Shaw. But when he got the call saying Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance wanted him to construct a Carolina Coop at 1 Observatory Circle, their residence in Washington, D.C., he got goosebumps.

"The rush, the euphoria, it's hard to describe what that feeling is like," DuBoise told Fox News Digital.

DuBoise quickly realized that he and his employees had their work cut out for them.

MORE AMERICANS SEEK EGGS AT HOME AS CHICKEN COOP INTEREST SURGES: WHAT EXPERTS WANT YOU TO KNOW

DuBoise said it was an "amazing opportunity" but came with a tight deadline.

"I can't thank my team enough," he said. "We had to work in the rain almost every single day to get that coop done in time."

The second family is making the most of the new chicken coop.

Matt DuBoise, left, and his Carolina Coops team built a custom Victorian-style chicken coop for Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance. (Carolina Coops)

"Our family has loved having a chicken coop on the property," Usha Vance told Fox News Digital. "Our children have especially enjoyed caring for the chickens as part of their daily routine. The beautifully designed coop fits seamlessly with the Naval Observatory and makes looking after the chickens so easy."

Carolina Coops designs and builds all of its coops by hand at its North Carolina facility. The company crafted a Victorian-style coop for the Vances that was designed to complement the historic house.

FORMER DIETITIAN'S HOMEGROWN FOOD HELPS FAMILY'S HELP AFTER CUTTING GROCERY TRIPS

"You can't miss that turret in the upper right-hand corner" of the house, DuBoise said. "And I went to my chief designer and said, 'Use that turret somehow.' He just said, 'I'm on it.'"

The Vances approved the design right away. Then, DuBoise said, "The real fun began."

"The second family is into it. They didn't just get chickens to be hip."

The large Carolina Coops are either shipped — sometimes around the world — on a pallet or, in this case, broken down methodically, stacked and delivered on a trailer.

"Keep in mind the hen house area is round," DuBoise said. "That made it that much more difficult, but we did it."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Carolina Coops donated the coop, valued at about $120,000, and installed it in June.

DuBoise said he "was kind of starstruck" when he met the Vances.

"When JD came out, he's in a T-shirt that says something about Lake Erie. And then Usha is in overalls," he said. "I was, like, 'Wow, I love this.' They are just such down-to-earth people. It was so much fun to talk to them."

The coop's distinctive round hen house added an extra challenge to the construction and installation process, said DuBoise. (Carolina Coops)

The Vances asked "all the normal questions most people have when they're brand-new to keeping chickens," DuBoise recalled.

Interest in the homesteading lifestyle and keeping backyard chickens has grown in recent years. About 11 million U.S. households kept chickens in 2025, nearly double the 5.8 million households recorded in 2018, according to American Pet Products Association data.

"The second family is into it," DuBoise said. "They didn't just get chickens to be hip. Especially the vice president. I didn't expect him to be so into the chickens, even though it makes sense because he's the one who wanted the chicken coop there. But I was just so happy [with] all the questions he had about them."

The Vance children are also very involved in keeping chickens, DuBoise revealed.

"They love those chickens," he said. "The second lady has an initiative for childhood literacy, and [the Vance children] painted their favorite books on some bricks for the coop-scaping art. Usha told us her children love to come out and read to the chickens."

Carolina Coops are built to accommodate modern standards, DuBoise said. People can have chickens and still go on vacation, for example.

DuBoise said the vice president showed a strong interest in learning about raising and caring for chickens. (Carolina Coops)

"I want everyone to be able to have a chicken coop — and we have a chicken coop for everyone, even people in the city," DuBoise said.

Carolina Coops recently donated a coop to a school in Harlem.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Their chickens are just thriving, and the kids are having so much fun," DuBoise said.

There's an "awakening" happening across America regarding the food industry, and the lessons learned from the pandemic have prompted people to think about sourcing their own food.

The turret at 1 Observatory Circle served as inspiration for the Vances' custom chicken coop, pictured here, DuBoise said. (Carolina Coops)

There are many advantages to homegrown eggs beyond their function as a reliable food source, DuBoise said.

"It's so much healthier for you when you're eating those fresh, backyard eggs," he said.

Chicken coops are also a place where families can come together to clean, handle the chickens and collect the eggs, DuBoise said.

"It's also such a great classroom for the kids," he added. "So I just absolutely love what the chicken coop and having chickens can do for families."

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Switzerland rave shooting kills 1, injures 5 as police hunt those responsible
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 22-year-old woman was killed and five other people were wounded in a shooting early Sunday at a rave in northern Swi...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 22-year-old woman was killed and five other people were wounded in a shooting early Sunday at a rave in northern Switzerland, authorities said, as police launched a large-scale search for those responsible.

The shooting happened in the Schachen area of Aarau, the capital of Switzerland’s Aargau canton, where the "Aarau Rave VOL. 7" was being held at a horse-racing track, according to Swiss broadcaster SRF.

Aargau cantonal police said the woman died from her injuries at the scene. Four men and another woman, all between the ages of 24 and 27, were taken to hospitals with injuries ranging from minor to serious.

All six victims are residents of Switzerland, police said.

ONE DEAD, 6 INJURED AFTER GUNFIRE ERUPTS AT UNSANCTIONED CALIFORNIA PARTY THAT DREW HUNDREDS: SHERIFF

Police officers patrol a street in downtown Aarau, Switzerland Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026, following a shooting at a rave. (Michael Buholzer/Keystone via AP)

Police spokesman Pascal Wenzel told SRF that authorities were alerted to the shooting shortly after 2:30 a.m. The event had been scheduled to end at 2 a.m., according to SRF, which cited information from the organizers’ website.

Authorities said the perpetrator or perpetrators remained unidentified and that possible motives and the circumstances surrounding the shooting were still unclear.

Police officers block a street near the Schachen horse racing track in Aarau following a shooting at a rave event near Aarau, Switzerland Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Michael Buholzer/Keystone via AP)

A large area surrounding the horse-racing track, swimming pool and nearby sports field was cordoned off as police searched the area. Authorities also increased their presence elsewhere in Aarau as a precaution and urged members of the public to stay away.

ALL 12 VICTIMS STABLE AFTER SHOOTING NEAR FESTIVAL AS TOLEDO POLICE PURSUE MULTIPLE LEADS

Armed police officers patrol near the Schachen horse racing track in Aarau following a shooting during a rave event near Aarau, Switzerland, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Michael Buholzer/Keystone via AP)

The response included police officers, firefighters and several emergency medical services, according to SRF. The broadcaster reported that a cantonal disaster-response unit, the Argus police special unit and a Swiss military Super Puma helicopter were also involved.

Police in neighboring Germany were also assisting with the search as part of routine cross-border cooperation, a spokesman in Freiburg told the German news agency dpa, according to SRF.

Police appealed to witnesses to provide investigators with videos or photographs from the event and established an information line for relatives and eyewitnesses.

Armed police officers patrol near the Schachen horse racing track in Aarau following a shooting during a rave event near Aarau, Switzerland, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Michael Buholzer/Keystone via AP)

Swiss DJ Tekibo, who performed at the rave, later wrote on Instagram that what happened was "absolutely heartbreaking" and said raves should be places of freedom and safety. He also said he had lost an "important friend," though SRF reported that it was not clear whom he was referring to.

Police said their investigation and search operation remained ongoing.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Bradford Betz is a Fox News Digital breaking reporter covering crime, political issues, and much more.

title: Israel’s Ben-Gvir lauds harsh conditions for Palestinian female prisoners
excerpt: Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has posted footage from a prison holding Palestinian women on social media, boasting that he is responsible for the harsh conditions imposed on them....
body_text:
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has posted footage from a prison holding Palestinian women on social media, boasting that he is responsible for the harsh conditions imposed on them.

The video, posted on Ben-Gvir’s X account on Sunday, shows him entering a section holding female prisoners and confronting them about their complaints regarding detention conditions.

One prisoner tells him: “This is our third day without showering. We are not receiving medical treatment, and our clothes are not clean.”

Ben-Gvir responds: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”

In a post accompanying the video, the far-right minister wrote that the “whining” of prisoners over their conditions would not influence him, arguing that Israeli captives held in Gaza had not enjoyed adequate conditions.

“I’ll continue to lead a policy of the bare minimum of the minimum,” he said.

Gaza’s Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs condemned Ben-Gvir’s visit, saying the filming of female prisoners amounted to intimidation and humiliation.

It said his entry into the women’s section of the facility was “not an inspection visit”, but rather a “political spectacle and public incitement against the female prisoners” aimed at intimidating them and breaking their will in front of cameras.

The Palestinian agency said Ben-Gvir’s remarks showed that conditions inside Israeli prisons were part of what it described as a systematic policy of retaliation based on “humiliation, torture, starvation and deprivation”.

The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society also condemned the footage, telling Al Jazeera that Ben-Gvir’s filming and publication of the women constituted “an assault on their human dignity”.

It said hundreds of testimonies from released detainees and prisoners had documented serious abuses inside Israeli prisons and detention facilities.

Since becoming national security minister in late 2022, Ben-Gvir has pushed for tougher conditions for Palestinian prisoners, including reducing food and water supplies, restricting family visits, limiting shower times and removing privileges inside prison sections.

He has also overseen the transfer of hundreds of Palestinian prisoners between facilities.

Ben-Gvir has previously rejected efforts to improve conditions for prisoners. In 2025, he publicly opposed an Israeli court ruling requiring authorities to ensure Palestinian prisoners received adequate food, insisting that harsh conditions should continue.

According to the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs, about 9,400 Palestinians are currently being held in Israeli prisons, including 88 women and more than 350 children.

title: Dodgers’ Edgardo Henriquez throws fastest strikeout pitch in team history against Tigers

body_text:
Rob Friedman says Mets pitcher Nolan McLean has the filthiest offspeed pitches in the MLB.

A 103.6 mph pitch would be a career-defining moment for nearly any pitcher. For Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez, it is increasingly becoming routine.

Henriquez, 24, froze Detroit Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler with a 103.6 mph front-door sinker in the eighth inning that clipped the edge of the strike zone for a called third strike. Dingler quickly challenged the call.

"Got him looking! A 104-mile-per-hour sinker," the television broadcaster announced.

Edgardo Henriquez (60) of the Los Angeles Dodgers pitches against the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park in Detroit, Michigan, on Aug. 29, 2026. (Zack Belsky/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

The review seemed to underscore the moment. Statcast clocked Henriquez’s sinker at 103.6 mph and 2,439 rpm.

According to MLB pitch-tracking data dating to 2008, it was the fastest strikeout pitch ever thrown by a Dodgers pitcher. The record-setting sinker was a highlight in an otherwise difficult 2-1 loss for Los Angeles.

BREWERS' FLAMETHROWER JACOB MISIOROWSKI LIGHTS UP RECORD BOOKS WITH TRIPLE-DIGIT SPEEDS IN GEM VS YANKEES

Henriquez already owned 14 of the Dodgers’ 16 fastest recorded strikeout pitches and 22 of the team’s fastest pitches overall. His 103.6 mph sinker Saturday matched a career high he first achieved during a June 2 matchup with the Arizona Diamondbacks.

Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Edgardo Henriquez (60) looks in for a sign during a game against the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park in Detroit, Michigan, on Aug. 29, 2026. (Zack Belsky/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Baseball Savant lists Henriquez’s average sinker at 100.8 mph this season and his four-seam fastball at an average of 100.5 mph. While most relievers strive to reach 100 mph, the right-handed flamethrower operates at that level with regularity.
