title: Nearly 1,400 missing, mostly tourists, after Nepal-Tibet flash flood kills at least 270
excerpt:
Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims

Have you been affected by the flash floods?

Rescuers are searching for nearl...
body_text:
Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims

Have you been affected by the flash floods?

Rescuers are searching for nearly 1,400 people, most of them tourists, who are missing after a catastrophic flash flood hit Nepal and Tibet, thundering down valleys, obliterating entire villages and killing at least 270 people.

Efforts to locate those missing – including hundreds of people from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and almost 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. Trucks were upended and houses, roads ⁠and power projects swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.

Rescue teams have found bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people have been transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care. By Thursday morning, the Nepali army had rescued more than 100 people from flood-affected areas by helicopter.

David Fisher, the head of the Nepal delegation of the International Federation of the Red Cross, said entire villages and market areas had been wiped out.

In the affected areas, houses, trees and vehicles were submerged or buried in mudslides. Helicopters hovered overhead all day, helping to rescue survivors.

The power, volume and speed of the surging waters gave little time for anyone to flee.

People from the hard-hit areas of Nuwakot and Dhading were seen gathering outside a Nepali army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.

Police were recording the names of the missing just outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity due to damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.

The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was virtually wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives live there. Desperate for information, he travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family.

“There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”

Almost 600 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted were 177 from India, 63 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.

Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.

Police in Nepal said 270 ⁠bodies had been recovered by Thursday afternoon local time, while Chinese state media reported three dead on the Tibet side of the border.

Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.

Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.

An initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery indicated a landslide of ice and rock triggered the debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, about 12 miles (20km) north-east of the Nepal-China Rasuwagadhi border crossing, Nepal’s national disaster authority said. Experts say the risk of such events is compounded by the extreme topography of the Himalayas.

People shared harrowing stories of how they managed to survive. “I started running. Then a wall of water came thundering down as if it was an earthquake,” said Bibek Kumal, a labourer who was working downstream from the worst-hit Rasuwa district, near Nepal’s Himalayan border with China’s Tibet.

From his hospital bed, Kumal said the torrent swept him downstream amid mud and debris but he survived by clinging to a mango tree. “Had there been no mango tree, I would ‌have been washed away to death,” he said.

Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor who was being treated at a small hospital, said: “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us. As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher.

“I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take ⁠her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud. Four or five hours later, a helicopter came to rescue me. My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud. She’s gone.”

The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, said UN teams and partners were mobilising supplies and personnel to support communities affected by the disaster. The US government said it would provide $500,000 in emergency assistance.

Tibet government officials deployed nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s official Xinhua news agency said.

The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, travelled to the affected area on the China-Nepal border on Thursday to oversee search efforts there.

The tour company Himalayan Glacier said 47 people, including two children, were missing from one of its groups in Nepal. Among them were 15 Australians, 10 Canadians, nine Nepalis, eight Americans, two Britons, two Singaporeans and one Russian-American dual citizen, its managing director, Sanket Pandey, said.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with those concerned about their loved ones, and that getting information about the status of missing people remained difficult.

title: Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say
excerpt:
Aerial footage shows floods on Nepal-Tibet border

Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier as the cause of the flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, highlighting the issue of r...
body_text:
Aerial footage shows floods on Nepal-Tibet border

Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier as the cause of the flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, highlighting the issue of rapidly melting Himalayan ice, scientists have told the BBC.

Initial reports of an earthquake led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the flood that has killed at least 177 people.

However, the US Geological Survey then clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.

The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.

Dr Simon Cook, a glacier expert with the University of Dundee, told the BBC his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.

He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a northwesterly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.

Scientists say a collapsed glacier near the Langtang Lirung peak likely caused the disaster

More than 800 missing in Nepal as authorities say glacial collapse triggered flash flood

People pulled from mud in Nepal after deadly flash floods

What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods

Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border

An analysis , externalby the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental scientific institution, found there could have been "an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude area".

This caused a "large volume of ice and rock debris" to enter the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, which in turn generated a sudden surge in the river carrying water, sediment and large boulders downstream.

The centre found that water levels in rivers downstream rose between seven to nine metres within a span of 30 minutes, and several water monitoring stations were washed away or damaged.

Mike Searle, a professor of earth sciences at Oxford University, said that this whole process - from landslide to flood - could have taken hours or even days.

"The sheer wave of debris suggests there could have been a landslide first; the water built up, dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC.

The topography of the area could have also exacerbated the flood. Searle pointed out that Langsang Lirung sits on the crest of the high Himalayas and there are "incredibly steep valleys" on both sides of the mountain, which could have funnelled the water at higher speeds.

Images from the scene show the steep sides of the affected valley

It is still unclear what caused the glacier to collapse on Wednesday.

Searle said that Langsang Lirung, like the rest of the Himalayas, has been slowly rising due to long-term tectonic movement, where one plate has been pushing another plate up. "It's like putting a jack under the car, and then jacking it up."

"As the mountain is rising, the glacier gets steeper and steeper, and it's inevitable that parts of it fall off."

But usually these are smaller chunks which temporarily block the rivers, and are easily flushed out, he said. However, in this disaster, the whole glacier seems to have collapsed "in one go", which Searle said is "very unusual". "These floods happen all the time, but not at this scale."

He said Wednesday's event likely happened because of "two different processes - tectonics with the Himalayas uplifting, and then climate change with increasingly high temperatures and melting of glaciers.

"The whole thing is combining to form these catastrophic disasters that we are now seeing at a regular basis."

Scientists for years have warned of melting ice and permafrost, which is centuries-old frozen soil, in the Himalayas due to climate change.

One analysis released by ICIMOD, external earlier this year found that the Hindu Kush Himalaya glaciers are now losing ice at double the rate since 2000. This in turn exacerbates dangers such as flooding.

Dr Cook pointed out that there have been similar incidents of floods and landslides caused by glacier collapses in India, Switzerland and Italy in recent years.

In 2021, a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people. Scientists later estimated that the impact of the collapse was equivalent to 15 atomic bombs.

Even in Nepal, the same region saw flooding last year caused by a glacial lake in Tibet bursting.

Mohd Farooq Azam, a specialist with ICIMOD, said the increasing frequency of hazards in the cryosphere - or the frozen parts of the Earth - "is becoming more visible than ever before. The pace of change is so rapid."

While it is difficult to say whether any single event is caused by climate change, "when you look at the pattern of these events, you do think climate change could have an impact," said Dr Cook.

"The logic is that with a warming planet, you will see shrinking glaciers, lots of snow melt. The permafrost that is partially holding some mountainsides together is warming and thawing and degrading."

"So you are going to get more landslides, debris flows, glacial meltwater, lake outbursts, glacier collapses, because climate warming ultimately destabilises these high mountain environments."

title: Search on for at least 33 Britons missing after flash floods in Nepal and Tibet
excerpt:
Rescue teams are searching for nearly 1,500 missing people, mostly tourists, after floods kill at least 165

Rescue teams in Nepal are searching for at least 33 British nationals who are among those m...
body_text:
Rescue teams are searching for nearly 1,500 missing people, mostly tourists, after floods kill at least 165

Rescue teams in Nepal are searching for at least 33 British nationals who are among those missing after flash floods ravaged its border with Tibet, killing at least 165 people.

Nearly 1,500 people are missing, the majority of them tourists, authorities have said, after a glacier collapse triggered devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, roaring down valleys and razing entire villages.

Tour company Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – travelling with the company.

Tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said a 13-year-old girl was among the missing British nationals, as well as two Irish citizens. They were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash and crossing into Tibet from Nepal when they became trapped at the border as the flash floods struck.

The other missing British nationals include a 13-year-old girl, three men aged 65, 64 and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63 and 65, according to travel logs.

The president of the Nepal Centre for Disaster Management, Bishal Nath Upreti, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the flash floods were like a “tsunami from the sky”.

He said: “It’s a huge debris, and in fact, after the 2015 earthquake, this is one of the largest disasters that we have [had] in Nepal.

He added: “It was such a huge amount of water. You can imagine it is 20 million cubic meters excess water on the river… Villages and villages along the almost 40 to 50 kilometres were completely wiped out.”

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the number of missing people had risen from 403 to 826, with the preliminary death toll standing at 165.

The Nepal Tourism Board said on Wednesday that 33 UK citizens were among the 466 foreign nationals unaccounted for out of 579 travellers missing from the affected area.

At least three people had died in Tibet, according to China’s state broadcaster CCTV, while the Xinhua news agency said 558 people were unaccounted for in the region.

Rescuers are racing to locate people missing in the mountainous Rasuwa region, which borders China’s autonomous region of Tibet and is popular with trekkers and pilgrims, including the hundreds of nationals from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

UK goverment minister Pat McFadden told Times Radio that the picture was “not completely clear yet”, with “many, many more” people understood to be missing than those reported by the Nepalese authorities, and no clear figures from the Chinese side yet.

He added: “In terms of missing Britons, my colleague the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has posted on social media phone numbers that people can call for further information. We are working as closely as we can with the Nepalese authorities. Consular assistance is available to families.

“But it’s a fast-moving picture. We don’t have a full picture yet of the numbers missing, and we will do everything we can to help the Nepalese authorities find them, and to support the families of those who are missing.”

McFadden told Sky News that the UK was likely to financially support Nepal’s flood response. “It’s in every country’s interest to do this. There’s been a number of international offers to the Nepalese government in the last few days, and of course the UK will play its part in that,” he said.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said it was “deeply saddened by the loss of life and devastation caused by the floods in Nepal”.

It added: “British nationals in Nepal should follow local authority advice and exercise caution while travelling. For consular assistance call (+44) (0)207 008 5000 or (+977) (0)14237100.”

title: 'View' host Ana Navarro rejects Hunter Biden's assertion that Trump is 'already' a 'dictator'
excerpt:
"The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared to disagree with Hunter Biden after he claimed that President Donald Trump was a dictator despite making similar claims.

"The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeare...
body_text:
"The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared to disagree with Hunter Biden after he claimed that President Donald Trump was a dictator despite making similar claims.

"The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared to disagree with former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, after he accused President Donald Trump of being a dictator on her podcast Monday.

In the second half of a two-part interview on "Bleep! with Ana Navarro," Hunter Biden told Navarro that the U.S. has "already" lost democracy under Trump regardless of who wins the midterm elections.

"He is a dictator ... in no uncertain terms," Biden said. "Everybody understands this. He has broken the system. It is gone. It is completely broken."

'THE VIEW' CO-HOST LAUDS HUNTER BIDEN AS 'RIVETING' AFTER PODCAST SIT-DOWN, CALLS HIM 'BIGGEST TROLL'

"The View" co-host Ana Navarro argued that President Donald Trump "would like" to be a dictator but stopped short of agreeing he already was one. (Lou Rocco / Getty)

"They’re going through confirmation hearings right now of his personal attorney to be the attorney general of the United States," he continued. "He has used his position as President of the United States to jail, to attempt to jail journalists. He is prosecuting Don Lemon for following someone into … and we’re not all sitting here up in arms?"

Trump's former personal attorney and Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was confirmed as attorney general earlier this month. Lemon, meanwhile, has pleaded not guilty to federal civil rights charges stemming from his coverage of an anti-ICE protest that disrupted a church service in St. Paul, Minnesota. Lemon maintains he was there as a journalist.

"He goes on Air Force One, and he gets a question that he doesn’t like, and he looks at a veteran woman reporter and tells her to ‘Be quiet, piggy,’ and no one says anything," Biden added. "We have lost our democracy at this point."

"Can you imagine if your father had ever done that?" Navarro asked.

"I can't even remotely imagine," Biden said.

However, Navarro stopped short of calling Trump a dictator, though said "he would like to be."

"I fled dictatorship," she said. "I fled the Sandinistas in 1980, and I live in Miami, where there’s a lot of Cuban-American exiles, a lot of Venezuelan-American exiles, a lot of Haitian-American exiles. I think he definitely would like to be a dictator and have no guardrails, have no pushback. I still have some hope in some of the courts. And I think we still have elections. And despite the fact that there's threats against the free press, we still do have the free press."

ANA NAVARRO AND FORMER TRUMP CAMPAIGN AIDE CLASH OVER PRESIDENT'S COMBATIVE EXCHANGES WITH FEMALE JOURNALISTS

The White House dismissed Hunter Biden's claims that President Donald Trump was a "dictator." (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

She argued that the larger problem was a lack of congressional oversight from Republicans to balance out Trump's power and questioned if Democrats retaking the House and Senate could make a difference.

"I don't know that they have the stomach to do some of the s--- that Republicans do without any qualms," Navarro said.

Navarro's response on the podcast marked a stark departure from her past comments on Trump, where she warned of him behaving like a dictator and suggested his actions were dictatorial.

During her speech at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, Navarro compared Trump to several communist dictators.

"Let me tell you what communist dictators do, and it's never just for one day," she said at the time. "They attack the free press. They call them the enemy of the people like Ortega does in Nicaragua. They put their unqualified relatives in cushy government jobs so they can get rich off their positions like the Castros do in Cuba."

"And they refuse to accept legitimate elections when they lose and call for violence to stay in power like Maduro is doing right now in Venezuela," Navarro continued. "Now, you tell me something, do any of those things sound familiar? Is there anybody running for president who reminds you of that?"

DAN RATHER AMONG 200 JOURNALISTS DEMANDING TRUMP BE CALLED OUT AT WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER

Ana Navarro previously compared President Donald Trump to communist dictators during her DNC speech in 2024. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

As recently as May, Navarro accused Trump on "The View" of being a "wannabe dictator" or having "small dictator energy" after a golden statue of Trump was installed at Trump National Doral golf course following the PGA Tour's Cadillac Championship.

Fox News Digital reached out to Navarro for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, however, dismissed the suggestion that Trump was a dictator and mocked Hunter Biden in a statement.

"Just like sleepy Joe, Hunter Biden’s brains are fried potatoes. We wish him and his family well during this difficult time," Ingle told Fox News Digital.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

title: Anthony Albanese says 34 Australians among hundreds of people missing in deadly Nepal flash floods
excerpt:
Powerful floods in Himalayan border area sweep away houses, roads and bridges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Doze...
body_text:
Powerful floods in Himalayan border area sweep away houses, roads and bridges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dozens of Australian tourists are reportedly missing in the deadly flash floods that swept through the Nepal-Tibet border, as the Australian government says it is urgently working to confirm their welfare.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said on Thursday morning there were 34 Australians missing.

According to the Nepal Tourist Board, as reported by Press Association, at least 403 people have been reported missing, with 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for.

According to the tourist board, 203 of the missing are male and 200 female.

Also among the missing were 47 people from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from the UK and 24 from Canada, according to the board’s figures.

They include one Australian who was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel.

Albanese said getting information from Nepal was “difficult” and “our thoughts are with all those who will be concerned about their loved ones today”.

He said the government was liaising with local authorities and tour operators to confirm the welfare of Australians in Nepal.

“We extend our deepest sympathies to those affected by the significant flooding in Nepal and Tibet, China,” he said in a statement.

Nepal’s embassy in Canberra has requested urgent assistance from the Australian government in response to the floods.

“We are reaching out to the Australian government and hopefully they will provide assistance to us. We are in communication with them,” said the embassy’s second secretary, Saroj Paneru.

Paneru said the government would be seeking financial assistance, but also technical support as it searches for missing people.

Australians in the region have been urged to follow the advice of local authorities.

In a statement on Thursday morning, Australia’s foreign minister, Penny Wong, said: “The loss of life and destruction caused by flash flooding in Nepal and China is devastating. Our thoughts are with the loved ones of those killed or missing and all affected by this disaster.

“Dfat officials are urgently working to confirm the welfare of Australians in the area.”

She said Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the consular emergency centre.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) said was is aware of a “number” of Australians in the area affected by the flooding, saying officials stood ready to provide consular assistance.

A Dfat spokesperson said: “We extend our deepest sympathies to those affected by the significant flooding in Nepal and Tibet, China.

Earlier, Australia’s ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, had said he was “deeply saddened” by the disaster.

A joint statement issued by the embassies of Australia, Finland, France, Norway, Switzerland and the UK in Nepal, posted on social media overnight by Ernst, said: “We are deeply saddened by the devastating flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts and surrounding areas.

“Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time.

“We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.”

title: HEAR IT: 911 call captures horrifying first moments of deadly shooting at Seattle’s Bite of Seattle festival
excerpt:
Newly obtained 911 audio captures a wounded caller pleading for help and dispatchers reporting multiple victims after gunfire erupted at Seattle’s Bite of Seattle festival. Credit: KCPQ

Newly obtaine...
body_text:
Newly obtained 911 audio captures a wounded caller pleading for help and dispatchers reporting multiple victims after gunfire erupted at Seattle’s Bite of Seattle festival. Credit: KCPQ

Newly obtained 911 calls shed new light on the deadly shooting at Seattle’s famed Bite of Seattle festival, capturing the frantic response as first responders raced to a scene with multiple people down.

"I’m losing blood," a caller who said they had been shot in the back told a dispatcher.

The caller said they did not know who opened fire.

GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED

"I don’t know who did it. I took cover. I see the officers down here," the caller said.

The dispatcher tried to keep the wounded person calm as help was sent toward the water fountain where the caller was believed to be waiting.

"It’s okay. Just breathe. Breathe with me. I’m going to stay with you," the dispatcher said.

Moments later, the caller said they were with an officer.

Other emergency transmissions capture dispatchers and first responders working to assess the scope of the unfolding violence near the Seattle Center Armory.

"Multiple people down at this point," one dispatcher said when asked whether anyone had been shot.

TOLEDO POLICE FOLLOWING 'MULTIPLE LEADS' AS MANHUNT ENTERS 3RD DAY AFTER FESTIVAL SHOOTING

Police officers keep watch after a mass shooting at the Bite of Seattle food festival on July 26, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. Two people are dead and multiple people are wounded. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said one suspect is in custody. (Getty Images)

As reports continued to come in, another dispatcher requested "as many aid units as possible," saying there were at least two people down — "but more than that."

Emergency crews initially treated the area as an active scene while officials worked to determine whether it was safe for responders to enter.

"Let’s treat that as an active scene for now," a dispatcher said.

A dispatcher later said there were "six confirmed gunshot wounds" amid the chaotic response.

MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes attend a vigil for victims the day after a shooting at Seattle Center during the Bite of Seattle food festival on Monday, July 27, 2026, in Seattle. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)

The calls come as Seattle police have offered few public updates on the investigation.

Fox 13 Seattle reported that interim Police Chief Andre Sayles said earlier this month that investigators had developed new information and expected to make an arrest, but he declined to disclose details.

SEATTLE MAYOR'S INTERVIEW CUT SHORT AS STAFF BLOCKS QUESTIONS ON GUN VIOLENCE, SURVEILLANCE

"I think the biggest thing is, you know, it’s going to cause a little bit of frustration, is the integrity of this investigation," Sayles said Aug. 7, according to the outlet. "There’s some information that we have. I want to make sure that we keep the integrity of that investigation close to the vest until we can make the appropriate arrest."

A 15-year-old suspect remains in custody in connection with the shooting.

TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'

The Mayor’s Office said in a statement to the outlet that the administration "continues to work closely with the Seattle Police Department to ensure information about critical events reach the public."

The shooting erupted last month outside the Seattle Center Armory during the Bite of Seattle food festival, near the Space Needle. Three people were killed and four others were wounded, including a 2-year-old boy, authorities previously said.

The dead included a 19-year-old man and a 44-year-old man who were pronounced dead at the scene. A 56-year-old woman later died after she was transported to a hospital in critical condition.

Wilson called the shooting "an act of horrific violence."

"Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection, and joy ended in gunfire," Wilson said at the time.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson listens to an attendee after a vigil a day after the Bite of Seattle food festival shooting at Seattle Center on July 27, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. Three people are dead and four are wounded. (Getty Images)

"No one should have to weigh the risk of being shot before attending an event, gathering with friends, or experiencing their city," she added.

Wilson said officials believed a 15-year-old had opened fire into the crowd, though details remained under investigation. The teen was booked into juvenile detention on suspicion of firearms violations and first-degree assault. No homicide charges had been filed as of the most recent update.

Former Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes said investigators believed gunfire was exchanged outside the Armory after a conflict involving small groups believed to be at odds with one another, leaving bystanders caught in the crossfire.

Investigators initially believed two gunmen were involved. But a juvenile-court document later indicated the detained teen and an acquaintance who was found dead at the scene may have exchanged gunfire with at least one other, unidentified suspect.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Seattle Police Department and mayor's office for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Australia news live: Victoria scraps secret public transport levy; former Treasury chief says WA GST deal might ‘break’ federal system
excerpt:
Ben Carroll announces he will ‘abolish the rail improvement charge’. Follow today’s news live

Nepal flash flood disaster – live updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

T...
body_text:
Ben Carroll announces he will ‘abolish the rail improvement charge’. Follow today’s news live

Nepal flash flood disaster – live updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced he will scrap a levy on public transport users the government secretly introduced to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop.

The report into the first stage of the SRL – from Cheltenham to Box Hill – revealed the government added a 1% levy on public transport fares on top of existing adjustments in line with inflation on 1 January 2025 but did not inform Victorians.

The auditor general said 60% of the revenue earned was meant go to SRL East but the levy was not been named as one of the government’s value capture methods for the project.

Speaking outside parliament, Carroll told reporters:

double quotation markI am a premier who levels with Victorians, and I’m going to level with Victorians today. I will abolish the rail improvement charge. There’ll be a proper cabinet process to come, but it’s my intention and the treasurer’s intention to abolish that charge. I’m a premier taking the state in a new direction. Victorians do deserve better public transport. They also deserve to know what their money is buying.

Asked when he first knew about the levy, he said:

double quotation markThe way this charge was created and implemented, there was a lack of transparency. That is why today I’m announcing I will abolish it.

Nepal embassy prepares request for Australian government assistance

Nepal’s embassy in Canberra is preparing an urgent request to the Australian government for financial and technical support.

The embassy’s second secretary, Saroj Paneru, said every Nepalese government official was working overtime to find and assist people displaced by the devastating floods.

Paneru said the Nepal government was scrambling to calculate the loss and damage caused by the floods and would be urgently seeking international assistance.

double quotation markWe are reaching out to the Australian government and hopefully they will provide assistance to us. We are in communication with them.

First of all, we are just calculating the loss back home. After that, we will have all the details. Then we expect financial, technical and responsive support. We expect all this support in this difficult time for Nepal

We are hoping all international communities and everyone will be providing assistance to us in this very sad time.

Coalition worried about ‘devastating’ Nepal floods

Opposition leader Angus Taylor and Coalition foreign affairs spokesperson Ted O’Brien have also voiced concern about the floods in Nepal and any Australians who may have been caught up in the disaster.

“Our thoughts are with all those affected by the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet, including the families who have lost loved ones and those still waiting for news. We are also thinking of the Australians caught up in this disaster and their families here at home,” Taylor wrote on social media.

O’Brien said in a separate statement: “News coming out of Nepal about horrific flash floods is devastating.”

double quotation markMy thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones and those still missing. We are particularly concerned by reports that Australians are among those unaccounted for and our thoughts are with their families and friends during this incredibly difficult time.

Both men echoed government advice, that Australians in the region should follow the advice of local authorities and contact Dfat’s Consular Emergency Centre if they need urgent assistance on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas.

Qantas profits slip to $2.06bn as US war on Iran adds to fuel bill

Qantas’ pre-tax profits have slipped $330m to land at $2.06bn for the year to June.

The airline said rising jet fuel costs from the US war on Iran added $610m to its fuel bill. It attracted an extra $190m in earnings from customers who switched to Qantas after cancellations on other airlines, with conflict on net costing Qantas $420m for the year.

Qantas and Jetstar domestic contributed a combined $1.44bn in underlying earnings. The company said Qantas’ unit (or per-flight) revenue increased 5% on the two local carriers from March to June. While Government and big business cut back, leisure customers and the Western Australian resources businesses continued to pay for flights.

Jetstar gained 11% more revenue despite increasing its flight capacity just 4%, supported by “value-conscious customers”, the company said. Half of Jetstar domestic customers paid under $150 per flight, it said.

International flights contributed $650m in underlying earnings, falling from the year before thanks to higher fuel costs. Qantas international revenue grew 8%, mostly from increased capacity, while Jetstar International grew its capacity by 11% and won a 14% revenue increase.

Qantas said its loyalty scheme had grown its underlying earnings by 12% in the year, to $625m, with a 6% growth in active members. Uber was the fastest-growing source of points.

Albanese confirms 34 Australians missing in Nepal, saying ‘information is difficult’ to get

Anthony Albanese just confirmed 34 Australians are missing in Nepal, echoing similar numbers from local authorities.

The prime minister said during an event in Dubbo:

double quotation markPeople would have seen some of the footage, which is a truly horrific event. At this point, there are 34 Australians who are missing.

Nepal, you know, is a developing country, it doesn’t have the resources that an event like that would have in Australia.

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced he will scrap a levy on public transport users the government secretly introduced to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop.

The report into the first stage of the SRL – from Cheltenham to Box Hill – revealed the government added a 1% levy on public transport fares on top of existing adjustments in line with inflation on 1 January 2025 but did not inform Victorians.

The auditor general said 60% of the revenue earned was meant go to SRL East but the levy was not been named as one of the government’s value capture methods for the project.

Speaking outside parliament, Carroll told reporters:

double quotation markI am a premier who levels with Victorians, and I’m going to level with Victorians today. I will abolish the rail improvement charge. There’ll be a proper cabinet process to come, but it’s my intention and the treasurer’s intention to abolish that charge. I’m a premier taking the state in a new direction. Victorians do deserve better public transport. They also deserve to know what their money is buying.

Asked when he first knew about the levy, he said:

double quotation markThe way this charge was created and implemented, there was a lack of transparency. That is why today I’m announcing I will abolish it.

The former Treasury secretary Ken Henry says the GST deal benefiting Western Australia is “stupid” and undermines the “integrity of the system of horizontal fiscal equalisation”.

Henry spoke to RN Breakfast this morning amid an ongoing stoush after the Productivity Commission said in an interim report the Morrison-era GST deal was a mistake that should be reversed. Western Australia has responded with fury, and Anthony Albanese said this week there would be no changes to the agreement while he is in power.

Henry, however, said he agreed the GST carve-out was hurting the nation, telling RN:

double quotation markIf a state, the wealthiest state in the nation, can come to Canberra with a begging bowl and get the rest of the country to put money into that begging bowl being held by the wealthiest people in the country, if that’s how this system is going to work, then this system is going to fail. And one day this system is going to break.

Without a high-integrity system of fiscal equalisation, the Australian federation is going to face some pretty serious challenges.

Home buyers have more power but new listings down as owners hold fire

Australia’s spring property season is shaping up to be unusually sluggish, as sellers retreat from a weak market and unsold homes pile up, AAP reports.

New property listings in the four weeks leading up to August 23 were 8.2% below the five-year average, property analytics firm Cotality data shows.

Advertised stock levels remain elevated overall, suggesting homeowners are holding back from adding to an already crowded market.

Sydney is leading the downturn, where new listings were 14% below the five-year average in the four-week period. Similar pullbacks were recorded in all capitals except Adelaide.

‘Reluctant’ approval for Tasmanian datacentre sets marker for national battle

The day before Anthony Albanese secured agreement with states and territories to develop national datacentre standards, a small council in Tasmania was grappling with the existing regulations in the face of strong community opposition to a new AI factory planned for its town.

The George Town council voted 6-1 to approve the plans of Australian developer Firmus to build a 288 megawatt (MW) datacentre at Long Reach, north of Launceston, but said it did so reluctantly.

The AI factory is planned on the former Gunns Pulp Mill site near the Tamar River, and has faced strong opposition from locals. A petition calling to stop the centre going ahead had nearly 6,000 signatures. More than 300 people wrote submissions on the application to the council.

Some photos from Nepal after the massive flooding

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says Dfat officials are ready to provide consular assistance to Australians in Nepal, after the devastating flooding in the country.

A local tourism official said they believed 34 Australians were missing in the area, among hundreds of foreign nationals. Australian officials were not confirming numbers at this stage, and were working to check on the welfare of people they know were in the affected region.

In a statement this morning Albanese urged Australians to listen to Nepalese authorities and said the government was aware of “a number” of people in the area.

“We extend our deepest sympathies to those affected by the significant flooding in Nepal and Tibet, China,” he said.

double quotation markAustralians in the affected area should follow the advice of local authorities. We are aware of a number of Australians in the area and Australian officials are urgently working to confirm their welfare. We are liaising with local authorities as well as tour operators.

We stand ready to provide consular assistance.

The PM said Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas).

Plibersek says government still determining how many Australians in Nepal floods

Tanya Plibersek, the minister for social services, said the federal government is very concerned about the flooding in Nepal.

She said the government was still trying to determine how many Australians are in the area and how many have been affected. Plibersek told RN Breakfast everyone in the region should follow the advice of local officials.

double quotation markThe images are very disturbing indeed. We do know that there are Australians in the area. We don’t know exactly how many.

Macquarie Group dealt a further blow to KMPG when the bank said it would reverse a decision to use the embattled consultancy as its auditor and instead will retain the services of PricewaterhouseCoopers.

In a statement to the ASX stock market yesterday, Macquarie said its decision followed scrutiny of KPMG Australia’s audit process as exposed by the recent parliamentary hearings in the leaking of client data.

Macquarie said it was concerned about KPMG’s “capacity to deliver the audit”, given that “several key members of the proposed KPMG Australia audit team have departed”, and “a culture that transparently discloses issues”.

Good morning, Nick Visser here to pick up the blog. Let’s get to it.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) says it is aware of a “number” of Australians in the area affected by the flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border, saying officials stand ready to provide consular assistance.

double quotation markWe extend our deepest sympathies to those affected by the significant flooding in Nepal and Tibet, China.

Australians in the affected area should follow the advice of local authorities.

We are aware of a number of Australians in the area and Australian officials are urgently working to confirm their welfare. We are liaising with local authorities as well as tour operators.

Australia’s ambassador to Nepal ‘deeply saddened’ by flood disaster

Australia’s ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, says he is “deeply saddened” by the disaster in Nepal.

A joint statement issued by the embassies of Australia, Finland, France, Norway, Switzerland the the UK in Nepal, posted on social media some hours ago by Ernst, says:

double quotation markWe are deeply saddened by the devastating flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts and surrounding areas.

Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time.

We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.

Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, says the government is urgently trying to confirm the welfare of Australians in Nepal, after reports dozens of Australian tourists were among those missing in flash floods.

In a statement issued this morning, Wong said:

double quotation markThe loss of life and destruction caused by flash flooding in Nepal and China is devastating. Our thoughts are with the loved ones of those killed or missing and all affected by this disaster.

DFAT officials are urgently working to confirm the welfare of Australians in the area.

Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas).

South Australian premier Peter Malinauskas has defended national cabinet’s decision to drop strict mandates requiring new AI data centres to be powered entirely by renewable energy.

After a meeting of national cabinet, prime minister Anthony Albanese flagged exemptions for jurisdictions including Queensland and the Northern Territory.

Speaking on ABC’s 7.30 on Wednesday evening, Malinauskas denied the PM had been rolled by state leaders, adding there was a “genuine desire” to manage the national rollout together.

“It’s pretty clear... to any objective observer that the way we’re going to see these datacentres roll out in an Australian context will be powered by renewables, because that is where the generation can come from,” he told host Sarah Ferguson.

double quotation markThat’s where the very large scale of energy is able to be procured at relatively quick speed... we can get renewables online sooner rather than later...

What you saw today was a nationally consistent position, that gas will have a role to play when it comes to the firming of renewables, which has always been South Australia’s view.

Malinauskas noted that different state energy profiles, such as Queensland’s state-owned generation, meant a federal mandate was unnecessary. However, he said all jurisdictions agreed that operators must construct new generation capacity.

double quotation markWe cannot have datacentres connecting to the grid without bringing their own new generation. Water is also clearly a consideration, but, frankly, energy is the main game. And that is accepted by all states and territories.

Dozens of Australian tourists are reportedly missing in the deadly flash floods that swept through the Nepal-Tibet border.

According to the Nepal Tourist Board, as reported by Agence France-Presse, at least 291 foreigners were among the missing, including one Australian who was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel.

However those numbers were quickly updated.

The Nepal Tourist Board said the number of missing people had risen from 384 to 403, with 33 UK citizens among 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for.

According to the tourist board, 203 of the missing are male and 200 female.

Also among the missing were 47 people from the US, 34 from Australia, and 24 from Canada.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

An estimated 34 Australians are believed missing amid devastating flash floods in Nepal. We will bring you more on this soon.

South Australian premier Peter Malinauskas has defended national cabinet’s decision to drop strict mandates requiring new AI datacentres to be powered entirely by renewable energy. More coming up.

Macquarie Group has dealt a further blow to KMPG when the bank said it would reverse a decision to use the embattled consultancy as its auditor and instead will retain the services of PricewaterhouseCoopers. More details shortly.

title: 2026 TOUR Championship picks for East Lake: Why Chris Gotterup, Hideki Matsuyama and Russell Henley stand out
excerpt:
Sam Burns would welcome back golfers like Bryson Dechambeau and Jon Rahm back on the PGA Tour despite committing to LIV years ago

The 2026 PGA TOUR season concludes this week anticlimactically with t...
body_text:
Sam Burns would welcome back golfers like Bryson Dechambeau and Jon Rahm back on the PGA Tour despite committing to LIV years ago

The 2026 PGA TOUR season concludes this week anticlimactically with the TOUR Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta, Georgia. After using a "starting strokes" format from 2019-24 that no one liked — not the fans nor the golfers — this is the second year all 30 guys in the TOUR Championship field will start at even-par.

Fortunately, new PGA TOUR commissioner Brian Rolapp announced a new postseason format earlier this week that will start in 2028. The top 90 players will compete in a final stroke-play event (the first round of the playoffs) before the top 32 advance to a two-week, match-play TOUR Championship.

'PAR TALK': WHY WYNDHAM CLARK DESERVES PGA TOUR PLAYER OF THE YEAR, LIV GOLF'S FINAL HOORAH, AND SCOTTIE SCHEFFLER'S MONEY

Designed by the legend Donald Ross, East Lake is a 7,455-yard, par-70 that has hosted the TOUR Championship every year since 2004. It is a driver-heavy layout with wide fairways, long approach shots and fast Bermuda greens, rewarding players who can bomb it off the tee and create birdie looks with their irons.

This has been a nightmare season for me betting on golf. I've donked off -50.94 units (u) in 2026, finished 4,133rd out of 5,297 entries in the Race for the Mayo Cup (one-and-done league) and I've only hit one outright: Nico Echavarria at the Cognizant Classic (+5900).

That said, I'm trying to minimize the loss and end the season on a high note by backing these three dudes.

The following odds are from when I bet on the golfers listed below. Subject to change.

🇺🇸 Chris Gotterup +2654 (0.75u) and Top-10 with ties +124 (1u), both at Kalshi

🇯🇵 Hideki Matsuyama +3200 at DraftKings (0.63u) and Top-10 with ties +146 at Kalshi (1u)

🇺🇸 Russell Henley +3500 (0.57u) and Top-10 with ties +167 (1u), both at Kalshi

I love Gotterup's price because, as I wrote last week, his game travels. His four wins over the last 13 months have been at different types of courses and conditions: 2025 Genesis Scottish Open, Sony Open in Hawaii, WM Phoenix Open in Arizona, and the John Deere Classic in Illinois.

East Lake is a driver-heavy course that favors distance over accuracy and has easy Bermuda greens, according to Betsperts Golf.

Well, Gotterup ranks second in this field for Strokes Gained (SG): Off-the-Tee (OTT) and second in driving distance over the last 30 rounds. He's picked up more than eight strokes on the greens last week in a T4 finish at the BMW Championship, and Bermuda is his best putting surface.

Chris Gotterup hits his tee shot during the first round of the 2025 TOUR Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta, Georgia. (Matthew Maxey/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Ultimately, we are getting such a good price on Gotterup because he's not as popular as the names ahead of him on the oddsboard, such as Tommy Fleetwood (+1900), Patrick Cantlay (+1700) and Ludvig Åberg (+1450). Yet, Gotterup is playing better than all of them, hence the value.

Hideki let me down last week by tying for 28th at the BMW Championship when I bet him outright (+3000) and to finish in the top 10.

Nonetheless, Matsuyama is getting a better price this week at Kalshi in a field with 20 fewer golfers, and he is third in my model at Betsperts Golf behind World No. 1 Scottie Scheffler and Gotterup.

My model includes stats for East Lake and comparable course history, putting on Bermuda greens, SG: OTT, approach shots from 200+ yards, birdie-or-better rate, etc. Over the last 24 rounds, Hideki is second in this field for total scoring, SG: T2G and SG: Ball-striking (driving and approach), per Betsperts Golf.

Hideki Matsuyama chips onto the seventh green during the 2025 TOUR Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta, Georgia. (Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)

Matsuyama’s short-game held him back last week at the BMW, but he gained strokes with his driver for a seventh straight tournament and with his irons for a fourth straight, according to DataGolf.com.

Driving has been the biggest weakness in Hideki's game, and I'm expecting his short-game to bounce back because he is a wizard around the green.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Granted, Matsuyama's TOUR Championship history is nothing to write home about (his best finish was T4 in 2018). But the 2021 Masters champion is knocking on the door, and this number is too good to pass up.

This is a "good number" for a few reasons.

First, Henley is a native Georgian who played college golf at the University of Georgia, so he’s familiar with East Lake’s agronomy and playing conditions, including Atlanta's hot, sticky summer weather. The Georgia Bulldog has gained strokes on the greens in five consecutive starts and Bermuda is his best putting surface.

Russell Henley hits a tee shot on the 11th hole during the 2025 TOUR Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta, Georgia. (Brett Davis-Imagn Images)

Henley has also finished higher on the leaderboard in the last three TOUR Championships: T14 in 2023, T4 in 2024, and T2 last year. Per DataGolf.com, he’s gained strokes across the board (driving, approach, chipping and putting) in the last two TOUR Championships and tee-to-green (driving, approach and around-the-green) in the last three.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Finally, Henley is underrated and playing better than several guys with shorter odds. He won the Charles Schwab Challenge in May and hasn’t missed the cut in his seven starts since, which includes a T9 at the British Open.

Follow me on X @Geoffery-Clark, and check out my "OutKick Bets Podcast" for more betting content and random rants.

Geoff Clark serves as OutKick’s sports betting guru.

title: Queensland woman gave birth to twins with different parents after surrogacy coincides with natural pregnancy
excerpt:
Both children were born on same day in November 2025 in situation so rare it had not been contemplated by state surrogacy laws

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking...
body_text:
Both children were born on same day in November 2025 in situation so rare it had not been contemplated by state surrogacy laws

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Queensland woman gave birth to twin children with separate sets of biological parents last year, in what is believed to be an Australian first situation so rare it had not been contemplated by state surrogacy laws.

The woman, anonymised in a court judgment, conceived an unplanned natural pregnancy about the same time as she received an IVF embryo transfer under a surrogacy arrangement with another couple.

Both children were born on the same day in November 2025 via caesarean section. There has been no dispute about the children’s parentage – both have been raised separately during the past 10 months by their respective biological parents.

But the situation has required a complex case in the Queensland children’s court because surrogacy rules were written to ban situations where “birth siblings” born from surrogate pregnancies were separated.

The court ultimately ruled that while the children were “gestational twins”, they were not birth siblings for the purpose of surrogacy laws, and made an order that formalised the parentage of the biological parents.

According to the judgment, the couples involved entered into an “altruistic” surrogacy arrangement after being connected by mutual friends.

One couple, anonymised as BNJ and DRJ in the court judgment, had been unable to conceive a natural child because BNJ has a medical condition where she was born without a uterus.

They met DZ and FZ, who already had five children. DZ agreed to become a surrogate, and an embryo was inserted via IVF in April 2025.

About two weeks later, an ultrasound identified that DZ was carrying two foetuses. Subsequent testing revealed that one child, a girl, was the biological child of BNJ and DRJ, and that the other, a boy, was the biological child of DZ and FZ.

The boy was “conceived separately to the … embryo implantation process, and without medical assistance”.
 “[DZ and FZ] had not intended to conceive a child at the time, however that is not to suggest the child is anything other than loved and wanted by [them]”, the court judgment says.

Earlier this year, the parties hired an independent counsellor to prepare a report for court proceedings that would be required to establish that BNJ and DRJ are the parents of the girl.

The report noted “the potential significance of [the children] being born of a twin birth, and that such relationship is likely to carry ongoing emotional and developmental significance for both children over time, notwithstanding the children are being raised in separate households”.

Both families told the counsellor they intended the children “will grow up knowing one another and be raised with an age-appropriate understanding of their place within the wider family network”.

“The parties also demonstrated a shared understanding that openness and honesty regarding [the girl’s] origins and parentage will be in her best interests over time,” the judgment said.

Judge Jodie Woodridge KC considered whether the language of the Queensland Surrogacy Act prevented her from making a parentage order in relation to the girl.

Under the act, a court cannot make a parentage order in relation to only one “birth sibling”, a term defined to mean a “brother or sister of the child who was born as a result of the same pregnancy”. If twins are born as a result of a surrogate pregnancy, any parentage order must be made in relation to both children “and to the same intended parents”.

Woodridge ruled that “in the unique circumstances presented by this case” the boy and girl were not birth siblings and that the act did not prevent the order sought by both sets of parents.

title: Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, dies at age 80
excerpt:
Tim Curry, the British actor best known for his star turn as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at age 80.

Curry, who had struggled with his health ...
body_text:
Tim Curry, the British actor best known for his star turn as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at age 80.

Curry, who had struggled with his health for more than a decade after a debilitating stroke, died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, California, according to a statement released by his longtime manager, Marcia Hurwitz, on Wednesday. No cause of death was disclosed.

The actor appeared in numerous movies, often as a hammy villain. He was nominated at the annual Tony Awards three times for Broadway roles and performed voice work in several animated films and television shows.

But his most iconic role was as Frank-N-Furter, a cross-dressing scientist in the rock musical The Rocky Horror Show, which premiered in 1973 at the Royal Court Theatre in London.

He took the show-stopping role to Broadway and then reprised his turn as Frank-N-Furter in the 1975 film adaptation, alongside Barry Bostwick, Meat Loaf and Susan Sarandon.

“I’m not much of a man by the light of day. But by night, I’m one hell of a lover. I’m just a sweet transvestite from transsexual Transylvania,” Curry sang in one scene, dressed in garish eye shadow, black corsetry and stockings topped with a garter belt.

In a 1975 television interview, Curry noted the risk of having his career defined by the role.

“When I read it, I just thought it was very, very witty and funny,” Curry said of the script, although he confessed to some initial reluctance to star in the role.

“I mean, I was hesitant in that, if it worked, it might be a difficult thing to shake off. But, really, I’ve always thought that [a part] wasn’t worth doing unless you took a risk.”

He later starred as the child-killing monster in the 1990 miniseries It, an adaptation of Stephen King’s horror novel.

That same year, he performed as a Soviet medical officer in the film The Hunt for Red October, based on the Cold War-era novel by Tom Clancy.

Later, he lent sneering gravitas to the role of the double-dealing Cardinal Richelieu in the 1993 adventure movie The Three Musketeers, with Kiefer Sutherland, Charlie Sheen and Chris O’Donnell.

“Tim Curry was someone I cared deeply about, he was someone I loved working with and I am so lucky to have these memories,” Sutherland said in a statement on Wednesday.

Born in the English village of Grappenhall, Cheshire, Curry studied drama at Birmingham University.

Critics argue he did much of his best work on stage. His first Tony nomination came in 1981 for his performance in the title role of Amadeus, a play fictionalising the great composer Mozart’s interactions with his rival, Antonio Salieri.

A second Tony nod came in 1993 for his leading role in the musical My Favorite Year. In 2005, he scooped up a third nomination for his portrayal of King Arthur in the zany musical Monty Python’s Spamalot.

Having a rich baritone voice, he was also in demand as a voice actor for animated films and television shows. He won a Daytime Emmy Award in 1991 for his voice work on the animated series Peter Pan and the Pirates.

Curry withdrew from a British stage production in 2011 due to ill health. In 2013, his agent said that he had suffered a stroke but was recovering “in great humor”.

From then on, he used a wheelchair and reduced his workload. In 2024, however, he returned to the big screen, appearing in the horror film Stream.

Curry, who lived in Los Angeles, never married and had no children. A composer and a singer, Curry also performed with his own rock band and released a handful of albums.

title: World Health Organization says Ebola outbreak in Uganda is over
excerpt:
Uganda has been declared free of Ebola, with the World Health Organization (WHO) confirming that the East African country had passed the mandatory 42-day monitoring period without any new cases.

WHO ...
body_text:
Uganda has been declared free of Ebola, with the World Health Organization (WHO) confirming that the East African country had passed the mandatory 42-day monitoring period without any new cases.

WHO made the announcement at a joint news conference on Tuesday with Uganda’s Ministry of Health.

But the declaration came roughly a month after Uganda had declared that the local outbreak was over, based on its own analysis of the virus’s spread.

“We had assessed the risk, we had assessed the whole chain of transmission and the dynamics of importation of the virus in the country, and we knew that we were free from Ebola,” Diana Atwine, the permanent secretary for Uganda’s Health Ministry, told national broadcaster NTV.

“However, WHO had to wait because that’s the process. That’s the guideline.”

Atwine called on countries that had imposed travel restrictions on Uganda during the outbreak to lift them.

“Unless they have other reasons, they should definitely lift the restrictions off the country, and Ugandans should be free to travel to any country,” she said.

Uganda reported 20 Ebola infections in total, with its last confirmed case recorded on June 21. Two people died from the virus during the outbreak.

The last patient was discharged from Mulago National Referral Isolation Centre on July 16, and the Health Ministry formally declared the outbreak over on July 28.

The outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), by contrast, is accelerating.

Confirmed cases in the DRC reached 5,656 as of August 25, an increase of 72 from a report released one day prior. A total of 2,715 deaths have been recorded, according to the latest government data cited by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.

Ituri province, in the northeast of the country, remains the epicentre of the outbreak, with more than 4,700 people infected.

Uganda shares a border with the northeast part of the DRC, stretching more than 877km (500 miles).

Kasonde Mwinga, the WHO’s representative for Uganda, said in Wednesday’s news conference that the country was supporting treatment and laboratory capacity at two sites across the border, in Aru and Kasenyi, both part of the Ituri province.

Mwinga added that the model for cross-border collaboration could be expanded regionally.

Already, Uganda has announced it would open two additional Ebola treatment centres in the DRC, bringing the total to four.

On Monday, Ugandan and Congolese officials also met in Kampala to review a bilateral memorandum of understanding on cross-border health security.

Kenneth Akiiri, the undersecretary for Uganda’s Health Ministry, called for the WHO and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to mobilise further resources.

“When you are vulnerable and you have littler resources, you are supposed to raise an alarm for help,” Akiiri said in a joint statement.

For his part, DRC delegation head Adelard Lufungula urged strong action to combat the virus. “We want to fight Ebola like a war,” he said.

title: Internet reacts to Georgia schoolteacher's groundbreaking invention, the 'fart corner'
excerpt: Kat Timpf delivers a humorous take on the alleged Sen. Chuck Schumer fart incident. She asserts that America desperately needed a new 'farter' to restore levity after former Rep. Eric Swalwell's previ...
body_text:
Kat Timpf delivers a humorous take on the alleged Sen. Chuck Schumer fart incident. She asserts that America desperately needed a new 'farter' to restore levity after former Rep. Eric Swalwell's previous allegations, which had tainted the humor of such jokes.

The old adage goes, "Necessity is the mother of invention," and nowhere is that perhaps more true than with one Georgia teacher’s invention: the "fart corner."

That's not a euphemism. It is indeed a corner one goes into to release a little gas.

But, like many pioneering inventions and technological breakthroughs, it is dividing — and at times clearing — the proverbial room.

'SPIDER-MAN' SHOWING WAS REPORTEDLY EVACUATED DUE TO SOMEONE'S UNCONTROLLED GAS RELEASE

A Georgia grade school teacher has developed a groundbreaking solution to classroom wind-breaking. (iStock)

According to NBC San Diego, second-grade teacher Candy Sydney-Browning had about enough of her students' inability to control their gas.

"I have a very weak stomach, so I cannot take it," Sydney-Browning told TODAY. "And so I was like, OK, I’m just gonna create this little area over here, and you just get up, you go over there, do your business, come back, and that’s just it."

The "Gusty Winds Area" is stocked with Febreze (veteran move) and gives innocent bystanders a significant buffer zone from wayward odors.

SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT'

But is this a good idea? I mean, are kids so coddled today that they don't understand the kind of intestinal fortitude it takes to hold a gasser in for several periods because you don't want it to escape in front of the girl you have a crush on in your biology class?

While some see it as a way to normalize a bodily function — by the way, why does everything have to be normalized? — fart corners are not winning over those with an old-school view on public flatulence.

I think fart corners are a slippery, rather foul-smelling slope.

Today they're using a fart corner; tomorrow they're crop-dusting entire elevators full of co-workers. (iStock)

Ripping one in front of the class is something that will haunt you for the rest of your life. I could rattle off several names of my grade school chums who did it, but I'm not going to because I'm a gentleman.

So, I think while this teacher's heart is in the right place, that stigma will still be there, just in a different form.

No longer will they be the "smelly kid who farted in class," but instead they'll be the "smelly kid who is constantly getting up to use the fart corner to the point that everyone else is like, 'Seriously, what the hell does that kid eat? Nothing but baked beans and kimchi?!'"

title: Justice Thomas recalls why he wasn't friends with Alito in law school: 'Clarence, you were scary'
excerpt:
Thomas recounted the moment during an interview with Sen. Ted Cruz (Verdict with Ted Cruz).

Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas recently recalled a funny conversation with Justice Samuel Alito abou...
body_text:
Thomas recounted the moment during an interview with Sen. Ted Cruz (Verdict with Ted Cruz).

Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas recently recalled a funny conversation with Justice Samuel Alito about why they weren't friends during their time at Yale Law School.

When asked why they were never friends at the Ivy League institution, Alito told Thomas he was "scary."

Thomas sat down with Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, for a rare interview in which the pair discussed race, politics and a variety of other issues on an episode of the "Verdict with Ted Cruz" podcast, which aired Wednesday.

CLARENCE THOMAS SCORCHES RACIAL LITMUS TESTS POLICING THOUGHT: ‘STAY BLACK AND DIE’

U.S. Supreme Court Associate Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito attend inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 20, 2025, in Washington, D.C. During an appearance on the "Verdict with Ted Cruz" podcast, Thomas recalled that Alito called him "scary," when he asked his colleague why they were never friends while attending Yale Law School. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool via REUTERS)

Thomas was talking about his Supreme Court colleagues when he noted that Alito attended Yale a year behind him.

"He was a year behind you. But you didn't know each other," Cruz said.

"He's a funny guy. He's brilliant. He was always nerdy. Princeton guy like you, right?" Thomas replied.

Thomas then recalled asking Alito about their time at the university: "So I said, 'Sam, how come we were there two years together? Why weren't we friends?'"

JUSTICE THOMAS REVEALS THIS ELITE INSTITUTION IS ‘OFF LIMITS’ TO HIM: ‘THAT'S THE WORLD WE'RE IN’

Supreme Court Associate Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas at the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"'Clarence, you were scary,'" Thomas said Alito told him.

The justice explained that he wore bib overalls and combat boots throughout law school. "I'm so glad they didn't have these phones where you could take a lot of pictures," he added.

During a Wednesday appearance on "The Will Cain Show," Cruz noted that Thomas was a "left-wing radical" in college before eventually embracing conservatism.

"He journeyed to become an extraordinary thinker," Cruz said. "No other justice has overcome so much adversity to reach the very pinnacle of American law."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Trump's lawyers put Dem AG on notice for targeting his family in NY fraud fight: 'Cannot stand'
excerpt:
Former Trump impeachment lawyer David Schoen explains why the cases against former FBI director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James were dismissed on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

On Wedn...
body_text:
Former Trump impeachment lawyer David Schoen explains why the cases against former FBI director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James were dismissed on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

On Wednesday, representatives of President Donald Trump filed a brief in the New York Court of Appeals, arguing that the court should throw out his liability finding in a $464 million civil fraud case that centered on Trump's real estate valuations.

The appeal argues that the case had several legal flaws that should have prevented it from being heard in the first place.

"This case should have never been brought, and the judgment cannot stand," the appeal reads. "This case is extremely unusual; it involves not only reams of improper statements targeting President Trump, his family, and his businesses, but also a decision to apply [New York law] against those targets in a completely unprecedented and unlawful way."

The appeal is the latest instance of President Donald Trump pushing back against what he has characterized as politically charged lawfare that he endured between his two administrations. It also gives Trump a renewed opportunity to push back against some of the penalties that still apply to him from that verdict.

LETITIA JAMES HAMMERED AFTER NY MEDICAID FRAUD UNIT FUNDING FROZEN OVER INEFFECTIVE ENFORCEMENT

NEW YORK, NY - FEBRUARY 16: Attorney General Letitia James speaks during a press conference following a verdict against former U.S. President Donald Trump in a civil fraud trial on February 16, 2024 in New York City. Justice Arthur Engoron ruled against the former president finding him liable for conspiring to manipulating his networth and fining him $335 million and imposing a three year ban from serving in top roles at any NY company. The judge also banned Eric and Donald Trump Jr. for two years as well as a fine of more than four million dollars. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

In 2022, New York Attorney General Letitia James sued Trump, alleging 200 instances of fraud. Specifically, her office alleged that Trump had routinely overvalued properties in New York City in order to secure favorable loans or insurance rates in violation of New York Executive Law § 63(12). The provision instructs the attorney general to prosecute cases of repeated fraudulent or illegal acts.

The law defines fraud as "any device, scheme or artifice to defraud and any deception, misrepresentation, concealment, suppression, false pretense, false promise or unconscionable contractual provision."

As a result, Trump was required to pay $355 million plus interest in damages and was banned from serving as an officer or director of any New York company for two years. He was also banned from applying for loans from any New York bank or financial institution for three years. Although an intermediate appeals court later vacated the monetary award, Trump's lawyers argue the underlying liability finding and the remaining restrictions should also be overturned.

APOLOGIES AND CASH HEADED TO ALLEGED ‘WEAPONIZATION’ VICTIMS IN BILLION-DOLLAR TRUMP SETTLEMENT

NEW YORK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 11: Former U.S. President Donald Trump speaks as he leaves the courtroom during his civil fraud trial at New York Supreme Court on January 11, 2024 in New York City. Trump won't make his own closing arguments after his lawyers objected to Judge Arthur Engoron's insistence that Trump stay within the bounds of "relevant, material facts that are in evidence" of the case. Trump faces a permanent ban from running a business in New York state and $370 million in penalties in the case brought by state Attorney General Letitia James. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

The appeal submitted on Wednesday argues against the verdict along five key lines.

The document argues that Attorney General James lacked the authority to bring the case, noting that the case involves private commercial transactions rather than harm to the public. It also contends that Trump’s valuations reflected subjective estimates that lenders independently evaluated rather than fraudulent misrepresentations.

"The only supposed 'victims' here are a handful of ultrasophisticated banks and insurers that have never claimed to be injured, were eager to do business with President Trump and his family, and made over $100 million from these transactions," the appeal states.

The appeal further argues that the prosecution’s premise of overvaluation is based on the misguided idea that real estate has one objective value — and that deviations from that value must be fraud.

"Under that breathtakingly broad theory, NYAG can second-guess any business transaction in this State on almost any imagined grounds," the filing reads.

And on the penalties, the appeal argues that the $450 million disgorgement is excessive, unlawful and even unconstitutional.

Finally, the appeal argues that the politically charged nature of the case, on its own, should have been enough to halt its consideration.

"NYAG cannot point to a single Section 63(12) enforcement action against similarly situated developers (or any other type of defendant) based on practices comparable to those alleged here," the filing states.

TRUMP PICKS JAMES MCDONALD TO LEAD POWERFUL SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK AFTER JAY CLAYTON'S DEPARTURE

NEW YORK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 04: Former U.S. President Donald Trump appears in the courtroom for the third day of his civil fraud trial at New York State Supreme Court on October 04, 2023 in New York City. Former President Trump may be forced to sell off his properties after Justice Arthur Engoron canceled his business certificates and ruled that he committed fraud for years while building his real estate empire after being sued by Attorney General Letitia James, who is seeking $250 million in damages. The trial will determine how much he and his companies will be penalized for the fraud. (Mary Altafeer-Pool/Getty Images)

"Ms. James repeatedly called President Trump a 'criminal'; promised to 'investigate President Trump and his business transactions,' 'review ... Trump-related real estate transactions,' and 'take on ... his business in New York'; and threatened President Trump's 'family' and 'anyone in his orbit," the document states.

James' office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

Spain’s tomato food fight leaves thousands covered in pulp

Thousands of people pelt each other with tomatoes as Spain’s famous ‘La Tomatina’ festival gets underway. Thousands of participants join the hour-long food fight, using around 150,000kg of tomatoes in a tradition dating back to 1945.
